talks.title: JDD: In-depth Mining of Java Deserialization Gadget Chains
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for JDD: In-depth Mining of Java Deserialization Gadget Chains.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Dr. Leilei Jiang, Dr. Yuan Zhang, and Dr. Min Yang from Fudan University present JDD (Java Deserialization Detector), an automated framework for mining deserialization gadget chains in Java enterprise software. The research explores the mechanics of object injection vulnerabilities, which continue to dominate high-impact risks like remote code execution across major application servers. The authors detail the construction of polymorphic gadget chains, analyze the shortcomings of conventional class blacklisting defenses, and demonstrate automated chain synthesis.

Key Topics:
- Core principles of Java object serialization and deserialization across network protocols (HTTP, RMI, Hessian)
- Mechanics of object injection vulnerabilities and arbitrary remote code execution via readObject entry points
- The anatomy of polymorphic gadget chains: Entry points, intermediate transformation calls, and execution sinks
- Limitations of static class blacklists and white-listing in enterprise application servers like Oracle WebLogic

Technical Details:
The presenters review the mechanics of Java serialization, where object graphs are encoded into byte streams for state transfer across network sockets (e.g., via RMI or HTTP using protocols like Hessian) and reconstructed on the receiving end. A Java deserialization vulnerability (CWE-502) occurs when an application deserializes untrusted input, allowing an attacker to manipulate object types and fields. When the target invokes the standard readObject method, the JVM reconstructs the serialized objects, executing underlying methods that can be chained toward arbitrary remote code execution.

The authors break down gadget chains into three structural components: an injection object, intermediate polymorphic method invocations, and a security-sensitive sink. In their motivating proof-of-concept, an attacker crafts a serialized HashMap containing custom objects. When the server invokes readObject, the HashMap recursively reconstructs its entries, ultimately calling put and executing key.equals to compare keys. By exploiting Java polymorphism, the attacker substitutes a malicious class whose overridden equals method chains into downstream logic, ultimately reaching an execution sink such as Runtime.getRuntime().exec(cmd).

Historically, software maintainers defended enterprise frameworks like Oracle WebLogic against deserialization CVEs by deploying blacklists of known dangerous classes. However, the researchers demonstrate that blacklists provide ineffective protection because attackers can easily identify alternative polymorphic paths that bypass blocked classes while reaching the same underlying execution sinks. To overcome manual analysis bottlenecks, the authors developed JDD, a graph-based mining framework that models Java class hierarchies and method call paths to automatically discover previously unknown gadget chains across complex enterprise libraries.

Key Takeaways:
Relying on class-name blacklists to mitigate Java deserialization vulnerabilities is fundamentally flawed, as alternative polymorphic gadget chains can circumvent filters. Organizations must replace native Java deserialization with secure, data-only serialization formats such as JSON or Protocol Buffers wherever feasible. When object deserialization is mandatory, developers should implement strict ObjectInputFilter look-ahead whitelisting and isolate network endpoints handling untrusted serialized payloads.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Keynote: Cyber Threats in the Age of AI

talks.summary:
Overview:
At Black Hat Asia in Singapore, founder Jeff Moss provides opening remarks on geopolitical technological decoupling, followed by a keynote address from Edward Chen, Deputy Chief Executive of National Cyber Resilience at the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA). Chen demystifies prevailing narratives surrounding artificial intelligence in offensive cyber operations, arguing that despite the hype around AI-generated zero-days, adversaries consistently achieve compromise through foundational security failures. The address details Singapore's whole-of-nation defense strategy across the "RSA" threat landscape: Ransomware, Scams, and Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs).

Key Topics:
- Geopolitical bifurcation of global technology stacks and regional regulatory pressures
- Foundational cyber hygiene failures versus novel AI-driven exploitation narratives
- Forensic analysis of automated, containerized transnational job scam syndicates
- Disruption of a multi-tier, multi-architecture global Mirai APT botnet and national defense frameworks

Technical Details:
Chen challenges the cybersecurity industry's fixation on complex AI exploits, illustrating that even cutting-edge AI platforms are repeatedly compromised via rudimentary operational oversights. He cites white-hat researcher Gal Nagli, who discovered critical vulnerabilities in ChatGPT stemming from standard web caching misconfigurations, and subsequently uncovered severe administrative access risks in DeepSeek caused by unauthenticated, publicly exposed database ports. These cases demonstrate that while adversaries may adopt AI to optimize reconnaissance and social engineering, their primary weapons of choice remain unpatched vulnerabilities, misconfigured cloud ports, and weak credentials.

To illustrate modern threat actor tradecraft, Chen presents two CSA investigative case studies. In the first, CSA disrupted a transnational job-scam syndicate that targeted over 3,000 victims across 110 campaigns over two years. Forensics revealed an automated, highly resilient infrastructure: scammers managed remote operations through Telegram bots, programmatically provisioning new hosting domains and environments within minutes. The syndicate deployed workloads using Docker containers and executed automated bash scripts that backed up application databases to Telegram channels every two hours, ensuring near-instant operational recovery following infrastructure takedowns.

In the second case study, CSA participated in an international law enforcement operation disrupting a global APT botnet that infected hundreds of thousands of devices, including 2,700 endpoints in Singapore. The malware, an advanced Mirai variant, operated across a robust three-tier architecture separating command-and-control (C2), payload distribution, and automated exploitation. The malware was compiled for diverse CPU architectures—including PowerPC and SuperH (SH4)—targeting enterprise routers, embedded controllers, and IoT cameras. Remarkably, the author had even submitted a patent application for the malware's cross-platform orchestration framework. CSA and global partners successfully tracked and neutralized the botnet by fingerprinting anomalous TLS certificate naming schemes and unique C2 callback ports.

Key Takeaways:
Organizations must master foundational security hygiene—prompt patch management, port exposure audits, and multi-factor authentication—as threat actors overwhelmingly exploit basic oversights rather than sophisticated AI exploits. Combating agile transnational syndicates that leverage automated cloud deployments requires rapid, cross-border intelligence sharing and synchronized infrastructure takedowns. National cyber resilience requires a comprehensive, whole-of-nation strategy combining updated regulatory mandates, critical infrastructure protections, and subsidized security support for small and medium enterprises.

talks.title: Weaponized Deception: Lessons from Indonesia's Muslim Cyber Army
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Weaponized Deception: Lessons from Indonesia's Muslim Cyber Army.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In this presentation, Tim Pappa—a former FBI supervisory special agent and profiler with the Behavioral Analysis Unit (BAU)—examines the operations, social dynamics, and psychological dimensions of the Indonesian threat group Muslim Cyber Army (MCA). Drawing on his background researching Islamic boarding schools (*pesantren*) in Indonesia and investigating cyber terrorism for the CIA, DIA, and FBI, Pappa demonstrates how behavioral profiling can be integrated into cyber threat intelligence (CTI). Although widely covered in 2018 due to arrests and government characterization of its members as "traitors," MCA has since been largely dismissed by authorities as no longer a threat. Pappa re-evaluates the group to understand how online influence and deception functioned within its localized social and religious context.

## Group Profile and Operational Methods

Contrary to sensationalized reports depicting MCA as an advanced cyber threat, Pappa highlights key distinctions regarding the group’s true capabilities and operational focus:

* **Target Audience and Community Roots:** MCA targeted *pesantren* (Islamic boarding school) communities. Because MCA members grew up and lived inside these specific neighborhoods, they possessed an intimate understanding of local religious nuances, dynamic interpretations of Islam, and regional social attitudes. This insider status made their messaging far more potent than external foreign influence operations (e.g., Russian or Iranian influence campaigns targeting the U.S.).
* **Content and Themes:** The group's primary output consisted of creating, repurposing, and amplifying content centered on religious persecution (e.g., portraying *ulama* as being targeted) and anti-LGBTQ messaging. They utilized myth, folklore, and historical events fused with emotion to make disinformation appear indisputable and provoke political tensions and violence.
* **Debunking Cyber Attack Capabilities:** Media reports frequently alleged that MCA maintained a "sniping team" conducting computer network operations (CNO), sending viruses, and hacking or compromising accounts. Pappa’s research found no evidence of computer network attacks. Instead, their organized functions focused on coordinated reporting to get target accounts banned, alongside content generation and dissemination.
* **Organizational Dynamic:** By their own accounts, several key admins never met in person until after their arrests in 2018.

## Behavioral Profiling Case Study: Tara RC Wardhani

To demonstrate behavioral threat intelligence, Pappa models a BAU personality assessment on Tara RC Wardhani, one of MCA's leading social media admins:

* **Background Discrepancies:** Indonesian media described Wardhani as a reclusive, friendless, antisocial figure. Artifact analysis revealed she was a middle-aged divorced single mother of four in her 40s (now deceased). Her personal social media showed extensive ties to friends and family, school reunions, and deep involvement in her children’s lives.
* **Self-Image Analysis:** BAU assessments evaluate observable personality traits derived from tangible artifacts:
  * *Anguish & Emotion:* Evident in her demeanor at police press conferences upon facing charges as a traitor.
  * *Celebratory & Nostalgic:* Documented through posts celebrating her adult child's wedding and regular reunions with middle and high school friends.
  * *Devoted & Persistent:* Exemplified by her securing a university lecturer position at a state Islamic college after what she termed a 30-year journey, as well as joint business endeavors (selling yogurt) with her former husband despite marital and financial strain.
* **Idealized / Aspirational Self:** Profiling explores how targets wish to see themselves and be perceived, which provides an entry point for engagement:
  * *Responsible & Secure:* Projecting stability, cheerfulness, and family responsibility even as her personal life and finances were collapsing prior to arrest.
  * *Distinguishable & Romanticized:* Evidenced by interests outside the norm (such as attending a heavy metal press conference) and sharing quotes regarding soulmates and fate, suggesting she may have viewed her involvement with MCA as meaningful or "meant to be."
* **Self-Actualization:** Evaluates life obstacles to determine vulnerability to behavioral exploitation, such as major disruptive life transitions (e.g., relocating from Jakarta to Yogyakarta at age 15).

## Deception Framework and Threat Intelligence Takeaways

Pappa connects MCA's activities to military deception doctrine, noting that the group executed nearly every technique described in the Bell-Whaley deception framework. Rather than acting as conventional technical hackers, MCA operated as sophisticated practitioners of deception and narrative warfare. Incorporating behavioral profiling and deception models allows CTI analysts to understand actor motivations, trace social engineering methods, and assess the psychological factors driving online influence networks.

talks.title: The Black Hat Asia Network Operations Center (NOC) Report
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in The Black Hat Asia Network Operations Center (NOC) Report.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Leaders of the Black Hat Asia Network Operations Center (NOC)—including Jessica, Jonathan from Arista Networks, Jimmy from Palo Alto Networks, and Mark from Corelight—provide an operational breakdown of designing, deploying, and defending the conference network. Tasked with delivering high-performance connectivity while monitoring hostile traffic, the NOC team operates under a unique threat model where attendees actively execute exploits and malware. The speakers detail their multi-vendor hardware deployment, continuous packet capture pipeline, centralized threat hunting workflows, and collaborative incident response.

Key Topics:
- Black Hat NOC architectural deployment: Venue infrastructure integration, Arista zero-touch provisioning, and network tapping
- Palo Alto Networks Cortex XSIAM centralized security operations and Next-Generation Firewall inspection policies
- High-assurance perimeter protection and SSL/TLS decryption for registration databases versus training network allowances
- Corelight Open NDR sensor integration: Zeek/Suricata logging, machine learning detection, and live packet capture

Technical Details:
The NOC engineering team details the physical and logical architecture deployed to support Black Hat Asia. Arista Networks provisions the underlying wired and wireless infrastructure, deploying 48 wireless Access Points (APs) and 11 enterprise switches tied directly into the venue's physical backbone. Hardware provisioning utilizes Arista CloudVision (CV-CUE) zero-touch automation, allowing unconfigured devices to boot, authenticate, pull predefined configurations, and establish segmented VLANs across the venue. Arista switches replicate all inbound, outbound, and inter-segment traffic via hardware network taps, aggregating data feeds directly to downstream inspection engines.

Network inspection is governed by a strategic dual policy implemented by Palo Alto Networks Next-Generation Firewalls. In public training classes, briefings, and the Arsenal demo area, the firewalls deliberately permit exploit traffic and malware payloads to traverse the network unhindered so attendees can conduct practical security research. Conversely, strict defensive controls, full SSL/TLS decryption, and active blocking are enforced around the conference registration infrastructure, protecting personal attendee data and internal databases. Palo Alto Networks Cortex XSIAM acts as the central security operations platform, ingesting telemetry, alerts, and system logs across all deployment partners.

Corelight provides Open Network Detection and Response (NDR) sensors connected to the Arista tap aggregators. The sensors parse raw network packets into structured Zeek connection logs, execute Suricata signature-based intrusion detection rules, and run behavioral machine learning heuristics. In addition to real-time logging, Corelight retains full packet captures (PCAP) for deep forensic investigation. Telemetry is streamed directly into Cortex XSIAM and Cisco XDR, enabling multi-vendor threat hunters to differentiate between benign classroom exercises and genuine unauthorized intrusions—described by the team as finding "needles in needle stacks."

Key Takeaways:
Securing complex environments requires clear segmentation between high-value operational assets (like registration databases) and open research networks. Integrating hardware taps, open NDR sensors (Zeek/Suricata), and centralized analytics (XSIAM/XDR) provides comprehensive visibility across massive traffic volumes. Multi-vendor operational collaboration and deep packet inspection remain essential for rapidly distinguishing between simulated training exploits and active adversarial attacks.

The ambiguous nature of automotive security leads to narratives that are polar opposites: either we’re all going to die or our cars are perfectly safe. In this talk, we will show the reality of car hacking by demonstrating exactly how a remote attack works against an unaltered, factory vehicle. Starting with remote exploitation, we will show ho

talks.title: Unveiling New Attack Vectors in Bluetooth Vulnerability Discovery through Protocol State Machine
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Unveiling New Attack Vectors in Bluetooth Vulnerability Discovery through Protocol State Machine.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Presented by researchers from SRAD—including Lidong Li, Oliver Dong, Xiao Wang, and Lewei Qu—this talk explores a novel vulnerability discovery methodology targeting Bluetooth protocol state machines. Classic Bluetooth architectures rely on layered protocol stacks built above the Host Controller Interface (HCI) and L2CAP, supporting protocols and profiles such as RFCOMM, SDP, A2DP, AVRCP, and OBEX. Because Bluetooth operates wirelessly over the air, implementation flaws expose devices to remote attacks without physical contact. The speakers demonstrate that breaking and reconstructing protocol state transitions uncovers severe, hidden flaws that traditional fuzzing techniques consistently miss.

## Limitations of Traditional TLV Fuzzing

Historically, Bluetooth security testing heavily relied on Type-Length-Value (TLV) mutation fuzzing (e.g., repeating tags, extending string lengths, setting values to extremes). While effective for discovering historical vulnerabilities like BlueBorne (2017), BleedingTooth (2020), and BlueFrag, the speakers identify four key reasons why TLV mutation is no longer sufficient against modern targets:

1. **High Volume of Invalid Packets:** Random fuzzing generates useless, invalid data that wastes execution time and fails to trigger deep logic.
2. **Driver-Level Packet Validation:** Modern Bluetooth drivers validate incoming packet formats and drop malformed inputs before they reach vulnerable core logic.
3. **Lack of Targeted Test Cases:** Unfocused test cases fail to reach deep protocol corner cases.
4. **Poor State Machine and Interdependency Awareness:** Without modeling complex protocol interactions, fuzzers suffer from low state-coverage and miss critical execution paths.

Modern vulnerabilities increasingly stem from improper state transitions, packet fragmentation, and session desynchronization rather than simple malformed field values.

## State Machine Disruption Methodology

The proposed approach identifies critical interaction nodes—such as connection setups, handshakes, authentication, and request/response sequences—and intentionally violates expected state transitions:

- **Protocol & Driver Discrepancies:** Bluetooth specifications are broad, leading vendors to implement custom driver behaviors that vary significantly across operating systems (e.g., Linux vs. Android) and SoC chipsets.
- **Pairing-Free Exploitation:** Several sub-protocols process packets prior to pairing. By modifying BlueZ source code to bypass pairing checks, attackers can send state-disrupting packets directly to target devices.
- **State Stalling and Rapid Flooding:** Rather than following normal handshake progression, the attacker sends valid initial negotiation frames and then rapidly repeats specific requests, triggering race conditions, state desynchronization, or resource exhaustion.

## Real-World Case Studies and Empirical Findings

The researchers validated their state-machine disruption techniques across multiple protocols and commercial platforms:

- **L2CAP Configuration Flooding (Smartphone Crash):** During an L2CAP connection setup (using PSM and channel identifiers), the initiator negotiates parameters like MTU. By sending an initial `Configuration Request` and rapidly flooding repeated MTU configuration requests instead of progressing to data transfer, the remote smartphone suffered driver-level crashes, bringing down the entire operating system.
- **AVRCP Browsing Channel Flooding (Automotive IVI Crash):** AVRCP browsing runs over AVCTP and A2DP. The browsing channel verifies link activity and disconnects if idle. By flooding `GetPlayStatus` requests at a high frequency immediately before the session timeout threshold, the researchers overloaded the protocol stack and crashed the in-vehicle infotainment (IVI) central control unit of a running Volkswagen vehicle without physical contact or pairing.
- **RFCOMM Multiplexer Abuse (Tesla IVI Reset Loop):** RFCOMM operates over L2CAP using PSM `0x0003`. After establishing an SABM/UA handshake on control channel `DLCI = 0`, the researchers continuously flooded SABM frames to force the device to repeatedly re-enter link setup. When tested on a Tesla IVI system, this attack forced the Bluetooth module into an endless, continuous reset loop.
- **SDP Connection Race (iOS Bluetooth Crash):** SDP operates on fixed PSM `0x0001` without pairing. The researchers exploited the brief transitional delay before an SDP connection completely closes by rapidly reconnecting and issuing new service queries during that short window. This forced the target device into a timeout state and crashed the Bluetooth service on iOS.

talks.title: Inbox Invasion: Exploiting MIME Ambiguities to Evade Email Attachment Detectors
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Inbox Invasion: Exploiting MIME Ambiguities to Evade Email Attachment Detectors.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Security researchers present MINER, an automated vulnerability mining framework designed to uncover protocol-level evasion attacks against email attachment detectors. Rather than relying on traditional malware obfuscation or file packing, the authors exploit structural and parsing discrepancies between email security filters and client software. By manipulating the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) protocol specifications, the researchers demonstrate how malformed message structures allow high-severity payloads—including the WannaCry ransomware—to slip past major email inspection engines into recipient inboxes.

Key Topics:
- Protocol-level evasion: Exploiting parsing ambiguities between email security detectors and end-user email clients
- MIME structural complexities: Header manipulation, transfer encodings, nested multipart boundaries, and RFC parsing differentials
- Demonstration of detection bypass: Delivering the WannaCry ransomware undetected to Gmail and retrieving it via Mozilla Thunderbird
- MINER framework architecture: RFC-guided grammar tree sample generation, heuristic filtering, and automated bypass verification

Technical Details:
The researchers analyze how email security gateways and client applications handle message formats. While traditional attackers rely on file-level evasion (such as packing, crypters, and binary obfuscation) to evade antivirus engines, defensive scanners have steadily hardened their file analysis capabilities. The authors introduce an alternative approach: protocol-level evasion. By exploiting ambiguities in how different implementations parse the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) standard, an attacker can craft an email message that appears structurally benign or unparseable to an inspection engine, yet correctly decodes into a malicious attachment when rendered by the recipient's mail user agent (MUA).

The presentation demonstrates this attack by delivering the WannaCry ransomware to a Gmail inbox. Under standard transmission, Gmail's antivirus engine immediately blocks the executable attachment. However, by introducing minor structural ambiguities—such as appending an extra base64 encoding value directly after a quoted-printable header (Content-Transfer-Encoding)—Gmail's scanning engine fails to recognize the embedded payload and delivers the email. When the victim opens the message using an email client like Mozilla Thunderbird, the client successfully parses the attachment, allowing the malware to execute. The researchers show that similar parsing failures occur in Microsoft Outlook when nested multipart boundaries reuse parent boundary identifiers.

talks.title: KernelSnitch: Leaking Kernel Heap Pointers by Exploiting Software-Induced Side-Channel Leakage
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning KernelSnitch: Leaking Kernel Heap Pointers by Exploiting Software-Induced Side-Channel Leakage.
talks.summary:
## Overview

**KernelSnitch** is an operating system side-channel attack targeting hash table implementations in the Linux kernel. Presented by Lukas Maar and Jonas Juffinger (PhD candidates at Graz University of Technology), the attack exploits timing differences that arise when iterating over kernel hash bucket linked lists. 

By leveraging this software-induced timing discrepancy, untrusted user-space applications can leak critical kernel heap pointers—specifically demonstrating a leak of the kernel's `mm_struct` in under one minute. This marks the first kernel heap pointer leak achieved via an operating system side-channel.

---

## Core Primitives and Timing Leakage

Kernel hash tables consist of multiple linked-list buckets indexed by hashing a combination of user-controlled inputs and internal kernel addresses. KernelSnitch interacts with these structures via two main primitives:

- **Access Primitives:** System calls (e.g., `clock_gettime` using POSIX timers) that compute a hash using an ID and a kernel structure address (such as `signal_struct`), resolve the corresponding bucket, and iterate through its linked list. When queried with an invalid ID, the kernel traverses the entire bucket without finding a match, causing execution time to reflect the bucket's total occupancy level.
- **Append / Remove Primitives:** System calls (e.g., `timer_create`) that add or remove elements within the kernel hash buckets from user space, allowing an attacker to artificially alter bucket length.

Measuring the raw system call duration (taking timestamps before and after execution) reveals occupancy levels. In an initial baseline test measuring 1,500 iterations of 512 accesses and averaging the 8 fastest runs, the authors distinguished empty buckets from single-timer buckets at ~165 timestamp units, though false positives and false negatives remained.

---

## Leakage Amplification via Microarchitectural Eviction

To eliminate measurement errors and achieve reliable user-space exploitation without false positives or negatives, the researchers amplified the timing discrepancy using two techniques:

1. **Increasing Bucket Occupancy:** Expanding bucket length (e.g., testing 5 elements versus 0) widens the execution duration gap significantly compared to a single-element difference.
2. **Enforcing Cache Misses via Big Array Eviction:** Because kernel linked-list elements become cached across repeated system calls, traversals normally speed up. Before every system call invocation, the researchers flush the CPU cache by accessing a large memory array. 
   - This evicts cached linked-list structures, forcing memory latency on every list iteration.
   - The technique is hardware-agnostic and functions reliably across x86, ARM, and RISC-V architectures without requiring specific CPU cache-replacement policy details.

Repeating the evaluation (1,400 runs of 512 accesses, averaging the 8 fastest) confirmed that 0 versus 1 element became clearly distinguishable, while 0 versus 5 elements yielded a massive timing separation with virtually zero false positives or false negatives.

---

## Exploitation Methodology: Kernel Heap Pointer Leak

Traditional kernel exploits rely on triggering memory corruption vulnerabilities to obtain an initial read primitive (leaking code and heap addresses). However, putting the kernel into an undefined state risks stability issues and system crashes/reboots. KernelSnitch substitutes this step with an architecturally valid, crash-free side-channel read primitive.

The attack operates across two phases:

1. **Online Phase:** The attacker invokes the access primitive across various user-controlled identifiers while the kernel pairs them with the same target kernel address. Because the hashing function maps these to bucket indices, certain identifier combinations produce hash collisions. KernelSnitch detects these collisions via bucket timing measurements, constructing a unique "fingerprint" of collisions.
2. **Offline Phase:** Because the Linux kernel source and hash functions are known and the user inputs are controlled, the attacker executes a local brute-force search over candidate kernel heap addresses to find the specific address that reproduces the exact collision fingerprint observed in the online phase.

The researchers apply this attack against Linux `futex` (fast userspace mutex) hash tables to recover kernel virtual addresses.

talks.title: CDN Cannon: Exploiting CDN Back-to-Origin Strategies for Amplification Attacks
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for CDN Cannon: Exploiting CDN Back-to-Origin Strategies for Amplification Attacks.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Network security researchers present research on "CDN Cannon," detailing a class of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) amplification attacks termed BTO-Amp. The presentation exposes how attackers can abuse legitimate Content Delivery Network (CDN) back-to-origin optimization strategies to flood backend servers with massive traffic volumes. By manipulating image processing features, request transformation rules, and HTTP method conversions, the authors demonstrate how threat actors achieve high amplification factors against origin servers without needing traditional botnets.

Key Topics:
- The economics of DDoS: Bypassing CDN DDoS mitigation layers without deploying expensive botnet infrastructure
- Core mechanics of BTO-Amp: Exploiting back-to-origin optimization features to create extreme request/response traffic asymmetry
- Attack Vector 1: Abusing dynamic CDN image optimization and cropping (e.g., crop=1,1) to force full-resolution origin retrievals
- Attack Vector 2: Request modification abuse, injecting oversized HTTP headers, and URL rewriting to amplify origin bandwidth consumption

Technical Details:
The researchers explore the dual-edged nature of modern CDN architectures. While CDNs are engineered to absorb volumetric DDoS attacks and shield origin servers through global edge caching and load balancing, their internal performance optimization mechanisms can be weaponized. Traditional volumetric attacks require large, resource-intensive botnets that are costly to maintain and largely ineffective against CDN edge networks. In contrast, the authors propose BTO-Amp (Back-to-Origin Amplification), an attack methodology that turns the CDN itself into an amplification proxy against target backend servers.

The first attack vector targets CDN dynamic image optimization. CDNs frequently offer on-the-fly image conversion and cropping to optimize mobile delivery (e.g., stripping query strings and converting PNGs to WebP or resizing dimensions). However, CDN edge nodes often fail to enforce strict lower bounds on client-requested image parameters. An attacker submits an image optimization request specifying extreme cropping parameters, such as crop=1,1. The CDN edge node strips the query parameters, fetches the entire high-resolution original image (often several megabytes) from the victim's origin server, crops the image down to a single pixel, and returns the single-byte result to the attacker. By repeatedly issuing these lightweight requests, an attacker consumes massive origin bandwidth while expending negligible client network resources.

The second attack vector exploits CDN request modification and URL rewriting features. An attacker registers a free trial account with a CDN provider and configures the victim's domain as the origin backend. The attacker then configures custom CDN edge transformation rules to append massive, oversized HTTP headers (such as padded X-Forwarded-For headers) and rewrite requested URLs into excessively long string sequences. When the attacker transmits a barrage of minimal, small HTTP POST requests to the CDN edge, the CDN expands each request into an oversized HTTP payload before forwarding it to the origin, rapidly exhausting backend processing capacity and network bandwidth.

Key Takeaways:
CDN providers must enforce strict validation, minimum size thresholds, and rate limits on dynamic image manipulation parameters to prevent back-to-origin bandwidth asymmetry. Cloud edge services must restrict user-configured request rewriting, capping the volume and size of injected HTTP headers forwarded to origin servers. Origin server administrators should monitor back-to-origin traffic patterns and establish mutual authentication and rate limiting between CDN edge nodes and backend servers.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Behind Closed Doors
talks.teaser: Bypassing RFID Readers details Behind Closed Doors.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In the Black Hat presentation *"Behind Closed Doors: Bypassing RFID Readers,"* speaker Julius Dunuk (IT security specialist and physical red teamer at Securing) examines attack vectors against physical access control systems (PACS). The talk highlights that physical security cannot rely solely on the strength of RFID locks or card encryption. Attackers and red teamers evaluate the entire physical setup, frequently prioritizing the simplest entry method—such as physical bypasses or wireline sniffing—over challenging cryptographic attacks.

---

## Physical and Autonomous Lock Bypasses

Before assessing digital or RF mechanisms, red teamers exploit baseline physical weaknesses:

- **Under-Door Tools:** Using a flexible wire inserted beneath the door gap, an operator can hook and pull the interior door handle, completely avoiding the RFID reader.
- **Autonomous RFID Locks:** Typically found in lower-security environments (e.g., apartment buildings, staircases), autonomous locks combine card authentication, memory, and latch control directly inside the reader unit. These units present several attack surfaces:
  - **Default Administrative PINs:** Many keypad-equipped readers retain factory default codes that allow attackers to enter programming mode and register unauthorized cards.
  - **Firmware Logic Flaws:** Demonstrating on a Mifare Classic autonomous lock using a Proxmark running Iceman firmware, Dunuk showed that while setting a card ID to all zeros (`00 00 00 00`) failed, setting it to all `F`s (`FF FF FF FF`) opened the lock. Even when using the administrator delete card to erase the credential, the lock continued to open with the all-`F` ID, likely due to a software bug where deleted card memory defaults to `0xFFFFFFFF`.
  - **EMP Generators:** Handheld electromagnetic pulse (EMP) devices can induce electrical surges to reset hardware or trigger lock release. However, the speaker cautions against practical operational use because EMP tools are unreliable and can permanently fry lock circuits or adjacent electronics.
  - **Wire Manipulation / Fail-Safe Exploitation:** Removing the unit from the wall exposes the wiring. If an electronic lock operates in a fail-safe configuration, cutting the control loop breaks the circuit and unlocks the door.

---

## Centralized Systems and Wiegand Protocol Attacks

Enterprise environments typically employ centralized access control systems. In these setups, the wall reader only handles tag excitation, RF communication, and credential decryption before passing card data over physical wires to a separate backend controller (such as an access panel or a Raspberry Pi running custom controller software).

- **The Wiegand Vulnerability:** 
  - Readers communicate with downstream controllers using the legacy **Wiegand** protocol. 
  - Wiegand utilizes two data lines—typically green (Data 0) and white (Data 1)—which rest in a high voltage state and pulse low to transmit individual bits.
  - **Plaintext Transmission:** Even when high-security cards like **iCLASS SEOS** (with non-default Elite encryption keys) prevent RF cloning via Flipper or Proxmark, the reader decrypts the credential internally and transmits the raw card identifier across the Wiegand wires in cleartext without encryption.
- **Wiegand Sniffing Tools:**
  - Red teamers intercept this communication using hardware bridge sniffers such as the **ESPKey**, **BLEKey**, or **TheDec** (developed by Jakob Kash with contributions from Dunuk).
  - Physical installation involves removing the reader from the wall to tap the Data 0, Data 1, and ground lines.

---

## Physical Defense Mechanisms: Tamper Alarms

To mitigate physical tampering and inline wire sniffing, readers incorporate **tamper sensors**:

- **Operation:** Optical or physical tamper switches monitor the back of the reader. When the unit is removed from the mounting bracket or wall, the sensor triggers an alarm (such as an audible alert or a notification to the central monitoring panel).
- **Red Team Considerations:** In the live demonstration, unscrewing the reader immediately activated an audible tamper alarm. Bypassing physical detection requires disarming or muffling the alert mechanism (e.g., disconnecting or untangling specific alarm lines) before splicing into the Wiegand bus.

talks.title: (Mis)adventures with Copilot+: Attacking and Exploiting Windows NPU Drivers
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of (Mis)adventures with Copilot+: Attacking and Exploiting Windows NPU Drivers.
talks.summary:
Overview:
A security researcher presents an analysis of the Windows Neural Processing Unit (NPU) driver attack surface within the Microsoft Copilot+ PC ecosystem. The talk explores how modern on-device artificial intelligence workloads—driven by 40+ TOPS hardware accelerators from Qualcomm, Intel, and AMD—are integrated into Windows 11. By examining the Windows Driver Device Model (WDDM) and the Microsoft Compute Driver Model (MCDM), the speaker details low-level driver architectures, kernel-mode communication paths, and methodologies for hunting local privilege escalation vulnerabilities.

Key Topics:
- Architectural motivations for on-device AI in Copilot+ PCs: Privacy concerns (e.g., Microsoft Recall), cloud inference costs, and latency
- The Windows AI execution stack: Application layer, ONNX Runtime, DirectML (DirectX 12/COM), WebNN, and underlying display/compute drivers
- Kernel mode driver communication: GDI32.dll, win32k.sys, and dxgkrnl.sys interactions with vendor WDDM and MCDM drivers
- Reverse engineering MCDM interfaces: Enumerating compute-only adapters via D3DKMTEnumAdapters3 and D3DKMTQueryAdapterInfo

Technical Details:
The speaker explores the shift toward local client-side AI processing in Windows Copilot+ systems. Running large language and computer vision models in the cloud incurs massive GPU operating costs, network latency, and privacy liabilities—highlighted by controversies surrounding Microsoft Recall telemetry. To resolve these challenges, Copilot+ PCs mandate specialized Neural Processing Units (NPUs) capable of delivering over 40 trillion operations per second (TOPS). While GPUs operate as high-power "sprinters," NPUs serve as power-efficient "marathon runners," sustaining continuous workloads like camera background blur, live translation, and super-resolution without rapidly draining laptop batteries.

The presentation maps the Windows on-device AI software stack. At the user layer, applications interact with the cross-platform ONNX Runtime or the upcoming browser-based WebNN API. These components call into DirectML, a hardware-acceleration API built on DirectX 12 and COM interfaces. While user-mode driver DLLs (UMDs) share the calling process's address space and offer no security boundary, the kernel driver represents a critical local privilege escalation boundary. System calls originate from user applications via GDI32.dll, traverse the win32k.sys subsystem, and pass through dxgkrnl.sys (DirectX Graphics Kernel), which validates parameters before invoking the hardware vendor's underlying driver.

Hardware manufacturers implement NPU support using the Microsoft Compute Driver Model (MCDM), introduced in 2021 as a specialized subset of the Windows Display Driver Model (WDDM). MCDM defines 38 mandatory functions, 42 optional functions, and explicitly forbids 29 display-centric functions. To obtain a handle to an NPU device from an unprivileged user process, an auditor constructs a D3DKMT_ENUMADAPTERS3 structure, sets the IncludeComputeOnly flag to 1, and invokes the d3dkmtenumadapters3 system call. The process then queries device capabilities by executing D3DKMTQueryAdapterInfo with the driver description type. The speaker notes that vendor implementations frequently fail to adhere strictly to MCDM restrictions, leaving deprecated or forbidden WDDM dispatch routines active and exposing significant kernel vulnerability surfaces.

Key Takeaways:
The rapid introduction of NPUs into consumer operating systems introduces complex kernel attack surfaces via the Microsoft Compute Driver Model (MCDM). Security researchers should audit the interaction between dxgkrnl.sys and vendor MCDM kernel drivers, as improper input validation creates viable paths for local privilege escalation. Hardware vendors must strictly enforce MCDM specification limits, stripping unsupported or legacy WDDM dispatch routines from production NPU drivers.

Running large language and computer vision models in the cloud incurs massive GPU operating costs, network latency, and privacy liabilities—highlighted by controversies surrounding Microsoft Recall telemetry. To resolve these challenges, Copilot+ PCs mandate specialized Neural Processing Units (NPUs) capable of delivering over 40 trillion operations per second (TOPS). While GPUs operate as high-power "sprinters," NPUs serve as power-efficient "marathon runners," sustaining continuous workloads like camera background blur, live translation, and super-resolution without rapidly draining laptop batteries.

The presentation maps the Windows on-device AI software stack. At the user layer, applications interact with the cross-platform ONNX Runtime or the upcoming browser-based WebNN API. These components call into DirectML, a hardware-acceleration API built on DirectX 12 and COM interfaces. While user-mode driver DLLs (UMDs) share the calling process's address space and offer no security boundary, the kernel driver represents a critical local privilege escalation boundary. System calls originate from user applications via GDI32.dll, traverse the win32k.sys subsystem, and pass through dxgkrnl.sys (DirectX Graphics Kernel), which validates parameters before invoking the hardware vendor's underlying driver.

Hardware manufacturers implement NPU support using the Microsoft Compute Driver Model (MCDM), introduced in 2021 as a specialized subset of the Windows Display Driver Model (WDDM). MCDM defines 38 mandatory functions, 42 optional functions, and explicitly forbids 29 display-centric functions. To obtain a handle to an NPU device from an unprivileged user process, an auditor constructs a D3DKMT_ENUMADAPTERS3 structure, sets the IncludeComputeOnly flag to 1, and invokes the d3dkmtenumadapters3 system call. The process then queries device capabilities by executing D3DKMTQueryAdapterInfo with the driver description type. The speaker notes that vendor implementations frequently fail to adhere strictly to MCDM restrictions, leaving deprecated or forbidden WDDM dispatch routines active and exposing significant kernel vulnerability surfaces.

Key Takeaways:
The rapid introduction of NPUs into consumer operating systems introduces complex kernel attack surfaces via the Microsoft Compute Driver Model (MCDM). Security researchers should audit the interaction between dxgkrnl.sys and vendor MCDM kernel drivers, as improper input validation creates viable paths for local privilege escalation. Hardware vendors must strictly enforce MCDM specification limits, stripping unsupported or legacy WDDM dispatch routines from production NPU drivers.

talks.title: Invisible Ink: Privacy Risks of CSS in Browsers and Emails
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Invisible Ink: Privacy Risks of CSS in Browsers and Emails.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In their presentation *"Invisible Ink: Privacy Risks of CSS in Browsers and Emails,"* Leon Trampert (PhD student at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security focusing on browser security) and Daniel Weber (researcher focusing on CPU security and side-channel attacks) examine how Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) can be abused for user tracking and fingerprinting. 

Traditional tracking protections, such as blocking third-party cookies with ad blockers (e.g., uBlock Origin) or disabling JavaScript with plugins like NoScript and privacy-focused modes like Tor Browser's high security settings, aim to neutralize client-side fingerprinting scripts. However, HTML email clients and script-restricted browsers still parse CSS. The speakers demonstrate that advanced CSS features can bypass script blockers entirely to fingerprint environments, leak viewing contexts, and detect when emails are forwarded or inspected.

## Motivation & Browser Fingerprinting Concepts

Tracking entities (such as major web platforms and ad networks) seek persistent identification to link user sessions across visits and correlate behavior across multiple devices. 

* **Benign Use Cases**: Risk-based authentication (e.g., banking systems prompting Bob for a second factor when correct login credentials arrive alongside an unfamiliar device fingerprint; Google suspicious-activity login alerts).
* **Malicious & Advertising Use Cases**: Ad tracking tailored to user browsing history (e.g., serving gaming ads based on past activities) or cloaking malicious content (e.g., serving malware only to target victims while serving benign content to automated crawlers or law enforcement).
* **Traditional Meta-Information Limitations**: Relying solely on IP address, User-Agent, and language headers provides low entropy and can easily be spoofed. Shared public Wi-Fi networks also cause multiple independent users to share the exact same IP address.
* **JavaScript-Based Fingerprinting**: Advanced scripts combine multiple high-entropy vectors, including:
  * **Installed Fonts**: Detecting installed software by querying font availability (e.g., Microsoft Office installs proprietary fonts like *Gill Sans*, separating Bob from Alice, who only has defaults like *Arial*, *Comic Sans*, and *Pacifico*).
  * **Canvas Rendering**: Rendering text, emoticons, and absolutely positioned shapes to expose minor rendering differences across operating systems (e.g., font thickness and emoji rendering between macOS and Linux).

## CSS-Based Fingerprinting Primitives

When JavaScript is completely disabled or unavailable (such as in Tor Browser, NoScript, or HTML email clients), tracking can be achieved directly via CSS conditional rules (at-rules) paired with conditional resource fetching. When a rule matches, the browser fetches an external resource (e.g., `background-image: url(...)`), revealing the matching property to the server controller.

Key CSS mechanisms include:

* **Arithmetic Functions (`calc()`)**: Used to perform dynamic calculations on values such as screen dimensions (e.g., subtracting fixed pixel values from viewport widths).
* **`@media` Queries**:
  * Measure screen dimensions and viewport width accurately via repeated conditional steps (e.g., serving a specific image only when screen width exceeds 720 pixels).
  * Detect user preferences, such as system color scheme (dark mode vs. light mode).
  * Identify device interaction capabilities, such as whether a device supports hovering or is a touch screen.
* **`@supports` Queries**:
  * Query support for specific CSS properties to identify browser vendor and engine (e.g., detecting `-moz-` vendor properties exclusive to Firefox-based browsers).
  * Determine precise browser version numbers based on the chronological introduction of standard CSS features.
* **`@container` Queries**:
  * Serve as a primitive for fine-grained width measurements of specific container elements rather than the whole viewport.
  * Allow tracking entities to evaluate dynamic sizing behaviors (e.g., measuring rendered element widths crossing thresholds like 400 pixels), which can expose user language settings and text rendering traits without executing scripts.

## Practical Applications in Email Security

Because email clients render HTML and CSS while stripping JavaScript, CSS fingerprinting introduces distinct capabilities within email workflows:

* **Email Leak Detection**: Creating uniquely targeted emails for a specific recipient (e.g., Alice). If the email is accessed or forwarded to a third party (e.g., Charlie), differences in the client environment trigger distinct resource requests that notify the sender or recipient of the leak.
* **Phishing Evasion and Cloaking**: Formatting an email so that it renders as an authentic phishing lure to targeted victims (e.g., PowerPoint users) while rendering as completely benign content to security analysts or automated mail scanners attempting detection.

talks.title: KernJC: Automated Vulnerable Environment Generation for Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning KernJC: Automated Vulnerable Environment Generation for Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Researchers Boan and co-speaker present KernJC, an automated framework designed to generate accurate vulnerable environments for Linux kernel vulnerability reproduction. Reproducing disclosed kernel flaws is notoriously challenging due to erroneous vulnerability records in public databases and intricate kernel build configuration dependencies. The authors detail how KernJC leverages git patch presence analysis and graph-based Kconfig resolution to automatically compile functional vulnerable kernels, enabling reliable vulnerability verification and mitigation testing.

Key Topics:
- The role of Linux kernel vulnerabilities in container escapes, virtualization breakouts, and cloud privilege escalation
- Impediments to kernel vulnerability reproduction: Erroneous NVD version ranges and missing Kconfig build options
- Case study of CVE-2021-22555: Heap out-of-bounds corruption in Netfilter and backported patch pitfalls in kernel 5.11.22
- KernJC architecture: Patch-driven vulnerable commit identification and directed graph modeling of Kconfig dependency networks

Technical Details:
The presenters analyze the impact of kernel vulnerabilities within modern cloud computing architectures. Attackers compromising unprivileged applications in user space or containers leverage kernel vulnerabilities to break out of container sandboxes, escalate to root within virtual machines, and exploit hypervisors (such as KVM) to reach the physical host. However, assessing these threats requires reproducing disclosed vulnerabilities, which security teams find exceptionally difficult. The authors demonstrate that reproduction attempts frequently fail due to two primary obstacles: incorrect version metadata in public repositories like the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), and incomplete kernel build configuration options (Kconfig).

To demonstrate the versioning challenge, the authors examine CVE-2021-22555, a high-severity heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability within the Linux kernel's Netfilter subsystem enabling local privilege escalation to root. While NVD listed kernel version 5.11.22 as vulnerable, code audits revealed that the vendor had already integrated the patch into that specific release, rendering reproduction impossible. Furthermore, even on genuinely vulnerable source trees, triggering the bug requires specific compilation flags—such as CONFIG_NETFILTER_XTABLES and CONFIG_COMPAT. Proof-of-concept exploits often depend on subsystem features like Netfilter Netlink Queue (CONFIG_NETFILTER_NETLINK_QUEUE / NFQ), which involve complex parent-child Kconfig dependency trees that researchers rarely document in advisories.

To solve this, the researchers developed KernJC, which automates environment generation using two core techniques. First, KernJC performs patch presence analysis: it extracts the fix diff and traces commit histories to verify the presence of vulnerable code lines, ensuring the compiled kernel is genuinely vulnerable rather than prematurely patched. Second, KernJC models the entire Linux Kconfig system as a directed dependency graph where configuration flags represent nodes and conditional requirements represent edges. By analyzing public proof-of-concept keywords and trace requirements, KernJC traverses the graph to resolve and enable all necessary parent and dependent Kconfig options, successfully compiling an accessible, functional vulnerable kernel environment.

Key Takeaways:
Security researchers cannot rely solely on public NVD version ranges for vulnerability reproduction, as vendor backports frequently patch code ahead of reported release bounds. Triggering kernel vulnerabilities requires identifying deep Kconfig dependency chains that make specific code paths accessible. Automated frameworks like KernJC streamline vulnerability validation, patch verification, and exploit mitigation testing by systematically resolving source versions and compiler configuration graphs.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Determining Exploitability of Vulnerabilities with SBOM and VEX
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Determining Exploitability of Vulnerabilities with SBOM and VEX.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In this presentation, Splunk security software engineers Srinija Kammari and Anusha Penumacha outline their journey from decentralized vulnerability scanning to a centralized platform combining Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX). While open-source adoption accelerates software delivery, it introduces significant vulnerability management challenges. In 2022, Splunk relied on a shift-left model where individual product teams managed CI/CD pipeline scans and shared results with product security. However, this model made gathering product-wide vulnerability insights difficult. Driven in part by the federal executive order mandating SBOMs, Splunk shifted to an asset inventory and centralized scanning model to efficiently track dependencies, assess exploitability, and alleviate alert fatigue for developers.

## Centralized Asset Inventory & Scanning Architecture

To overcome data fragmentation, the team introduced internal tooling and centralized infrastructure:

- **CTS Portal & Asset Inventory:** An internal portal allowing developers to onboard and offboard code repositories and build artifacts. Teams provide scan parameters such as target branches, ticket assignees, and severity thresholds. This created a scalable asset inventory with product-level telemetry, though it required operational effort to maintain fresh metadata.
- **Centralized Scan Platform:** A central program fetches product data from the inventory, triggers scans across repositories, parses Software Composition Analysis (SCA) findings, assigns owners, and persists results in central storage. Supported scan types include SAST, open-source software (OSS), threat modeling, and credential management.
- **SBOM Generation & Security Central:** Centralized data enabled rapid generation of formatted SBOMs. It also powered "Security Central," an analytics dashboard providing metrics on ticket distribution by severity and scan type, three-month closure trends, product/employee filters, and organization-wide vulnerability rollups. It features single-CVE search (e.g., Log4j) to pinpoint all affected products across the company instantly.

## The Exploitability Challenge & VEX Integration

Despite successful centralization, automated scanning generated a flood of tickets. Internal analysis revealed that **over 26% (more than one-fourth)** of discovered vulnerabilities were either not exploitable or not actionable, causing severe developer friction amid an ever-growing annual CVE count.

To evaluate actual risk, the team evaluated three exploitability determination methods:
1. Public database lookups.
2. Reachability analysis (verifying if product execution paths reach vulnerable functions).
3. Direct developer feedback via **VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange)**.

VEX provides machine-readable status statements that complement and embed directly into SBOMs. Splunk adopted standard VEX statuses: *Not Affected*, *Affected*, *Fixed*, and *Under Investigation*. Generating VEX required capturing developer-validated remediation information and linking it back to the product inventory.

## Implementation via Issue Trackers & Key Takeaways

Rather than introducing a separate security tool or forcing developers to navigate disparate scanners, Splunk integrated VEX data collection directly into existing issue tracking systems:

- **Abstraction & Enforcement:** The issue tracker acts as an abstraction layer above the scanning tools. Requiring VEX metadata fields prior to ticket closure ensured complete data capture with minimal learning curve.
- **Standardized Templates & Audit Trails:** A standardized ticket template provided explicit exploitability determinations, component usage context, ownership records, and complete audit histories.
- **Automated VEX-Embedded SBOMs:** Captured remediation data is stored in a central database and correlated with the product inventory to generate VEX-embedded SBOMs automatically.
- **Context-Driven Remediation:** Aggregated historical remediation records enable Splunk to build package-level context from both external sources (e.g., auto-closing issues where no upstream fix exists) and internal institutional knowledge (generating dependency graphs, codifying patterns, and automating remediation decisions to shield developers from non-actionable alerts).

talks.title: The Illusion of Isolation: How Isolation Failures in CI/CD Servers Lead to RCE and Privacy Risks
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding The Illusion of Isolation: How Isolation Failures in CI/CD Servers Lead to RCE and Privacy Risks.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Security researchers investigate isolation failures in Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) systems, focusing on vulnerabilities that allow attackers to breach server-side infrastructure. While existing research heavily targets worker-level compromises (such as Poisoned Pipeline Execution), this presentation examines how Source Code Management (SCM) integrations expose the central CI/CD server itself. Analyzing Atlassian Bamboo as a primary case study, the researchers demonstrate how configuration-as-code features and symlink manipulation lead to arbitrary server-side file disclosure and remote code execution.

Key Topics:
- CI/CD architecture and isolation models: Server/controller responsibilities versus worker/agent/runner task execution
- Attack limitations of Poisoned Pipeline Execution (PPE) and dependency supply-chain attacks on worker nodes
- SCM integration as an unauthenticated server-side attack surface: Repository URLs, branch parameters, and server-side clones
- Vulnerability case study in Atlassian Bamboo: Exploiting "Bamboo Specs" and Git symlink parsing to achieve arbitrary server file reads

Technical Details:
The presentation analyzes the architectural division within modern CI/CD systems, which rely on a central server (or controller) coordinating with distributed workers (agents or runners). While workers execute build pipelines inside containers, virtual machines, or pods, the central server manages source code integrations, stores build logs, orchestrates jobs, and holds enterprise credentials. Most common CI/CD attack paths—including Poisoned Pipeline Execution (PPE), where malicious code is injected into repository pipeline configurations, and dependency chain abuse—only grant initial access to the isolated worker environment. Attackers seeking high-impact server control still face container escapes and lateral movement hurdles.

The researchers shift focus toward attacking the central server directly through Source Code Management (SCM) integrations. SCM connections present an overlooked attack surface: repository URLs, branch names, and repository contents are user-controllable, while the server must actively interact with these inputs using local git clients or parsing engines. To illustrate the risk, the authors analyze Atlassian Bamboo, a CI server that utilizes "plans" to orchestrate builds. Bamboo features a configuration-as-code mechanism called "Bamboo Specs," which allows developers to define build plans using YAML or Java files stored directly inside a repository directory named bamboo-specs.

To process Bamboo Specs, the Bamboo server automatically clones the remote git repository to its local server filesystem under a temporary checkout directory. This architectural design completely lacks file-system-level isolation between the untrusted repository contents and the host server operating system. When scanning the repository, Bamboo reads bamboo.yaml using a read-file method and parses the content with SnakeYAML. The researchers exploit this by committing a symbolic link named bamboo.yaml pointing directly to /etc/passwd (abusing Git's core.symlinks default setting). When the Bamboo server clones the repository and reads the YAML file, it traverses the symlink and ingests /etc/passwd. While SnakeYAML throws a parsing exception due to invalid syntax, the resulting error output or server execution trace discloses sensitive system file contents, creating an exploit primitive that can be chained into full server compromise.

Key Takeaways:
CI/CD architectures must strictly enforce file-system and process isolation between central management servers and untrusted source code repositories. Management servers should never clone or parse user-supplied repository files directly on host controllers; instead, all repository parsing and build plan generation must execute inside disposable, sandboxed worker containers. SCM integration pipelines must disable Git symlink processing (e.g., setting core.symlinks to false) and sanitize all user-controllable repository parameters to prevent server-side traversal and execution attacks.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Bridging the Gap: Type Confusion and Boundary Vulnerabilities Between WebAssembly and JavaScript
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Bridging the Gap: Type Confusion and Boundary Vulnerabilities Between WebAssembly and JavaScript.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Security researchers Neng (Sakura) and Jian Han-Sa from Tsinghua University and Seraph Tech investigate the emerging attack surface at the boundary between WebAssembly (Wasm) and JavaScript within Google Chrome's V8 engine. Highlighting new Wasm specifications—specifically Garbage Collection (WasmGC) and JavaScript Promise Integration (JSPI)—the authors analyze the complex wrapper architecture mediating cross-language interaction. Through an enhanced grammar-based fuzzer incorporating type, scope, and context analysis, the researchers uncover severe vulnerabilities spanning type confusion in prototype traversal and inline caching, use-after-free bugs in garbage collection, and wrapper mismatches in asynchronous promise boundaries.

Key Topics:
- Wasm-JavaScript interaction architecture: JS2WASM, WASM2JS, and JS2JS wrapper mechanisms
- Type-aware and context-guided fuzzing strategies targeting the WasmGC and JSPI boundaries
- Type confusion in V8 prototype chain iteration (has_only_simple_elements) and StoreIC inline caches
- Use-after-free in JIT-optimized Wasm internal function code references and JSPI wrapper mismatches

Technical Details:
The integration between WebAssembly and JavaScript in V8 relies on bridging wrappers: JS2WASM converts JavaScript arguments to Wasm types, WASM2JS adapts Wasm outputs to JavaScript objects, and JS2JS mediates re-exported calls. The introduction of WasmGC allows Wasm to handle structured objects, arrays, and garbage-collected references. To find cross-language boundary defects, the researchers enhanced their grammar-based JavaScript fuzzer with type, scope, and context analysis, deliberately mutating JavaScript prototype chains and function invocations by substituting WasmGC objects into traditional JavaScript object locations.

This strategy revealed a critical type confusion vulnerability in prototype chain traversal. When an attacker assigns a WasmGC object to the __proto__ property of a JavaScript Array, V8 invokes has_only_simple_elements during element iteration. The engine checked whether an object was a JSProxy; if not, it assumed the object was a standard JSObject and forcefully cast it. Because WasmGC objects feature completely distinct memory layouts, this cast triggered memory corruption. A related type confusion occurred in V8's JIT compiler during fast instanceof optimization (TryBuildFastInstanceOf / BuildHasInPrototypeChain), where the compiler directly cast prototype objects as JSObject, failing when encountering Wasm structs.

The authors also discovered type confusion within V8's Store Inline Cache (StoreIC). Because Wasm objects are opaque, setting properties on them should throw an error. However, StoreIC invoked UpdateCache before Object::SetProperty, recording the Wasm object map despite the error. By alternately setting properties on JavaScript arrays and Wasm arrays, the IC transitioned into a polymorphic state where the fast store handler for JS arrays was mistakenly applied to Wasm arrays. In the Wasm array layout, the third 4-byte word represents array length, whereas in a JS array it points to elements backing store. The mismatched handler wrote an element pointer into the Wasm array's length field, expanding it to an enormous value and providing a trivial out-of-bounds read/write primitive for full RCE. Furthermore, the authors uncovered a use-after-free bug where JIT-optimized WasmInternalFunction code pointers were not tracked as strong references during garbage collection, alongside wrapper mismatch flaws when circular JS-to-Wasm-to-JS exports intersected with JSPI promise wrappers.

Key Takeaways:
Complex cross-language boundaries between WebAssembly and JavaScript introduce subtle type-confusion risks when engine optimization paths assume uniform object hierarchies. JIT compilers and runtime helpers must explicitly validate that prototype objects and inline cache targets are authentic JavaScript objects rather than merely verifying they are not proxies. Fuzzing harnesses should incorporate semantic type and scope tracking to systematically swap WasmGC structures into JavaScript APIs. Additionally, memory management must treat JIT-compiled cross-language wrappers as strong roots during garbage collection to prevent use-after-free vulnerabilities.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: The Oversights Under the Flow: Discovering the Vulnerable Tooling Suites From Azure MLOps
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning The Oversights Under the Flow: Discovering the Vulnerable Tooling Suites From Azure MLOps.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In this presentation, Peng Zhou from Shanghai University explores security oversights within tooling suites supporting Azure Machine Learning Operations (MLOps). While traditional DevOps spans planning, coding, testing, release, deployment, and customer feedback monitoring, MLOps introduces an integrated machine learning lifecycle covering model training, testing, evaluation, and synthesis. Microsoft supports this ecosystem through the Azure Machine Learning workspace, client-side/cloud SDKs, and tooling suites used across on-premises environments and cloud AI workspaces.

The research focuses on six specific tooling suites within the Azure stack where developer oversights introduced vulnerabilities: Prompt Flow, traditional Azure client tools, Azure DevOps tools, Azure AI Generative (part of the Azure SDK ecosystem), DeepSpeed (used in model training), and TorchGeo. 

---

## Developer Oversights & Flawed Assumptions

The speaker notes that these vulnerabilities stem from simple, recurring coding oversights rather than complex architectural flaws. Contributing factors include:
- **Diverse Community Contributions:** Although maintained by Microsoft personnel, repositories accept contributions from the broader open-source and machine learning communities, where developers prioritize software performance and ML functionality over secure coding practices.
- **Inconsistent Application of Existing Secure Patterns:** Secure coding practices—such as using safe path joins, validating types, or avoiding shell execution—were already implemented in parts of the codebases, but contributors repeatedly overlooked applying them across all components.
- **Flawed Patching and Coordination:** When vulnerabilities were disclosed to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC), subsequent patches applied by maintainers were sometimes incomplete or overlooked underlying root causes.

---

## Key Vulnerabilities and Techniques

The presentation highlights concrete technical examples primarily centered on **Prompt Flow**, an MLOps tool used in VS Code and Azure Machine Learning Studio for building LLM applications via execution graphs:

1. **Command / Code Injection via Shell Execution:**
   - **Flaw:** Code joined a list of arguments back into a string and executed it with `shell=True`. 
   - **Contrast with Secure Code:** Elsewhere in the codebase, developers correctly passed parameter lists without `shell=True` and strongly typed parameters (e.g., casting port parameters to integers).
   - **Impact Path:** The vulnerable execution path traced through the `start_experiment` function and the Prompt Flow client (`pf`). While execution directly via the CLI client required local access for privilege escalation, developers incorporating `start_experiment` into Azure applications exposed to REST APIs or LLM inputs (e.g., Azure OpenAI) effectively converted it into a remote code injection vulnerability.

2. **Path Traversal via String Concatenation:**
   - **Flaw:** Image data writing routines constructed target file paths using manual string concatenation (`directory + filename + extension`) rather than safe path-joining functions (such as `safe_join`). Developers assumed the filename was a safe hash object and sanitized the directory, but neglected to validate the extension.
   - **Impact Path:** This vulnerability was exposed to Prompt Flow backend API endpoints. In a proof-of-concept demonstration, an attacker sent an HTTP request to write a malicious dynamic-link library (`.dll`) directly into the victim's `System32` directory.

---

## Local vs. Remote Exposure Dynamics

A central discussion in the talk involves whether tooling vulnerabilities are strictly "local" or practically "remote":
- **Default Configurations:** Maintainers originally classified Prompt Flow issues as local because backend services defaulted to listening on `localhost` (`127.0.0.1`).
- **Real-World Configurations:** Due to feature requests on GitHub, maintainers enabled binding to `0.0.0.0`, allowing instances to listen on public/remote interfaces across network environments.
- **Pipeline Exposure:** Exposing functions like `start_experiment` to external inputs, web APIs, or LLM-generated prompts transforms local tooling flaws into remote attack vectors across software supply chains.

talks.title: ObfusQate: Where Quantum Magic Meets Code Security - Say Goodbye to Easy Cracking!
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in ObfusQate: Where Quantum Magic Meets Code Security - Say Goodbye to Easy Cracking!.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Associate Professor Vivek from SIT and Michael introduce ObfusQate, an intellectual property protection and code obfuscation framework designed specifically for quantum algorithms. As the computing ecosystem advances beyond classical computing milestones toward commercial quantum advantage, quantum software will encapsulate valuable proprietary trade secrets. The speakers analyze the architectural layers of modern quantum computing stacks and explain how ObfusQate operates at the algorithmic layer to protect quantum circuits from reverse engineering and cracking.

Key Topics:
- The transition from classical supercomputing to quantum computing ("beyond classical")
- Architectural abstraction layers of quantum computing systems
- The quantum algorithm development pipeline using frameworks like Qiskit and PennyLane
- ObfusQate's role in obfuscating and protecting quantum circuit intellectual property

Technical Details:
The presentation benchmarks the performance frontier between high-performance classical supercomputers and emerging quantum systems. The top supercomputer, El Capitan, achieves 1.742 exaflops, while advanced AI clusters like the Nvidia DGX GB300 deliver 35 exaflops. However, solving specific complex benchmark problems that would require quadrillions of years on classical supercomputers can be accomplished in seconds on quantum platforms, such as Google's Quantum Willow in five seconds. Industry projections from Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Continuum suggest practical quantum systems addressing quantum simulation, materials science, optimization, and cryptographic factoring (such as Shor's algorithm targeting RSA) will emerge within years to two decades.

The authors decompose the quantum computing stack into distinct operational tiers: physical hardware comprising the Quantum Processing Unit (QPU) at the base, followed by quantum error correction and readout controls, logical qubits, and logical quantum processor management. Sitting atop this hierarchy is the Quantum Algorithms layer. Using modern middleware frameworks like IBM Qiskit and PennyLane, developers can formulate classical problems into hybrid quantum-classical algorithms (such as Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms, or QAOA) deployed across QPUs from vendors like IBM, Google, Rigetti, and SpinQ.

Because quantum code is compiled into open intermediate circuit representations and gate schedules, deployed quantum algorithms are completely transparent to reverse engineering and intellectual property theft. ObfusQate directly addresses this vulnerability at the quantum algorithms tier. The framework applies mathematical transformations and circuit rewriting rules to the high-level quantum instructions, masking proprietary algorithmic logic and state preparation routines without degrading quantum computational fidelity or altering execution results on target QPUs.

Key Takeaways:
Security architects and quantum software developers must begin engineering intellectual property protection into quantum circuits as applications transition from academic theory into commercial deployment. Relying on the novelty of quantum hardware is insufficient to protect proprietary algorithms from decompilation and structural reverse engineering. Frameworks like ObfusQate demonstrate that software obfuscation must be adapted to quantum circuit gate operations to safeguard quantum software assets.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)
