talks.title: See Like a Bat: Using Echo-Analysis to Detect Man-in-the-Middle Attacks in LANs
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning See Like a Bat: Using Echo-Analysis to Detect Man-in-the-Middle Attacks in LANs.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Yisroel Mirsky from Ben-Gurion University presents Vesper, an active defense tool that uses acoustic echolocation principles to detect Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks within Local Area Networks (LANs). Mirsky explains how traditional LAN defenses struggle because attackers can tamper with network protocols such as ARP, DNS, ICMP, or STP without leaving reliable forensic traces. By transmitting virtual acoustic probe signals and analyzing the physical channel's impulse response, Vesper identifies when an attacker has inserted themselves into the communication path between hosts.

Key Topics:
- LAN Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack vectors (ARP, DNS, ICMP, DHCP spoofing)
- Channel impulse response and network physical layer profiling
- Maximum Length Sequences (MLS) and nanosecond-precision probing
- Vesper architecture, feature extraction, and deployment models

Technical Details:
Traditional network intrusion detection systems rely on inspecting packet payloads, monitoring MAC-to-IP bindings (e.g., dynamic ARP inspection), or checking routing tables. However, skilled attackers can forge ARP replies, poison DNS caches, abuse ICMP redirects, manipulate Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), or insert physical hardware taps without violating high-level protocol rules. Vesper approaches the problem from a physics-inspired perspective, analogizing network packet round-trips to bat echolocation. In any physical LAN, the transmission path between two endpoints (switches, transceivers, network cards, cables) establishes a unique channel impulse response characterized by propagation delay, hardware processing latency, and micro-jitter.

When an attacker establishes a MitM position, they inevitably alter this physical transmission channel by introducing an intermediate network interface, OS packet processing queues, and routing overhead. Vesper transmits low-overhead probe packets containing pseudo-random sequences, specifically Maximum Length Sequences (MLS). By correlating the transmitted sequence with the received echo, Vesper computes the channel's impulse response with nanosecond timing precision. The system extracts three distinct statistical features from each probe echo: one tracking temporal delay, one measuring channel distortion, and one detecting sequence manipulation. This multi-feature analysis prevents adversarial bypasses such as sequence replay or selective packet relaying.

The authors evaluated Vesper across hundreds of diverse network devices and operating systems, as well as a testbed of 48 identical Raspberry Pi devices. For mixed device environments, Vesper detected MitM spoofing attacks almost instantaneously; for the identical Raspberry Pis, it successfully fingerprinted and differentiated 75% of them after five minutes of continuous probing. The prototype is implemented in Python with a Cython/C++ wrapper for raw socket generation and nanosecond timing. Deployment options include running on individual LAN endpoints to monitor subnet hosts, or running directly on network routers and public Wi-Fi gateways to secure outbound traffic against interception.

Key Takeaways:
Network defenders can detect local MitM attacks without relying on signature inspection or protocol-specific heuristics by monitoring channel impulse response changes. Vesper provides an effective, protocol-agnostic defense capable of exposing ARP poisoning, DNS spoofing, and rogue inline hardware. High-precision timing coupled with multi-feature averaging mitigates transient network noise and CPU load variations, making echo-analysis viable for enterprise LAN and gateway monitoring.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Worm Charming: Harvesting Malware Lures for Fun and Profit.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In the presentation *"Worm Charming: Harvesting Malware Lures for Fun and Profit,"* Pedram Amini (from InQuest) discusses the methodology of collecting and sifting through vast amounts of daily malware uploads to isolate high-value, interesting attack lures and potential zero-day exploits. Drawing an analogy to the East Texas sport of "worm charming"—in which competitors vibrate or thump the ground to drive worms to the surface—Amini demonstrates how defenders can use targeted filtering rules and syntactic anomalies to coax stealthy or experimental malware lures out of massive data streams.

## Attack Lures and Collection Sources

Amini notes that while writing chained software exploits is costly and time-intensive, attackers frequently achieve initial compromise by attacking endpoints and end users via malicious document attachments (e.g., Office documents, PDFs, Java, Flash) or drive-by downloads. Notable threat vectors include:
- **Encapsulated/Matryoshka Lures:** Layering payloads inside documents (such as Flash embedded in documents delivered via email) to evade sandbox detonation while requiring user interaction.
- **Abuse of Features:** Exploiting Microsoft Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) for command execution, or relying on uninformed user consent (e.g., enabling malicious macros).
- **Metadata Payloads:** Embedding base64-encoded executables directly inside file metadata that macros pivot to and launch.

Researchers can harvest samples from sources such as open sandboxes (Hybrid Analysis, Any.Run), enterprise email spools, attacker infrastructure tracking (monitoring domain registrations, reverse DNS, shared SSL certificate IDs, Google Analytics tracking IDs, and Shodan/Censys searches), or VirusTotal Intelligence (VTI).

## Sifting the Corpus: Filtering Rules & Metrics

Addressing the daily volume on VirusTotal—approximately 1.2 to 1.3 million uploads per day (around 1 million distinct, ~409,000 newly seen, and ~400,000 malicious)—Amini highlights the challenge of manual analysis across the roughly 470,000 daily documents and lures (e.g., 400,000 PDFs, 40,000 Office docs, 15,000 Java files).

To reduce this dataset to a manageable volume, defenders deploy specialized YARA hunting rules against incoming feeds:
- **Macro-bearing Documents:** Matches documents with macros regardless of classification (~1,000 samples/day).
- **ActiveX or AV Detections:** Identifies Office documents embedding ActiveX or having at least one positive antivirus detection (~500 samples/day).
- **Active Content in PDFs, RTFs, and Java:** Captures Java files of interest (~500/day), RTFs (~20–50/day), PDFs containing JavaScript/active content, and documents embedding Flash.

Applying these heuristics narrows the daily intake from over 1.2 million samples down to roughly 2,500 lures per day (less than 1% of the original volume).

## Surface Vibrations: Exploiting Parser Tolerance and Evasion Anomaly

To isolate high-fidelity targets within the filtered subset, defenders search for structural anomalies that indicate manual file crafting or deliberate evasion:
- **Parser Robustness vs. Strict Signatures:** Attackers exploit the leniency of Microsoft parsers. For example, standard RTF files begin with `{\rtf1`, but the Microsoft parser will successfully open files beginning simply with `{\rt`. Security tools relying on strict MIME typing or full-header magic signatures fail to recognize these as RTF, allowing them to slip past standard detections.
- **Anomalous Features as Detection Signals:** When malware authors modify headers (comparable to concepts from the "Tiny PE" project) or deploy unconventional obfuscation to evade static checks, they inadvertently create distinct signatures. These structural deviations stand out against benign software, providing defenders with high-signal indicators to catch experimental malware campaigns and early zero-days before full production rollout.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning I'm Unique, Just Like You: Human Side-Channels and Their Implications for Security and Privacy.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Ian Coldwater, Lead Platform Security Engineer at Heroku, and Duffy Cooley, Staff Cloud Native Architect at VMware, present a technical deconstruction of Kubernetes core architecture and the vulnerabilities inherent in out-of-the-box configurations. Demonstrating live attacks against clusters deployed via kubeadm and kind (Kubernetes in Docker), the speakers debunk the assumption that Kubernetes is secure by default. The presentation dissects internal control plane communications, component-level attack surfaces, and privilege escalation techniques targeting the API server, etcd, and worker node kubelets.

Key Topics:
- Architectural security assumptions: dissecting the lack of secure defaults in standard Kubernetes deployments
- Cluster component topology: the operational roles of the API server, etcd, controller-manager, scheduler, and kubelet
- High-value attack surfaces: reading and writing cluster state and credentials directly within etcd
- Exploiting the kubelet API, container runtime interactions, and escalating privileges across worker nodes

Technical Details:
The presentation explores the core internal architecture of Kubernetes, illustrating how container orchestration components interact across the control plane and worker nodes. A standard deployment encompasses five fundamental services: etcd (the backing distributed key-value datastore storing complete cluster state, manifests, and secrets), kube-apiserver (the central administrative gateway handling authentication, authorization, and manifest admission), kube-scheduler (responsible for assigning pod workloads to nodes), kube-controller-manager (executing core lifecycle reconciliation control loops), and the kubelet (the node-level agent executing on each worker to manage container runtimes such as Docker). The speakers emphasize that while tools like kubeadm implement baseline security controls, raw cluster configurations frequently leave internal ports exposed without mandatory mutual TLS or authentication.

The speakers highlight etcd as an exceptionally high-value target for adversaries. Because etcd maintains complete cluster state—including configuration maps, persistent volume configurations, and sensitive service account tokens and secrets—unauthorized read access allows an attacker to exfiltrate critical cluster credentials. More critically, because Kubernetes is a loosely coupled, declarative distributed system where etcd is the authoritative source of truth, write access to etcd allows an attacker to manipulate cluster state directly. By injecting or altering records within etcd, an attacker bypasses the API server's admission controllers and authorization checks entirely, causing the controller-manager to deploy malicious containers or alter security policies automatically.

On the worker nodes, the kubelet represents a vital execution target. Kubelet operates an independent HTTP API to receive workload instructions from the API server and supervise container engines. If the kubelet API is left accessible without strict client certificate authentication or webhook authorization, attackers on the local node or adjacent network can execute arbitrary commands inside running containers, dump container logs, and inspect local pod volumes. Furthermore, gaining control over the kubelet or its credentials enables attackers to forge node authorizations, assign unauthorized roles, alter RBAC bindings, and leverage service account tokens to compromise the central API server, achieving complete control over the entire container cluster.

Key Takeaways:
Organizations must never assume that Kubernetes clusters or containerized workloads are secure by default upon deployment. Administrators must isolate and restrict network access to etcd using strong mutual TLS authentication and strictly enforce encryption at rest for stored secrets. Cluster operators must harden worker nodes by disabling anonymous authentication on kubelet APIs, enforcing least-privilege Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), and regularly auditing cluster configurations against established security benchmarks.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Arm IDA and Cross Check: Reversing the Boeing 787's Core Network
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Arm IDA and Cross Check: Reversing the Boeing 787's Core Network.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In this presentation, researcher Ruben Santamarta analyzes the core network architecture of the Boeing 787, focusing on the boundary mechanisms designed to isolate critical flight avionics from passenger and external systems. While aircraft communications historically relied on physical isolation, modern network-centric airframes share interconnects regulated by security boundaries. Santamarta examines the primary intermediary device responsible for this segregation: the Core Network Cabinet (CNC). 

The research was initiated after discovering an exposed, public Boeing server in September 2018 containing documentation, a virtual machine used by Boeing engineers to VPN into their network, and production-grade ("black level") firmware for both the Boeing 787 Core Network Cabinet and parts of the Boeing 737. Lacking direct physical access to an aircraft, the research methodology combined binary reverse engineering, technical documentation analysis, multimedia materials, and key US patents.

## Boeing 787 Network Architecture and Segregation

The Boeing 787's internal architecture links multiple distinct network domains:
* **Common Data Network (CDN):** The high-integrity avionics network hosting safety-critical functions via the Common Core System (CCS). Built on ARINC 664 (avionics Ethernet), it relies on General Processing Modules (GPMs) running a type-1 bare-metal hypervisor (VxWorks 653) with partitioned applications, alongside Remote Data Concentrators (RDCs) bridging CAN bus and legacy sensor buses.
* **Isolated Data Network (IDN):** Connects secure devices not directly critical to flight safety, such as the flight data recorder (black box) and electronic flight bags.
* **Open Data Network (ODN):** Connects non-critical, potentially hostile systems, including passenger In-Flight Entertainment (IFE).

The **Core Network Cabinet (CNC)** serves as the gateway between the outside world / non-critical networks and the internal avionics. Inside the CNC, the **Crew Information System (CIS)** manages communication between these three domains using key hardware modules:
1. **Ethernet Gateway Module (EGM):** An embedded Linux device implementing boundary firewalls and packet routing via `iptables`.
2. **CIS/MS File Server Module:** A commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) board powered by a Pentium M CPU running an uncertified version of VxWorks 6.2. It supports user-mode real-time processes (RTPs) and kernel-mode operations, utilizing custom packet filtering (`F_only_U_believe`).
3. **Network Interface Module (NIM):** The end system connecting directly to ARINC 664 and the CDN, configured by proprietary Level A certified binary rules.

## Attack Path and Vulnerability Findings

The primary attack scenario attempts to breach safety boundaries starting from an untrusted domain (ODN) and pivoting step-by-step into the critical avionics network (CDN):
* **Attack Flow:** `ODN (e.g., IFE)` $\rightarrow$ `EGM Firewall Rule Abuse` $\rightarrow$ `CIS Network Service Exploitation` $\rightarrow$ `IDN Switch` $\rightarrow$ `NIM Filtering Rules` $\rightarrow$ `CDN Switch / Avionics`.

Reverse engineering the uncertified VxWorks 6.2 environment revealed significant security debt across the CIS firmware (14 real-time processes and 15 shared libraries, including a custom-compiled `libc`):
* **Vulnerability Landscape:** Hundreds of calls to insecure standard C functions (`sprintf`, `strcpy`, `strcat`), leading to potential integer overflows, out-of-bounds reads/writes, buffer overflows, and memory corruption.
* **EGM Firewall Bypass & Remote Code Execution (RCE):** The EGM configuration (`S24_EGM_config`) explicitly permitted traffic from the IFE router on the ODN (`.40.2`) to the CIS via the `FTS_manager` service on port `16005`.
* **TFTP Opcode Exploitation:** The `FTS_manager` service, which handles TFTP-based transfers, reads an incoming packet up to 200 bytes. It indexes an opcode byte directly into an array to locate strings for log generation into a 400-byte buffer. While the 200-byte input payload itself cannot directly overflow the 400-byte buffer, Santamarta demonstrated that an out-of-bounds opcode index allows referencing arbitrary strings located across adjacent `.data` and `.bss` sections, supplying a long enough target string to overflow the stack buffer and achieve remote code execution in user mode.

## Research Takeaways

* **Architectural Boundaries vs. Physical Isolation:** Despite historical industry claims of physical isolation, modern avionics rely heavily on logical segregation implemented across intermediate gateway devices and COTS hardware.
* **Avionics vs. COTS Gateway Rigor:** While the core avionics (CDN) adhere to rigorous DO-178C Level A assurance standards and certified RTOS hypervisors (VxWorks 653), the boundary gateway modules (such as the CIS file server) ran uncertified software stacks lacking basic modern exploit mitigations.
* **Pivoting Feasibility:** Misconfigured firewall rules combined with memory corruption bugs in non-safety-certified gateway firmware create theoretical pathways for an attacker situated in the passenger domain (ODN) to bridge into core aircraft networks.

talks.title: Hacking Your Non-Compete
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Hacking Your Non-Compete.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Brian Dykstra, CEO of Atlantic Data Forensics and former DoD counterintelligence investigator, and Gregory Stone, intellectual property partner at Whiteford, Taylor & Preston, present the intersection of digital forensics, intellectual property law, and employee non-compete agreements. Examining the cybersecurity industry's high mobility workforce, the speakers evaluate how departing personnel and hiring employers can navigate restrictive covenants without triggering trade secret litigation. The presentation dissects real-world legal disputes involving forensic artifacts, bring-your-own-device (BYOD) complications, and the legal standards governing non-compete enforceability.

Key Topics:
- The legal mechanics and enforceability criteria of non-compete agreements: geographic and temporal reasonableness
- Digital forensics discovery in trade secret litigation: analyzing commingled data on personal BYOD laptops
- Legal distinctions between proprietary information, confidential business data, and protected trade secrets
- Defensive strategies and operational checklists for tech employees and hiring firms to avoid intellectual property disputes

Technical Details:
The speakers examine the operational dynamics of non-compete agreements through a case study involving a cybersecurity sales representative transitioning between competing endpoint security vendors. Company A attempted to enforce a generic non-compete agreement downloaded from the internet that barred the former employee from working for any cybersecurity company selling endpoint solutions anywhere in the market. The speakers explain that to be legally enforceable, non-compete covenants must be strictly reasonable in temporal duration, geographic scope, and the specific definition of prohibited competitive activities. Courts routinely strike down overly broad agreements that operate as blanket prohibitions on an individual's right to earn a livelihood. Furthermore, legal enforceability varies significantly across state jurisdictions, ranging from employee-favorable states like California (which generally bans non-competes) to states like Maryland that enforce reasonable contractual restrictions.

The case study illustrates the forensic complications introduced by lax corporate IT policies and Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) practices. Company A failed to issue corporate hardware, requiring the employee to conduct business on a personally owned laptop. When Company A initiated litigation alleging data theft, the legal discovery process subjected the employee's personal device to comprehensive forensic imaging and analysis. The speakers emphasize that while an employer retains proprietary ownership over company data residing on an employee's machine, the commingling of personal and corporate records does not grant the employer ownership of the hardware or personal files. However, during adversarial litigation, forensic examination exposes all personal communications, financial records, and private data to opposing counsel.

To prevent trade secret misappropriation claims, hiring firms must establish rigorous onboarding protocols. In the case study, Company B insulated itself by issuing a clean corporate laptop, strictly prohibiting the new hire from importing files, contacts, or client databases from Company A, and formally restricting the employee from soliciting former clients. The speakers warn that taking customer lists, pricing sheets, or proprietary source code constitutes civil misappropriation and potential criminal theft under federal trade secret statutes. Employees must negotiate precise non-compete definitions prior to signing, secure explicit definitions of confidential boundaries, and ensure all former employer data is formally returned or purged prior to accepting a new role.

Key Takeaways:
Employers must replace generic, internet-downloaded non-compete forms with customized, jurisdiction-specific agreements that define reasonable scopes of duration, geography, and competitive activity. Organizations must establish strict BYOD data-handling policies and issue dedicated corporate hardware to prevent the commingling of corporate trade secrets with personal employee data. Departing employees and hiring firms must implement clean-slate transitions, ensuring no proprietary documents, client databases, or confidential files are retained or transferred between employers.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Preloading Insecurity In Your Electron.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Luca examines the architecture and security implications of the Electron desktop application framework, focusing on how developers bridge the gap between web technologies and desktop environments. The talk evaluates core framework mechanics, contrasting the security models of Electron with traditional web browsers like Chromium. The presentation specifically investigates the security boundaries established by preload scripts and the critical role of context isolation.

Key Topics:
- Electron architecture and packaging: Chromium, Node.js, and .asar archives
- Process model: Main process, renderer processes, and render creation methods
- Preload script execution and DOM augmentation mechanisms
- contextIsolation security controls and Node.js API exposure

Technical Details:
Electron applications bundle Chromium, Node.js, core framework libraries, application code, and third-party NPM dependencies into uncompressed .asar archive files. During execution, the framework inspects package.json to launch the main process, which subsequently creates renderer processes to display HTML, JavaScript, and CSS web content. Renderers can be instantiated through BrowserWindow, BrowserView (which serves as the modern replacement for the legacy <webview> tag), or <webview>. Before web content finishes bootstrapping and rendering, Electron allows developers to execute a preload script to customize the execution environment.

Preload scripts have access to Node.js APIs by default and are frequently employed to augment the DOM by injecting custom properties or overriding built-in methods, such as window.open, on the global window object. However, security risks emerge when renderer scripts can access or tamper with these privileged functions. To address this, Electron provides the contextIsolation configuration flag. When contextIsolation is disabled (historically the default configuration), the preload script and renderer context share the exact same global window object, exposing internal structures and Node.js primitives to potentially untrusted content. When enabled, contextIsolation executes the preload script and renderer code in mutually isolated JavaScript execution contexts, preventing renderer scripts from accessing preload internals or modifying augmented functions.

The speaker highlights fundamental differences between the security posture of standard web browsers and Electron applications. While web browsers are hardened to safely navigate arbitrary untrusted web content from the internet, Electron is designed for purpose-built desktop applications that integrate deeply with operating system features. Using testing tools like Electron Fiddle to demonstrate configuration behaviors across versions, the talk emphasizes that building general-purpose web browsers in Electron is strongly discouraged due to the inherent exposure of native system APIs.

Key Takeaways:
Developers building desktop applications with Electron must enable contextIsolation and disable nodeIntegration across all renderer instances to establish hard security boundaries between web code and underlying Node.js capabilities. Preload scripts must never expose raw Node.js modules or unvalidated native execution primitives directly onto the renderer's window object. Security teams must audit .asar packages and evaluate whether applications load untrusted remote web resources into privileged renderer contexts.

talks.title: Transparency in the Software Supply Chain: Making SBOM a Reality
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Transparency in the Software Supply Chain: Making SBOM a Reality.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Dr. Allan Friedman, representing the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) at the U.S. Department of Commerce, delivers a briefing at Black Hat on operationalizing Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs). Friedman examines the acute transparency deficit across modern software ecosystems, where embedded devices, critical infrastructure, and enterprise applications incorporate vast webs of unmanaged third-party dependencies. The talk outlines the NTIA multi-stakeholder consensus model, standardized machine-readable formats, and practical approaches for navigating vulnerability prioritization and procurement governance.

Key Topics:
- Software supply chain opacity, left-pad dependencies, and widespread embedded risks
- Economic market failures and the NTIA open multi-stakeholder model
- Core SBOM technical framing, standardized formats (SPDX, CycloneDX, SWID), and data fields
- Resolving the gap between vulnerability presence and exploitability (VEX frameworks)

Technical Details:
Friedman contextualizes modern software supply chain risk by contrasting software development with traditional heavy industry. While capital equipment such as industrial diesel generators has included comprehensive bills of materials for over eight decades, network-connected software products regularly conceal deeply nested dependencies. Critical vulnerabilities, such as the Urgent/11 flaws in the ubiquitous VxWorks real-time operating system or historical vulnerabilities like Heartbleed in OpenSSL, expose how systemic blind spots prevent organizations from determining whether their environments are compromised. The software ecosystem's opacity creates distinct operational burdens across three key roles: software producers (tracking license compliance, code bloat, and shipping vulnerabilities), software buyers (evaluating procurement risk and end-of-life components), and software operators (managing rapid incident response).

Because producers lacked commercial incentives to voluntarily disclose component details and buyers historically failed to demand them, a classic market failure emerged. Operating without direct regulatory authority or enforcement budgets, the NTIA established an open, multi-stakeholder initiative convening software vendors, security researchers, healthcare networks, and international partners from the UK, Netherlands, and Japan. The initiative established four technical working groups: Framing (defining minimum required data fields including supplier name, component name, version string, unique cryptographic hash, and dependency relationships), Use Cases, Formats, and Healthcare Proof-of-Concept.

The technical working group aligned industry consensus around three established, machine-readable data formats: SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange), CycloneDX, and SWID (Software Identification) tags. A major operational challenge tackled by the framework is distinguishing raw vulnerability presence from actual exploitability. For example, while OpenSSL contains hundreds of exposed functions, only a minute subset was vulnerable to Heartbleed. This insight spurred the development of Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX) mechanisms, enabling vendors to cryptographically signal whether a flagged downstream CVE is truly reachable and exploitable within their compiled binary context.

Key Takeaways:
SBOM transparency provides the essential baseline data required to automate software asset inventories, manage open-source licensing liabilities, and accelerate enterprise incident response. Organizations should mandate standardized machine-readable SBOM formats (SPDX or CycloneDX) in procurement contracts rather than accepting static documentation like PDFs. Integrating VEX advisories alongside SBOM ingestion prevents operational fatigue by allowing security teams to filter out unreachable vulnerabilities and prioritize actively exploitable components.

talks.title: Attacking Electric Motors for Fun and Profit
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Attacking Electric Motors for Fun and Profit.
talks.summary:
Overview:
This presentation introduces a comprehensive threat model for attacking electric motors deployed across robotics, drones, and SCADA industrial systems. The speaker contrasts traditional safety controls—which manage accidental physical failures—with security controls focused on mitigating intentional adversarial manipulation. Using a commercial drone delivery fleet as a case study, the talk explores how exploiting motor drive electronics can induce kinetic damage, catastrophic overheating, and hardware destruction.

Key Topics:
- Threat modeling motion systems: Industrial SCADA, autonomous drones, and robotics
- Safety controls versus security risks in moving electro-mechanical systems
- Pulse Width Modulation (PWM), duty cycle manipulation, and motor electrical physics
- Motor operational limits: Stall torque, no-load conditions, and unauthenticated control paths

Technical Details:
The presentation frames its threat model around a hypothetical worldwide package delivery fleet operating over 30 proprietary drone models managed by hundreds of operators. The analyzed systems rely on dual communications channels (4G LTE over the Internet and 2.4 GHz line-of-sight wireless), onboard sensor arrays (GPS, accelerometers, inertial measurement units), and a central Linux-based controller communicating with Electronic Speed Controllers (ESCs). In motion systems, safety frameworks governed by bodies such as the FAA rely on training and deterministic failsafes for unexpected physical events, but fail to account for deliberate cyber sabotage.

At the physical and electronic layer, all electric motors connect to drives—such as ESCs, Variable Speed Drives (VSDs), or Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs)—that supply electrical power. Motor speed and torque are modulated via Pulse Width Modulation (PWM), which toggles voltage at specific clock frequencies. The proportion of time voltage remains active during each switching cycle defines the duty cycle, which is governed through hardware and software routines. Electrical current flowing through motor windings interacts with permanent magnets to create an electromagnetic field between the stationary stator and moving rotor, converting electrical input into mechanical power.

Analyzing motor datasheets (such as brushed DC motors) reveals critical operating extremes: "stall torque," where torque is maximized while rotational speed is zero, and "no-load" conditions, where speed is maximized at zero torque. The speaker demonstrates that prolonged operation under stall torque conditions forces high continuous current draw through internal windings, rapidly overheating the motor, burning out electrical components, and causing physical fires. Crucially, digital control signals regulating PWM duty cycles across ESCs and motor drives lack cryptographic authentication. An attacker gaining access to the flight controller or drive interface can manipulate duty cycles and clock timings, weaponizing normal control loops to induce physical stall conditions or in-flight mechanical failure.

Key Takeaways:
Control links driving Electronic Speed Controllers and motor drives require cryptographic authentication and command integrity checks to prevent unauthorized manipulation of PWM parameters. System architects must implement hardware-level thermal cutoffs and current-limiting safeguards that operate independently of software controllers to prevent catastrophic burnouts caused by forced stall torque states. Threat models for autonomous and robotic vehicles must treat physical actuator dynamics and electrical drive buses as critical attack surfaces.

talks.title: SSO Wars: The Token Menace
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding SSO Wars: The Token Menace.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Alex Emeril and Alvaro Muñoz present an in-depth security analysis of delegated authentication and Single Sign-On (SSO) token processing within the Microsoft .NET Framework. The researchers investigate how Service Providers parse and validate cryptographic tokens, identifying severe design flaws in .NET token handling libraries. Their talk demonstrates two critical vulnerabilities: an arbitrary constructor invocation flaw via unvalidated cryptographic algorithm resolution and a complete SAML signature bypass arising from "key confusion."

Key Topics:
- Delegated authentication architecture: Identity Providers (IdP), Service Providers (SP), and signed tokens
- Arbitrary constructor injection via CryptoConfig.CreateFromName in .NET
- Target exploitation on Microsoft SharePoint and Microsoft Exchange Server
- SAML XML signature bypass via asymmetric ResolveSecurityKey and ResolveSecurityToken evaluation

Technical Details:
In delegated authentication architectures, a Service Provider offloads user verification to an Identity Provider, which issues signed tokens (such as SAML, JWT, or Simple Web Tokens). The researchers focused their vulnerability research on the Service Provider's token intake and verification pipeline, targeting flaws that execute prior to or directly subvert cryptographic signature validation.

The first vulnerability involves cryptographic token parsing in the .NET Framework. To instantiate objects representing cryptographic algorithms, libraries routinely invoke CryptoConfig.CreateFromName. However, the researchers discovered that CreateFromName failed to restrict type names, allowing callers to execute any public, parameterless constructor of any class accessible in the application context. This unvalidated reflection entry point can be reached before signature verification via untrusted token headers, such as the alg attribute in System.IdentityModel.Tokens.Jwt or the Algorithm attribute within SAML SignatureMethod elements. When tested against Microsoft SharePoint, this primitive allowed unauthenticated attackers to fingerprint installed software components, determine exact versions, and trigger denial-of-service exceptions; against Microsoft Exchange Server, authenticated users could instantiate arbitrary constructors across local DLLs.

The second vulnerability exploits architectural asymmetry during SAML XML signature verification in Windows Communication Foundation (WCF) and SamlAssertion handlers. XML signatures contain a KeyInfo element that specifies the key or key reference required for verification. The .NET implementation queries KeyInfo twice: first calling ResolveSecurityKey to obtain the cryptographic key for mathematical signature validation, and subsequently calling ResolveSecurityToken to establish the identity of the signing party. However, ResolveSecurityKey traverses candidate keys using a depth-first search (iterating through all keys in KeyInfo first), whereas ResolveSecurityToken iterates through available resolvers first. By crafting a malformed KeyInfo element containing competing key definitions, an attacker creates a "key confusion" state where the server verifies the mathematical signature using an attacker-supplied key while simultaneously validating the token's origin as the legitimate Identity Provider, completely bypassing SAML authentication.

Key Takeaways:
Developers using .NET cryptographic frameworks must ensure type resolution routines enforce strict whitelists of permitted algorithm identifiers rather than accepting arbitrary class names from unauthenticated token headers. Security teams must ensure SAML and XML signature libraries use atomic, consistent key resolution pathways that bind cryptographic validation directly to identity verification. Systems processing federated identity tokens must be patched to prevent key confusion attacks that allow complete signature circumvention.

talks.title: Attacking and Defending the Microsoft Cloud (Office 365 & Azure AD)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Attacking and Defending the Microsoft Cloud (Office 365 & Azure AD).
talks.summary:
## Overview

Presented at Black Hat by Sean Metcalf (Founder of Trimark Security) and Mark Morowczynski (Principal Program Manager, Microsoft Identity Division), this session examines attack surfaces and defense strategies when integrating on-premises Active Directory with Office 365 and Azure Active Directory (Azure AD). Using a hypothetical enterprise scenario—Acme, an organization with 500,000 employees across 140 countries migrating to Office 365 and deploying Azure MFA—the speakers demonstrate how cloud adoption often stalls over niche edge cases while leaving critical hybrid identity components exposed to reconnaissance and exploitation.

## External Reconnaissance via DNS and Federation Discovery

An attacker begins by profiling an organization without generating internal network noise:
- **MX Records:** Scanning mail exchanger records (evaluated across Fortune 1000 targets) exposes email filtering vendors (e.g., Proofpoint, Cisco, Office 365), allowing adversaries to tailor phishing payloads against matching defenses.
- **DNS TXT Records:** Third-party domain/site verification records frequently linger indefinitely in public DNS, revealing adoption of SaaS platforms such as Atlassian, Cisco, Citrix, Dropbox, and WebEx. Attackers exploit these insights to craft targeted lures (e.g., urgent WebEx updates) or identify vulnerable associated platforms (such as misconfigured Atlassian JIRA instances).
- **Federation Fingerprinting:** Attackers enumerate standard host prefixes (`FS`, `SSO`, `STS`) to locate Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) endpoints and determine how authentication flows are structured.

## Compromising Hybrid Identity Infrastructure

The talk details high-impact techniques targeting hybrid identity mechanisms:
- **AD FS Token Forgery ("Golden SAML"):** Stealing the token-signing certificate from an AD FS server enables an attacker to forge SAML tokens and access any federated cloud service (e.g., Salesforce, Workday) under arbitrary user identities. Tools like `ADFSpoof` (developed by Doug Bienstock and Austin) automate extracting certificate data and generating forged tokens.
- **Malicious AD FS Adapters:** Third-party MFA integrations (such as Duo Security) utilize custom DLL adapters in AD FS. Attackers can decompile and alter the adapter's code to intercept authentication flows and execute arbitrary commands (such as malicious PowerShell scripts) whenever users log in.
- **Azure AD Connect Exploitation:** Express installations of Azure AD Connect configure password hash synchronization (syncing a hash of the hash). The process creates an `MSOL` service account and populates installation host details directly into the account's description field.
- **Privilege Escalation via AD ACLs:** Tools like PowerView (`Invoke-ACLScanner`, `Find-GPOComputerAdmin`) can locate `MSOL` accounts with directory replication permissions (`DS-Replication-Get-Changes` and `DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All`—the same permissions used in Mimikatz DCSync attacks). Attackers can then audit GPO delegations (such as finding delegated modify rights assigned to lower-tier server admin groups) to compromise the Azure AD Connect host, manipulate local administrative groups, and pivot to domain-level access.

## Defense and Operational Takeaways

- **Treat Hybrid Identity as Tier 0:** Systems like AD FS and Azure AD Connect hold administrative power equivalent to domain controllers. Compromise of an Azure AD Connect server or its delegating GPOs leads directly to total domain compromise.
- **Secure and Rotate Certificates:** Protect AD FS token-signing certificates rigorously, restricting local administrative access to federation hosts.
- **Centralize Identity Telemetry:** Ingest and correlate logs from on-premises Active Directory, AD FS, and Azure AD into a centralized SIEM to detect suspicious token requests and administrative anomalies.
- **DNS Hygiene:** Routinely clean up domain verification TXT records after SaaS onboarding is complete to prevent external recon of the enterprise tech stack.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Biometric Authentication Under Threat: Liveness Detection Hacking.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Researchers from Tencent Security Keen Lab present technical methodologies for circumventing biometric authentication systems deployed across mobile devices and financial services. The presentation examines how contemporary biometric pipelines perform liveness and attention detection to prevent identity spoofing. The authors detail a hardware-level signal injection framework that directly inputs synthetic video and audio feeds into device sensor buses, bypassing optical and acoustic defense mechanisms.

Key Topics:
- Biometric verification pipeline: Sensor collection, pre-processing, liveness detection, and feature matching
- Optical, textural, and interactive liveness checks versus 3D physical spoofing
- Limitations of presentation attacks: Color space loss, focus blur, and acoustic reverberation
- Hardware-level video (HDMI to MIPI CSI) and audio signal injection architectures

Technical Details:
Biometric authentication systems on modern smartphones and real-name identification apps process user verification through sequential stages: sensor data collection, digital pre-processing, liveness detection, and final biometric feature matching against stored templates. Liveness detection mechanisms verify that the biometric subject is a living person physically present before the sensor. Common defenses include human skin texture analysis, optical flow tracking, material frequency response, hardware infrared depth mapping, and interactive challenges requiring the user to blink, open their mouth, nod, or shake their head. Additional layers include attention detection, which verifies whether the user is actively gazing directly at the front-facing camera.

Prior research on bypassing facial recognition relied primarily on physical presentation attacks, such as displaying photos, replaying video recordings, or constructing complex 3D facial masks. However, these methods suffer from severe physical degradation: camera re-recording causes color space loss (in RGB and HSV spectrums), display moiré patterns, focus blur, and unnatural optical flow, while audio replays introduce room reverberation and inconsistent background acoustic noise. Furthermore, 3D facial molds are expensive and exceptionally difficult to reproduce reliably.

To eliminate optical and acoustic degradation, the researchers developed a transparent, hardware-level signal injection platform. Instead of presenting artifacts to external sensors, the attack intercepts the device's internal sensor buses. For video injection, an attacker PC generates synthetic video frames and routes the digital output through a hardware converter that transforms HDMI signals into native MIPI CSI (Camera Serial Interface) signals, connecting directly into the smartphone's camera connector socket. For audio verification, the PC routes synthesized voice responses directly into the microphone hardware pins. By monitoring interactive screen prompts over a secondary debug line, the attacker executes software on the PC to animate a single 2D static portrait in real time—generating head turns, nods, and blinks—and streams uncompressed native sensor data directly into the mobile processor with zero latency, completely bypassing liveness and attention checks.

Key Takeaways:
Biometric security architectures cannot rely exclusively on optical and acoustic software checks if the underlying sensor hardware buses remain unauthenticated and physically accessible. Device manufacturers must establish end-to-end cryptographic mutual authentication and encrypted data transport between camera/microphone sensor modules and the system application processor. Multi-factor verification combining biometric input with hardware-backed cryptographic tokens should be mandated for high-value financial and real-name authentication transactions.

talks.title: Battle of Windows Service: A Silver Bullet to Discover File Privilege Escalation Bugs Automatically
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Battle of Windows Service: A Silver Bullet to Discover File Privilege Escalation Bugs Automatically.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In this talk, Wenxu Wu from Tencent Security Xuanwu Lab presents research focused on discovering Windows logical privilege escalation vulnerabilities, specifically file privilege escalation bugs. Logical flaws occur when a restricted user interacts with a privileged system service via mechanisms like ALPC (Advanced Local Procedure Call) or COM, prompting the service to perform sensitive file operations (such as granting access, altering ownership, or creating/deleting/writing files) under a `SYSTEM` token. Traditional fuzzers target memory corruption rather than logical design issues, while manual reverse engineering of hundreds of ALPC interfaces and thousands of functions is resource-intensive. Wu introduces an automated approach using UI interactions and filesystem link manipulation to discover these flaws without relying on extensive manual reverse engineering.

---

## Historical Case Studies and Core Vulnerability Patterns

Wu examines historical vulnerabilities and common developer mistakes regarding token impersonation and file handling:

- **Task Scheduler DACL Modification**: A vulnerability reported in the Task Scheduler service allowed a restricted user to gain full control of arbitrary files. The service accepted an SDDL string parameter, canonicalized the path, converted the SDDL into a security descriptor, and reverted to a `SYSTEM` token before applying a new DACL via `AddRemovePrincipalAce`. Exploitation required creating a hard link to the target file and triggering the routine.
- **Installer Service TOCTOU**: In the Windows Installer service, file-copying routines introduced a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race condition. The service temporarily impersonated the current user to verify read permissions, reverted to `SYSTEM`, and then copied the target file into a readable Windows Installer directory. Attackers could exploit this window using opportunistic locks (OpLocks via `DeviceIoControl`) to reliably win the race condition, or brute-force the timing window using `ReadDirectoryChangesW`.
- **Assistant Service ALPC Metadata Read**: A semi-automated analysis of ALPC functions documented or gathered via spiders from MSDN revealed a vulnerability in the Assistant service. The service called `CreateFileW` under user impersonation to check read access, reverted to `SYSTEM`, and then read metadata from the file—repeating the improper impersonation pattern.

---

## The "Silver Bullet": Automated Discovery Framework via UI Interactions

Recognizing that manual reverse engineering of ALPC interfaces yields diminishing returns, Wu designed an automated testing framework based on triggering system operations via user interface interactions (such as opening Windows Store applications or interacting with system context menus):

1. **Triggering Execution**: The framework launches system applications and Windows Store applications from system and user directories, automating UI actions (e.g., button clicks).
2. **Monitoring Operations**: It hooks into or monitors system activity (using Process Monitor) to detect sensitive file actions, specifically `SetSecurity` calls that alter a target's DACL.
3. **Link Substitution**: The framework replaces target configuration and data paths with symbolic links (softlinks) or hard links pointing to restricted target files.
4. **Validation and Logging**: It evaluates whether the target file's DACL was modified under `SYSTEM` privileges, logging successful privilege escalations across multiple automated virtual machines.

---

## Vulnerabilities Discovered via the Framework

Using this automated framework, Wu identified several previously unknown vulnerabilities:

- **AppX / FX Development Services**: Launching default Windows applications (such as Windows Camera or Xbox Live) touched application settings files under the user's directory. By deleting the settings file and replacing it with a hard link pointing to a protected target file, launching the app triggered `SetSecurity` through internal object interfaces, granting the user full control over the target file.
- **Standard Collector Service**: Triggered via menu button clicks, this service created a file and subsequently set a DACL on a file sharing the same base name without an extension. The service operated directly under `SYSTEM` privileges without impersonating the caller, exposing a race condition exploitable via hard links.
- **Windows Defender Service**: When an unprivileged user initiates a scan on files across the system (including files in other user or system directories), Windows Defender invokes a system service to manage infected items. The service attempts to delete detected files via `SetFileDisposition`; if deletion fails, it applies a DACL to restrict access. By creating a text file detected as malicious and substituting it with a softlink before deletion occurred, the service altered the DACL on the link's target, borrowing `SYSTEM` privileges to modify permissions on arbitrary files.

talks.title: ClickOnce and You're in - When Appref-ms Abuse is Operating as Intended
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding ClickOnce and You're in - When Appref-ms Abuse is Operating as Intended.
talks.summary:
Overview:
William Burke, Red Team Lead at CISA and adjunct graduate professor at Marymount University, presents research on abusing Microsoft ClickOnce technology for initial access and payload delivery. The talk details how security advancements in Windows Defender, antivirus engines, and email gateways have diminished the efficacy of traditional phishing vectors like macro-enabled Office documents and blocked OLE formats. The author demonstrates how legitimate ClickOnce .appref-ms deployment files can be weaponized to achieve reliable code execution on fully patched Windows 7 and Windows 10 systems.

Key Topics:
- Evolution of phishing attack surfaces and defenses against legacy OLE file formats
- ClickOnce deployment architecture: manifests, publish.htm, and .application files
- Abuse of .appref-ms (Application Reference) files as unblocked OLE attachments
- Post-exploitation and persistence: silent background updates without user interaction

Technical Details:
Traditional initial access techniques, such as embedding PowerShell one-liners inside batch files packaged within Word or Excel Object Linking and Embedding (OLE) containers, have become largely ineffective. Modern defenses—including hardened Windows Defender definitions, commercial endpoint detection, and email scanners like Gmail—routinely detect and block these legacy delivery chains. Seeking a reliable alternative that operates seamlessly against fully patched Windows 7 and Windows 10 environments with active antivirus protections, the author investigated Microsoft's OLE blacklists to identify permitted file extensions capable of invoking system execution engines, building upon earlier research into .settingcontent-ms by Matt Nelson.

While Microsoft explicitly blocked direct execution of ClickOnce .application deployment manifests within OLE packages, the author discovered that .appref-ms (Application Reference) files remained fully permitted. Microsoft ClickOnce is designed to facilitate rapid web-based deployment of .NET applications across HTTP servers and UNC shares. A standard ClickOnce publication directory includes a landing page (publish.htm), an application manifest (.application), a generic installer (setup.exe), and supporting dependencies stored inside an Application Files directory. ClickOnce supports two deployment availability settings: "online only," which displays a "Run" prompt to the user, and "online or offline," which displays an "Install" prompt and automatically generates a local .appref-ms shortcut in the user's Start Menu.

The author demonstrates that delivering a weaponized .appref-ms file (either directly or encapsulated within permitted Office OLE containers) triggers the standard ClickOnce application launch workflow. When the target user clicks "Install" or "Run" once, ClickOnce downloads and executes the application from the remote host. Crucially, applications deployed with "online or offline" availability establish persistent auto-update connections: any subsequent application updates pushed to the remote web server—including forced update configurations—are retrieved and executed automatically by the operating system without displaying any warning dialogues or requiring further user authorization.

Key Takeaways:
Defenders and system administrators must monitor and restrict the execution of ClickOnce deployment mechanisms and .appref-ms file handlers across enterprise workstations. Email security gateways and content inspection firewalls should treat incoming .appref-ms attachments and ClickOnce deployment manifests with the same high-risk restrictions applied to executable binaries. Security teams should audit application execution logs for anomalous parent-child process relationships originating from ClickOnce runtime binaries (dfshim.dll and dfsvc.exe).

talks.title: I Block You Because I Love You: Social Account Identification Attack Against a Website Visitor
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning I Block You Because I Love You: Social Account Identification Attack Against a Website Visitor.
talks.summary:
## Overview

The presentation addresses social account identification attacks aimed at website visitors, exploring how interactions between web visitors and social platforms can de-anonymize individuals. The transcript touches on themes of stalking, social engineering, and the manipulation of user identity through web services, CRM systems, and online platforms. The talk specifically focuses on distinguishing and tracking individuals via social accounts and web tracking mechanisms, referencing marketing campaigns, live shopping, gaming, and betting environments.

## Mechanisms and Identification Techniques

The core attack methodology discussed revolves around contrasting blocking and non-blocking account states to differentiate and profile targets:

* **Blocking vs. Non-Blocking States:** The mechanism leverages differences between a "blocking" and "non-blocking" account status (noted in relation to services and platforms like pokernews.com and Facebook). The variation between these states acts as a differentiator to identify specific accounts or visitor profiles.
* **Interface and Social Actions:** The procedure examines user interfaces, social actions, and CRM system integrations to monitor how a targeted account reacts.
* **Cross-Media and Web Tracking:** The attack model references tracking user page views (noting page view metrics such as eighth page view), content sources like YouTube, and cross-media tracking vectors across web domains (referencing sites like pz-news.de, pokernews.com, and dgap.de).
* **Platform and Device Context:** The technique evaluates mobile platforms, multi-platform display sources, and account derivations across social environments, including tests observing movements into Facebook accounts.

## Experimental Setup and Observations

The speaker outlines experimental parameters and observations assessing the realism of the attack:

* **Experimental Design:** An IT distributor experiment was structured to test whether aggressive account blocking and interaction behaviors could simulate realistic social actions.
* **Account Differentiation:** The methodology tests how an ideal target account is differentiated across visits, evaluating whether specific profiles (e.g., historical user data, archive materials, or targeted content streams) can be isolated.
* **Contextual Variables:** The experiments observed account status under varied visitor environments, tracking device conditions, mobile usage in different regional contexts, and service provider integrations.

## Impact on Anonymity and Privacy

The primary outcome highlighted is the compromise of user anonymity:

* **Destruction of Anonymity:** The attack demonstrates that manipulating social account states (such as blocking mechanisms) can destroy expected anonymity, particularly in private browsing situations.
* **Visitor De-anonymization:** By associating website visitor behaviors with distinct social platform states, an attacker or tracking entity can identify the specific social account of an otherwise anonymous web visitor.

talks.title: Where 2 Worlds Collide: Bringing Mimikatz et al to UNIX
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Where 2 Worlds Collide: Bringing Mimikatz et al to UNIX.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Tim, a security engineer at Cisco with two decades of experience in operational security and penetration testing, explores the security consequences of integrating UNIX and Linux enterprise systems into Microsoft Active Directory (AD). The presentation examines the architectural trust relationships formed when corporate AD domains are extended across heterogeneous data center environments. The speaker reveals how misconfigurations, disparate security models, and local credential caching software expose enterprise Active Directory forests to lateral movement and privilege escalation originating from compromised UNIX hosts.

Key Topics:
- Active Directory integration architectures in UNIX/Linux enterprise environments
- Behavioral disconnects between Windows Enterprise Admins and UNIX system administrators
- Authentication daemon architectures: SSSD versus Quest/Dell Vintela (vasd)
- Credential caching vulnerabilities on local UNIX filesystems and memory dumping techniques

Technical Details:
Enterprise infrastructure has largely transitioned from legacy UNIX identity management systems (such as Tivoli and scripted /etc/passwd synchronization) to joining Linux and UNIX servers directly to corporate Active Directory domains for unified single sign-on. This convergence introduces severe architectural friction between Windows enterprise administrators—who manage domain policies and the overarching AD forest—and UNIX systems administrators. Centralized Active Directory Group Policies (GPOs), password enforcement rules, and native event telemetry do not automatically apply to UNIX hosts over the network; instead, UNIX hosts enforce security locally through tools like sudo, PAM, and SELinux, creating substantial auditing blind spots.

Furthermore, enterprise organizations routinely join low-trust environments (such as non-production SAP development clusters) to the corporate AD domain. Because trust relationships in Active Directory span across all joined endpoints, compromising an under-secured Linux server in a development zone provides an attacker with a direct foothold into the broader AD infrastructure. 

The author analyzes the software stacks that enable Linux AD integration, highlighting Red Hat's System Security Services Daemon (SSSD) and Quest/Dell Vintela Authentication Services (vasd), noting that these daemons function effectively as the Linux counterpart to the Windows Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). When a user logs in via SSH or SMB, authentication requests pass through Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) across a local UNIX domain socket to vasd or SSSD. The daemon coordinates Kerberos, LDAP, and DNS communications with the domain controller. Crucially, to accommodate offline access and performance requirements, these services maintain local cached credential stores—including SQLite databases and configuration files located on the local filesystem. Attackers who gain administrative access on a Linux host can harvest cached domain credentials, Kerberos tickets, and authentication artifacts, reproducing Windows-style Mimikatz credential extraction directly on UNIX endpoints.

Key Takeaways:
Enterprises must avoid treating UNIX and Linux endpoints as isolated security silos when they are joined to Active Directory domains, as domain-level trust relationships extend across all joined assets. Security operations teams must deploy unified host-based monitoring to capture authentication telemetry, PAM modifications, and anomalous credential access targeting SSSD or vasd stores on Linux systems. Organizations should isolate development environments from production AD forests and enforce dedicated, restricted service accounts for UNIX authentication infrastructure.

talks.title: Eternal War in XNU Kernel Objects
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Eternal War in XNU Kernel Objects.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In the presentation **"Eternal War in XNU Kernel Objects,"** Min Zheng (Spark) and teammate Xiaoning from Alibaba discuss the evolution of exploitation techniques and mitigations within Apple's hybrid XNU kernel across iOS and macOS. While Apple introduced mitigations such as Data Execution Prevention (DEP), Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (kASLR), freelist randomization (iOS 9.2 / macOS 10.11.2), and zone metadata region integrity checks (iOS / OS X 10.11), attackers shifted their attention toward kernel objects that remain vulnerable to manipulation. Specifically, the talk focuses on how attackers leverage `ipc_port` kernel objects via **Mach Port-Oriented Programming (MPOP)** to bypass modern protections.

---

## Mach Port-Oriented Programming (MPOP) Primitives

MPOP systematizes techniques found in public exploits that manipulate Mach ports—represented in kernel space by pointers to `ipc_port` structures (containing fields such as `io_bits`, `io_references`, `io_lock_data`, and `kobject`). By invoking user-mode system calls with manipulated Mach ports, attackers construct four main categories of primitives:

1. **General-Purpose Primitives:**  
   Utilizes standard Mach system calls as originally designed without hijacking control flow. For instance, obtaining rights to privileged host ports (e.g., via `host_processor_set_priv`) allows acquisition of powerful processor set ports. Furthermore, `mach_vm_*` APIs enable full memory manipulation of another process or kernel space once the target task port pointer is obtained.
2. **Querying Primitives:**  
   Abuses system call logic to disclose kernel layout information and defeat kASLR. Examples include:
   - `mach_port_kobject`: Historically leaked kernel object addresses (used in the Pangu jailbreak; later patched).
   - `clock_sleep_trap`: Combined with a corrupted `kobject` field pointing to the global system clock, returns `KERN_SUCCESS` on a match, enabling side-channel brute-forcing of kASLR.
3. **Memory Inter-operation & Type-Confusion Primitives:**  
   Enables unauthorized data transfer between kernel and user space:
   - `pid_for_task`: Retrieves the PID without validating whether the task object is legitimate. By pointing a fake port to a crafted user-space fake task structure, an attacker can read 32 bytes of arbitrary kernel memory at a specific offset (`bsd_info->p_pid`).
   - Dangling ports: Using APIs like `mach_port_set_context` / `mach_port_get_context` on dangling (freed) ports allows reading or writing a 64-bit value in kernel space.
4. **Arbitrary Code Execution Primitives:**  
   - Hijacking control flow via `clock_get_attributes` by corrupting global function pointers or crafting fake objects (used in the Pegasus APT attack on iOS 9.3.3).
   - Overwriting C++ virtual method table (`vtable`) pointers inside I/O Kit user clients (`IOUserClient`) to redirect control flow to ROP gadgets.

---

## Case Study: The Yalu OS X Exploit

The speakers walk through the Yalu exploit targeting OS X:
- **Vulnerability:** A heap buffer overflow in `mach_port_extract_right_trap` where `kalloc` allocates a buffer sized via an `sd` value read from user space, but `copyin` uses `receipt_size` (a user pointer that can represent a much larger size).
- **Exploitation:** The overflow corrupts `ipc_port` pointers inside an array of Mach messages to point to a crafted fake `ipc_port` in user space.
- **kASLR Bypass:** Uses `clock_sleep_trap` to brute-force the global system clock address.
- **Arbitrary Kernel Read:** Sets `io_bits` to `IKOT_TASK` and configures a fake task offset to read arbitrary 32-bit kernel values using `pid_for_task` without any ROP gadgets.
- **Control:** Historically, exploits obtained the `kernel_task` port via `task_for_pid` or `processor_set_tasks`. When iOS 11 blocked resolution of `kernel_task`, Ian Beer's `async_wake` exploit bypassed the restriction by cloning the kernel's `vm_map` reference pointer into a fake task to retain arbitrary read/write via `mach_vm_*`.

---

## Defense: XNU Kernel Object Protector (XKOP)

Because enterprise MacBooks are not forced to upgrade like iOS devices, lack certain hardware protections, and feature looser sandboxing, they are uniquely exposed to APT and MPOP attacks. To defend these systems, the speakers designed **XKOP (XNU Kernel Object Protector)**:
- Deployed as a kernel extension (KEXT) that implements inline hooking on critical system calls and performs runtime integrity checks on `ipc_port` kernel objects.
- Uses dedicated examiner functions at strategic kernel execution points, working around the functional limitations of standard MACF (Mandatory Access Control Framework) APIs to backport modern security checks to older macOS installations.

talks.title: DeepPhish: Simulating Malicious AI
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning DeepPhish: Simulating Malicious AI.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Alejandro Correa Bahnsen, VP of Research at Cyxtera Technologies, presents empirical research on applying machine learning and deep learning to cyber defense and phishing detection. The talk analyzes why traditional content-based phishing detection mechanisms struggle to scale on edge and mobile devices due to latency, compute, and privacy constraints. The author outlines a character-level recurrent neural network for high-accuracy URL classification and examines the growing exploitation of TLS web certificates by malicious actors.

Key Topics:
- Phishing threat statistics and evolving evasion techniques (from HTML clones to screenshots)
- Computational bottlenecks of traditional DOM, image, and text-based machine learning classifiers
- Character-level Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN/LSTM) for lightweight URL classification
- TLS certificate abuse in phishing campaigns and browser indicator trust misconceptions

Technical Details:
Phishing remains the foundational initial compromise vector, serving as the entry point for 91% of modern cyberattacks. Attackers continually adapt their evasion techniques against security scanners: when automated detectors relied on text keywords, phishers substituted webpage screenshots to thwart OCR and keyword parsing, forcing defenders to implement complex computer vision classifiers. Comprehensive modern phishing analysis pipelines evaluate website source code, rendered screenshots, extracted text, and DOM references using algorithms like Random Forest. While effective, these multimodal systems require substantial computational resources, specialized GPUs, and high network bandwidth, making them unsuitable for real-time mobile execution or privacy-restricted environments where outbound website telemetry is prohibited.

To provide a lightweight, real-time alternative, the author developed a deep learning architecture that classifies phishing threats purely from the raw character sequence of the URL string. The training dataset comprised two million samples: one million confirmed phishing URLs (harvested from PhishTank and internal telemetry) and one million legitimate URLs (curated from Common Crawl). The model employs a character-level Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) featuring Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layers. The raw URL string undergoes one-hot encoding and embedding before being processed through LSTM layers, outputting a probability score via a final sigmoid activation. This architecture achieved an impressive 98% to 99% classification accuracy using only the URL string, completely eliminating the need for page rendering, network round-trips, or heavy processing overhead.

The presentation also investigates emerging trends in adversary infrastructure, noting that by late 2017 nearly 25% of phishing campaigns had integrated TLS web certificates. Attackers exploit automated, free certificate authorities to secure their domains programmatically. Citing a Forrester consumer survey, the author highlights that 82% of users erroneously believe that a browser's "green padlock" and "Secure" label indicate that a website is intrinsically safe and trustworthy, rather than merely indicating an encrypted communications channel. Attackers systematically leverage this psychological vulnerability to instill false confidence and harvest credentials.

Key Takeaways:
Character-level LSTM models provide highly efficient, low-latency phishing detection that can operate directly on mobile devices without relying on external cloud APIs or full-page rendering. Security training programs must educate users that TLS certificates and browser padlocks only establish channel encryption, not domain legitimacy or website safety. Defenders should incorporate lightweight URL-based neural network models into endpoint inspection points to filter malicious infrastructure before page content loads.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

The iPhone and Android have accelerated the mass adoption of smart devices, mobile applications, and high speed mobile networks. Meanwhile, mobile devices are now a material target: they contain sensitive personal and corporate data, access privileged networks, and routinely perform financial transactions. The question remains, how do we keep these devices safe
