talks.title: There will be Glitches: Extracting and Analyzing Automotive Firmware Efficiently
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of There will be Glitches: Extracting and Analyzing Automotive Firmware Efficiently.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Niek Shenk and Elisa from the Riscure automotive security team present an end-to-end methodology for extracting and reverse engineering automotive microcontroller firmware. Focusing on an automotive instrument cluster Electronic Control Unit (ECU), the speakers demonstrate how voltage fault injection (voltage glitching) bypasses standard diagnostic security mechanisms. Furthermore, they discuss developing custom CPU emulators and peripheral models to dynamically analyze complex, monolithic automotive binary blobs.

Key Topics:
- Automotive ECU hardware architecture and physical acquisition from salvage vehicles
- Unified Diagnostic Services (UDS / ISO 14229) Service 0x23 and Service 0x27
- Voltage fault injection (voltage glitching) mechanics and instruction skipping
- Firmware reverse engineering challenges with AUTOSAR, Simulink, and custom emulation

Technical Details:
Automotive ECUs, such as digital instrument clusters, operate as dedicated embedded systems communicating across CAN buses. When hardware debug interfaces (JTAG/SWD) are physically locked and external EEPROMs contain only configuration data rather than executable code, security researchers must extract firmware stored within the microcontroller's internal flash. The speakers leveraged the Unified Diagnostic Services (UDS, ISO 14229) protocol, specifically Service 0x23 (ReadMemoryByAddress). Normally, Service 0x23 is gated by Service 0x27 (SecurityAccess), which enforces a seed-key challenge-response cryptographic handshake. However, attempting to glitch the seed-key calculation directly was impractical because firmware enforces a strict 10-minute lockout penalty after three consecutive failed attempts, preventing high-frequency fault injection experimentation.

To bypass this barrier, the researchers targeted the internal authorization check executed within Service 0x23. While calling ReadMemoryByAddress without authentication yields a negative response, it does not trigger any lockout timer. By taking control of the microcontroller's power supply rails (normally operating between 1.8V and 5.5V) and precisely dropping the VDD voltage for brief nanosecond intervals, they induced transient hardware faults. This voltage glitching caused the processor to skip conditional branch instructions verifying authentication state or corrupt the authorization comparison register. By automating this glitch over thousands of iterations, the team successfully bypassed access controls and dumped internal memory 40 to 500 bytes per request across 500 KB to 4 MB flash memories, successfully performing a live firmware dump on stage.

Analyzing the dumped firmware presented substantial reverse engineering hurdles. Automotive firmware is heavily synthesized from high-level MATLAB Simulink models and AUTOSAR architectures, resulting in monolithic binary blobs devoid of conventional operating system abstractions (such as standard QNX, VxWorks, or Linux boundaries). Because the specific microcontroller architecture was unsupported by standard dynamic analysis platforms like QEMU, the researchers engineered a bespoke instruction set emulator. Their emulator integrated customized peripheral models covering system timers, interrupt controllers, I2C buses (for EEPROM and display components), and CAN interfaces, enabling dynamic execution and vulnerability research on the proprietary binary.

Key Takeaways:
Automotive hardware manufacturers must incorporate hardware-level brownout detectors, core voltage monitoring, and clock glitch sensors to thwart fault injection attacks. In ECU software architectures, diagnostic security checks must implement defensive coding standards, including double-condition verification, randomized delays (jitter), and unified rate-limiting across all unauthenticated diagnostic requests. Security assessments of embedded automotive components must combine physical fault injection testing with customized dynamic emulation environments.

Firmware Attack Vectors: BMC, UEFI, BIOS, and Remote Management Vulnerabilities

**Overview**

Security researchers from Eclipse iam present comprehensive analysis of firmware attack vectors targeting Baseboard Management Controllers (BMC), UEFI firmware, BIOS, and Advanced Management Technology (AMT) on server and client platforms. Core thesis: firmware components represent blind spot in modern security architecture; isolated from traditional security boundaries (user/kernel separation); often running untrusted code, unpatched for years, with full hardware access and minimal audit trails. Attack vectors span remote (network), software-local (host OS), and physical categories. Remote attack vectors primary focus: BMC accessible via IPMI (Intelligent Platform Management Interface), SMM (System Management Mode), web interfaces over plaintext HTTP; UEFI/BIOS featuring network capabilities (TCP/IP stack, HTTP boot, SMTP, Bluetooth) enabling firmware download and update mechanisms vulnerable to man-in-the-middle and buffer overflow exploits. Demonstrated vulnerabilities: ASUS and ASROCK motherboards vulnerable to buffer overflows in HTTP-based firmware update checking mechanism; pre-OS execution enables arbitrary code execution with ring -2 privileges (SMM code). Historical firmware vulnerabilities: HP Integrated Lights-Out (ILO) 4 authentication bypass, Hewlett-Packard Default More than Farmer (2013) affecting 53,000 exposed BMCs, Intel MEI AM Team (2015) 17-day authentication bypass. Hardware management components (BMC, AMT) represent privileged out-of-band access points; compromise provides complete system control independent of OS security. Firmware supply chain: third-party components (controllers, microcode vendors) run proprietary firmware often unupdatable, compiled without exploit protections (NX, ASLR, stack canaries), potentially years old and never patched. Cover story for firmware vulnerabilities: "performance optimization" patches enable vendors to pre-position updates before public disclosure. Debugging challenges: absence of kernel-level debugging tools; researchers must leverage hardware debug interfaces (XTP, Closed Chassis Adapter, USB 3 Debug cable) to trace firmware execution during exploitation. Detection and defense: firmware monitoring absent on most systems; attack surface spans BMC management network, IPMI/ICMP interfaces, web/VNC ports, and serial connections. Risk stratification: firmware compromise enables persistent root kit-like implants, BIOS modification (survives OS reinstall), exfiltration of unencrypted data, lateral movement within data center management networks. Vendor implementations diverge: no standard HTTP boot, firmware update checking, Bluetooth, WiFi implementations in UEFI; each vendor custom solution introduces unique vulnerabilities (buffer overflows, authentication bypasses). Reference implementation (Tianocore UEFI) provides baseline; vendors extend with proprietary features, doubling attack surface.

**Technical Details**

Firmware Attack Surface, Component Vulnerabilities, and Remote Exploitation:

1. **Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) Architecture**:
   - Dedicated independent computing system: separate CPU, SRAM, flash memory
   - Persistence: boots immediately on power cable insertion; operates independent of host OS
   - Management protocols: IPMI (Intelligent Platform Management Interface) for server management
   - Capabilities: KVM (remote VNC), BIOS configuration, ISO image mounting, power control, firmware flashing
   - Network access: dedicated NIC (separate from host) or shared network port; VNC, web interface, IPMI ports
   - Licensing models: feature-based (Super Micro) or tier-based (Dell iDRAC: Basic/Express/Enterprise)
   - Challenge: Hardware scanning difficult (high latency); network enumeration limited to port detection

2. **IPMI (Intelligent Platform Management Interface) Protocol**:
   - Historical evolution: 1998 initial specification, 2001 LAN support, 2004 VLAN/firewall support
   - Vulnerability history: 2013 Shodan-based scan revealed 300,000 exposed BMCs; 53,000 vulnerable to zero-auth bypass
   - Authentication mechanisms: default credentials, zero-authentication bypass (digest authentication misconfiguration)
   - Modern vulnerabilities: HP iLO 4 authentication bypass (2015), 27-day embargo
   - Privilege level: full BMC access enables complete system control (power management, BIOS modification, OS installation)
   - Deployment gap: data center segregation (management VLAN separate from host VLAN) not always enforced; network pivoting enables BMC access

3. **Intel AMT (Active Management Technology) on Client Platforms**:
   - Functional equivalent: AMT for enterprise clients (desktops/laptops); functionally similar to BMC but different platform
   - Capabilities: remote provisioning, OS installation, BIOS configuration, KVM (remote desktop access), wireless support (2007+)
   - Provisioning: out-of-band network provisioning (2008+), remote KVM (2010+)
   - Vulnerability timeline: 2015 authentication bypass (empty digest attack), 2017 first major vulnerability disclosed, 2018 Intel internal vulnerabilities
   - Web interface vulnerability (2015): authentication bypass enabling full remote access
   - Use case: enables IT to provision corporate laptops without physical access; remote management at scale

4. **BIOS/UEFI Firmware Role and Trust Model**:
   - Definition: early-stage code executing before OS boot; configures hardware, enables security policies
   - Functionality: register configuration, memory protection (ECC/SEC), SMM (System Management Mode) locking, hardware protection bit locking
   - Root of trust: BIOS is Trust Core; all post-boot security depends on BIOS integrity
   - Attack consequence: BIOS compromise enables complete system takeover; survives OS reinstall, disk wipe
   - Evolution: proprietary implementations (1990s) consolidated into UEFI Forum standardization (2007+)
   - Tianocore: reference implementation enabling third-party BIOS vendors to build secure boot

5. **UEFI Specification Evolution and Reference Implementation**:
   - Historical development: EFI 1.0 (1998), 2.0 (2002), UEFI Forum standardization (2007)
   - Feature additions: cryptography (2007), network/authentication (2007), WiFi/Bluetooth support (2015), HTTP boot/OpenSSL (2016)
   - Tianocore: open-source reference implementation; provides baseline functionality
   - Standards compliance: UEFI 2.4 specification includes TCP/IP, UDP, DHCP, IPv4/IPv6, DNS, TLS
   - Reference implementations: vendors use Tianocore as base; extend with proprietary features

6. **Vendor-Specific UEFI Extensions and Feature Addition**:
   - HTTP boot (HP custom, later standardized): replaces PXE boot; downloads UEFI app or ISO via HTTP/HTTPS
   - Signature verification: HTTP boot verifies code signature before execution (policy-based: internal/external source determination)
   - WiFi stack (AMI custom): parallel implementation when reference code incomplete; open network + WPA2 but missing EAP implementation
   - Bluetooth stack (AMI custom): proprietary implementation; allows connection pre-OS boot (use case unclear)
   - Intelligent Provisioning (HP): embedded system enabling firmware update download, driver injection into installed OS, system provisioning wizard
   - SMTP (HP/OEM custom): email from BIOS before OS boot; attached file system access via NTFS driver; diagnostic reporting

7. **HP Remote Diagnostic Download Feature**:
   - Functionality: BIOS triggers network boot; downloads executable from remote server; signature verification before execution
   - Scheduling: automatic scheduling possible (weekly check); triggers on reboot if threshold time exceeded
   - Upload capability: results returned to remote server (FTP with optional password protection)
   - Risk: allows firmware-level remote command execution before OS boot; bypasses OS-level security monitoring

8. **Automated BIOS Update Features (Vendor-Specific)**:
   - Challenge: BIOS updates historically manual and risky; users skip updates
   - Solution: pre-OS update checking; brings up network, queries remote server for newer BIOS version
   - Implementations vary: ASUS, ASROCK, HP all custom implementations with no standard approach
   - Network requests: plain HTTP to vendor servers (no HTTPS in some cases)
   - Vulnerability potential: update mechanism without standardization increases exploit surface
   - Responsive design: ASUS/ASROCK update checkers vulnerable to buffer overflow (long string fields crash update process)

9. **Buffer Overflow in ASUS/ASROCK Firmware Update Checking**:
   - Vulnerability type: classic buffer overflow in pre-OS code
   - Trigger: checking for firmware updates (not applying updates); check alone triggers overflow
   - Exploit mechanism: plain HTTP response from server under attacker control (man-in-the-middle)
   - Payload insertion: oversized URL field in XML response causes buffer overflow
   - Code execution: arbitrary code execution at SMM privilege level (ring -2)
   - Affected systems: ASUS, ASROCK models; approximately 300 motherboard variants (Haswell onward); AMD processors also affected

10. **ASROCK Update Protocol and Exploitation**:
    - Plain HTTP request: to asrock.com/web/live_update endpoint; includes motherboard model
    - XML response: contains URLs, region information, BIOS update availability list
    - Vulnerability point: URL field unbounded; long string causes overflow during parsing
    - Man-in-the-middle requirement: attacker intercepts plain HTTP traffic; injects malicious response
    - Malicious UI: crafted XML description shows "malicious BIOS" in firmware update UI; user can click to apply
    - Silent exploitation: payload can execute without visual indication; continues boot after compromise

11. **ASUS Update Protocol and Exploitation**:
    - Plain HTTP request: motherboard-specific path to ASUS website; different structure from ASROCK
    - Response format: XML with similar structure; vulnerable to same buffer overflow attack
    - Hang behavior: oversized fields cause update process to hang; indicates memory corruption
    - Debugging requirement: hardware debug interface needed to trace execution; kernel debuggers unavailable for firmware

12. **Firmware Debugging Challenges**:
    - XTP (extreme debug port): older hardware debug interface; socket on motherboard; requires case opening; expensive equipment
    - Closed Chassis Adapter: enables debugging via USB without case opening; simpler than XTP
    - USB 3 Debug: native debug capability on modern platforms; USB 3 cable enables runtime tracing
    - Absence of kernel debugging: no gdb equivalent for firmware; hardware debug interfaces required for execution tracing
    - Research barrier: firmware security research requires specialized hardware; limits researcher community

13. **SMM (System Management Mode) Privilege Level**:
   - Definition: CPU privilege mode (ring -2); higher privilege than kernel (ring 0)
   - Invocation: triggered by System Management Interrupt (SMI); firmware code runs with full hardware access
   - Isolation: SMM code isolated from OS monitoring; no visibility into SMM execution
   - Consequence: SMM compromise enables rootkit-like persistence; OS-level monitoring cannot detect SMM activity
   - BIOS lock: write protection prevents runtime modification of BIOS flash; SMM code can bypass (owns flash controller)
   - Control: SMM code can modify page tables, intercept CPU instructions, control hardware (DMA, memory, registers)

14. **Firmware Update Mechanisms and Signature Verification**:
   - Secure boot requirement: signature verification of UEFI applications before execution
   - Policy-based verification: internal sources (policy bit unset) bypass signature checking; external sources require verification
   - HTTP boot: downloads ISO image or UEFI app; signature check enforced for remote sources
   - Vendor extensions: each vendor implements update checking with own signature scheme
   - Vulnerability in signature verification: buffer overflow before signature check; code execution before validation

15. **Reference Implementation Vulnerabilities (Tianocore)**:
   - DHCP buffer overflow (2016): missing size check in DHCP packet parsing; affected multiple vendors
   - Discovery: researcher (Topher Timson) identified missing bounds check; assert/check logic inverted
   - Root cause: complexity of UEFI network stack; reference implementation focus on functionality over security
   - Impact: any firmware using Tianocore DHCP code vulnerable unless patched
   - Lesson: reference implementations used as-is by multiple vendors; security bugs propagate widely

16. **Firmware Supply Chain Vulnerabilities**:
   - Component origin: BMC, AMT, SMM code from CPU vendors; other controllers from third-party manufacturers
   - Firmware updates: third-party component firmware often unupdatable; vendor proprietary; no visibility
   - Compilation: code compiled without security flags (NX, ASLR, stack canaries); no exploit protections
   - Age: firmware dated; years since compilation; pre-dates modern security practices
   - Consequence: third-party component compromise enables system compromise; supply chain weak link
   - Example: Super Micro firmware updates affecting all servers; third-party firmware updates via BMC

17. **Firmware Cover Story and Pre-Positioning**:
   - Strategy: vendors release firmware updates weeks before public disclosure of vulnerability
   - Narrative: "performance optimization," "cache behavior improvement," "microcode update"
   - Purpose: enable internal testing, pre-position fixes, avoid surprise at disclosure deadline
   - Risk: attacker can analyze firmware deltas; identify vulnerability from patch comparison
   - Deployment: cover story patches applied widely without revealing vulnerability; patch rollback prevents exploitation

18. **Firmware Network Capabilities and Attack Surface**:
   - TCP/IP stack: Tianocore reference; vendors build on top; enables network boot (PXE/DHCP)
   - HTTP boot: downloads UEFI app or ISO; HTTPS variant for security
   - SMTP: email capability from firmware; requires network access
   - WiFi/Bluetooth: pre-OS network connectivity; enables management access before OS boots
   - Consequence: network-accessible firmware attack surface; no OS firewall protections applicable
   - Remote management: BMC, AMT, IPMI all network-accessible; default routing in many data centers

19. **BIOS/Firmware Update Strategies and Risks**:
   - Manual updates: users skip BIOS updates (historically tedious, risky)
   - Automated checking: pre-OS checks for newer version; user-initiated or scheduled update
   - Rollback protection: write protection prevents downgrade; security ratchet mechanism
   - Recovery mechanism: recovery image stored on separate flash; enables factory reset
   - Risk: automated update without staging increases attack surface; immediate application of update

20. **Data Center Network Segmentation and Attack Scenarios**:
   - Typical topology: management network (BMC/AMT) separated from host network
   - Assumption: management network isolated; attackers cannot reach it
   - Failure case: misconfiguration allows management network access from host network
   - Compromise scenario: host OS compromise enables pivot to management network; BMC compromise enables host OS control
   - Bidirectional risk: host OS access via host network + BMC access via management network = symmetric compromise
   - Enterprise scale: data center with thousands of servers; single exploitable firmware vulnerability affects all
   - Persistence: firmware compromise survives OS reinstall, disk wipe, password reset

**Defense & Takeaways**

Defending firmware components and management interfaces against remote exploitation and persistence: (1) Firmware baseline monitoring—establish firmware checksums/hashes of BIOS, BMC, microcode; detect unauthorized modifications; verify vendor signatures; (2) Network segmentation—strictly isolate management networks (BMC, IPMI, AMT) from host networks; no cross-segment routing; air-gap if possible; (3) Firmware update signing—require cryptographic signature verification; disable unsigned firmware execution; enforce chain of trust; (4) Default credential elimination—change all default BMC, AMT, BIOS passwords; enforce strong authentication; (5) IPMI hardening—disable IPMI where not required; require authentication for all operations; disable cipher suite weaknesses; (6) HTTP to HTTPS transition—firmware update mechanisms must use HTTPS; no plaintext HTTP for firmware download; (7) Certificate pinning—pin HTTPS certificates for firmware servers; prevent man-in-the-middle; (8) Disable unnecessary network protocols—disable SMTP, WiFi, Bluetooth from BIOS if not required; reduce attack surface; (9) Hardware debugging control—restrict physical debug port access; Closed Chassis Adapter requires physical access; XTP/USB3 debug vulnerable to physical compromise; (10) Firmware update validation—implement staged firmware updates; validate new firmware before boot; recovery mechanism if update corrupts; (11) SMM protection—enforce SMM Code Access Check (SMRR); prevent DMA attacks; isolate SMM from DMA devices; (12) Microcode verification—validate CPU microcode signature; prevent backdoor microcode insertion; (13) UEFI Secure Boot enforcement—sign boot loaders; prevent unsigned OS loading; maintain chain of trust; (14) TPM integration—store firmware measurements in TPM; detect tampering; attest firmware integrity remotely; (15) Firmware audit logging—enable firmware logging of configuration changes; authenticate log writes; prevent log tampering; (16) Supply chain verification—verify firmware binaries from third-party component vendors; no unsigned code; validate compilation environment; (17) Exploit protection hardening—enable ASLR, NX, stack canaries in firmware code; recompile with security flags; (18) Firmware update patching—apply UEFI Tianocore patches promptly (DHCP buffer overflow example); validate vendors release patches; (19) Management protocol disabling—disable IPMI, ICMP, IMPI bridges where not required; limit access to privileged users; (20) Incident response procedures—firmware compromise requires out-of-band recovery; maintain recovery media; prepare secure BIOS recovery process. The critical insight: firmware represents blind spot in modern security; isolated from OS-level monitoring; often unpatched, unupdatable, full hardware access. Remote attack vectors ubiquitous: HTTP firmware update checking over plaintext HTTP; IPMI authentication bypasses; AMT web interface vulnerabilities. Pre-OS code execution enables SMM privilege (ring -2) exploitation; compromise survives OS reinstall. Network-accessible firmware contradicts data center isolation assumptions; management network compromise enables symmetric OS compromise. Reference implementation vulnerabilities propagate widely: Tianocore DHCP buffer overflow affects multiple vendors; no vendor-specific fix needed. Vendor extensions beyond reference implementation double attack surface: HTTP boot (HP), WiFi (AMI), Bluetooth (AMI), SMTP; each custom implementation introduces unique vulnerabilities. Buffer overflow in pre-OS code enables arbitrary SMM execution: ASUS/ASROCK firmware update vulnerability demonstrates classic memory safety bugs in firmware context. Hardware debugging challenges limit firmware security research: XTP/Closed Chassis Adapter/USB3 debug required; constrains researcher community. The broader lesson: firmware security lagging OS security by decade; no standard security practices, exploit protections, or update mechanisms. Vendor fragmentation: three major firmware vendors (ASUS, ASROCK, HP) implement update checking three different ways; standardization necessary. Supply chain risk amplified: third-party component firmware often proprietary, unupdatable, unverifiable; backdoor risk. Management interface design prioritizes functionality over security: blanket remote access (KVM, power control, firmware update) enables wholesale compromise. The asymmetry: defender must patch all firmware variants; attacker needs exploit for single model. Network-accessible firmware fundamentally problematic: attack surface unavoidable; defense must focus on authentication, encryption, and signature verification. The future: firmware security requires standardized update mechanisms, exploit protections, and monitoring; currently missing across industry. Hardware debug access (physical) controls firmware security: XTP/Closed Chassis ports enable firmware modification; physical security essential. Firmware compromise persistence (SMM, BIOS survives OS wipe) demands architectural change: trusted boot, firmware attestation, secure recovery mechanisms required.

    - Vulnerability point: URL field unbounded; long string causes overflow during parsing
    - Man-in-the-middle requirement: attacker intercepts plain HTTP traffic; injects malicious response
    - Malicious UI: crafted XML description shows "malicious BIOS" in firmware update UI; user can click to apply
    - Silent exploitation: payload can execute without visual indication; continues boot after compromise

11. **ASUS Update Protocol and Exploitation**:
    - Plain HTTP request: motherboard-specific path to ASUS website; different structure from ASROCK
    - Response format: XML with similar structure; vulnerable to same buffer overflow attack
    - Hang behavior: oversized fields cause update process to hang; indicates memory corruption
    - Debugging requirement: hardware debug interface needed to trace execution; kernel debuggers unavailable for firmware

12. **Firmware Debugging Challenges**:
    - XTP (extreme debug port): older hardware debug interface; socket on motherboard; requires case opening; expensive equipment
    - Closed Chassis Adapter: enables debugging via USB without case opening; simpler than XTP
    - USB 3 Debug: native debug capability on modern platforms; USB 3 cable enables runtime tracing
    - Absence of kernel debugging: no gdb equivalent for firmware; hardware debug interfaces required for execution tracing
    - Research barrier: firmware security research requires specialized hardware; limits researcher community

13. **SMM (System Management Mode) Privilege Level**:
   - Definition: CPU privilege mode (ring -2); higher privilege than kernel (ring 0)
   - Invocation: triggered by System Management Interrupt (SMI); firmware code runs with full hardware access
   - Isolation: SMM code isolated from OS monitoring; no visibility into SMM execution
   - Consequence: SMM compromise enables rootkit-like persistence; OS-level monitoring cannot detect SMM activity
   - BIOS lock: write protection prevents runtime modification of BIOS flash; SMM code can bypass (owns flash controller)
   - Control: SMM code can modify page tables, intercept CPU instructions, control hardware (DMA, memory, registers)

14. **Firmware Update Mechanisms and Signature Verification**:
   - Secure boot requirement: signature verification of UEFI applications before execution
   - Policy-based verification: internal sources (policy bit unset) bypass signature checking; external sources require verification
   - HTTP boot: downloads ISO image or UEFI app; signature check enforced for remote sources
   - Vendor extensions: each vendor implements update checking with own signature scheme
   - Vulnerability in signature verification: buffer overflow before signature check; code execution before validation

15. **Reference Implementation Vulnerabilities (Tianocore)**:
   - DHCP buffer overflow (2016): missing size check in DHCP packet parsing; affected multiple vendors
   - Discovery: researcher (Topher Timson) identified missing bounds check; assert/check logic inverted
   - Root cause: complexity of UEFI network stack; reference implementation focus on functionality over security
   - Impact: any firmware using Tianocore DHCP code vulnerable unless patched
   - Lesson: reference implementations used as-is by multiple vendors; security bugs propagate widely

16. **Firmware Supply Chain Vulnerabilities**:
   - Component origin: BMC, AMT, SMM code from CPU vendors; other controllers from third-party manufacturers
   - Firmware updates: third-party component firmware often unupdatable; vendor proprietary; no visibility
   - Compilation: code compiled without security flags (NX, ASLR, stack canaries); no exploit protections
   - Age: firmware dated; years since compilation; pre-dates modern security practices
   - Consequence: third-party component compromise enables system compromise; supply chain weak link
   - Example: Super Micro firmware updates affecting all servers; third-party firmware updates via BMC

17. **Firmware Cover Story and Pre-Positioning**:
   - Strategy: vendors release firmware updates weeks before public disclosure of vulnerability
   - Narrative: "performance optimization," "cache behavior improvement," "microcode update"
   - Purpose: enable internal testing, pre-position fixes, avoid surprise at disclosure deadline
   - Risk: attacker can analyze firmware deltas; identify vulnerability from patch comparison
   - Deployment: cover story patches applied widely without revealing vulnerability; patch rollback prevents exploitation

18. **Firmware Network Capabilities and Attack Surface**:
   - TCP/IP stack: Tianocore reference; vendors build on top; enables network boot (PXE/DHCP)
   - HTTP boot: downloads UEFI app or ISO; HTTPS variant for security
   - SMTP: email capability from firmware; requires network access
   - WiFi/Bluetooth: pre-OS network connectivity; enables management access before OS boots
   - Consequence: network-accessible firmware attack surface; no OS firewall protections applicable
   - Remote management: BMC, AMT, IPMI all network-accessible; default routing in many data centers

19. **BIOS/Firmware Update Strategies and Risks**:
   - Manual updates: users skip BIOS updates (historically tedious, risky)
   - Automated checking: pre-OS checks for newer version; user-initiated or scheduled update
   - Rollback protection: write protection prevents downgrade; security ratchet mechanism
   - Recovery mechanism: recovery image stored on separate flash; enables factory reset
   - Risk: automated update without staging increases attack surface; immediate application of update

20. **Data Center Network Segmentation and Attack Scenarios**:
   - Typical topology: management network (BMC/AMT) separated from host network
   - Assumption: management network isolated; attackers cannot reach it
   - Failure case: misconfiguration allows management network access from host network
   - Compromise scenario: host OS compromise enables pivot to management network; BMC compromise enables host OS control
   - Bidirectional risk: host OS access via host network + BMC access via management network = symmetric compromise
   - Enterprise scale: data center with thousands of servers; single exploitable firmware vulnerability affects all
   - Persistence: firmware compromise survives OS reinstall, disk wipe, password reset

**Defense & Takeaways**

Defending firmware components and management interfaces against remote exploitation and persistence: (1) Firmware baseline monitoring—establish firmware checksums/hashes of BIOS, BMC, microcode; detect unauthorized modifications; verify vendor signatures; (2) Network segmentation—strictly isolate management networks (BMC, IPMI, AMT) from host networks; no cross-segment routing; air-gap if possible; (3) Firmware update signing—require cryptographic signature verification; disable unsigned firmware execution; enforce chain of trust; (4) Default credential elimination—change all default BMC, AMT, BIOS passwords; enforce strong authentication; (5) IPMI hardening—disable IPMI where not required; require authentication for all operations; disable cipher suite weaknesses; (6) HTTP to HTTPS transition—firmware update mechanisms must use HTTPS; no plaintext HTTP for firmware download; (7) Certificate pinning—pin HTTPS certificates for firmware servers; prevent man-in-the-middle; (8) Disable unnecessary network protocols—disable SMTP, WiFi, Bluetooth from BIOS if not required; reduce attack surface; (9) Hardware debugging control—restrict physical debug port access; Closed Chassis Adapter requires physical access; XTP/USB3 debug vulnerable to physical compromise; (10) Firmware update validation—implement staged firmware updates; validate new firmware before boot; recovery mechanism if update corrupts; (11) SMM protection—enforce SMM Code Access Check (SMRR); prevent DMA attacks; isolate SMM from DMA devices; (12) Microcode verification—validate CPU microcode signature; prevent backdoor microcode insertion; (13) UEFI Secure Boot enforcement—sign boot loaders; prevent unsigned OS loading; maintain chain of trust; (14) TPM integration—store firmware measurements in TPM; detect tampering; attest firmware integrity remotely; (15) Firmware audit logging—enable firmware logging of configuration changes; authenticate log writes; prevent log tampering; (16) Supply chain verification—verify firmware binaries from third-party component vendors; no unsigned code; validate compilation environment; (17) Exploit protection hardening—enable ASLR, NX, stack canaries in firmware code; recompile with security flags; (18) Firmware update patching—apply UEFI Tianocore patches promptly (DHCP buffer overflow example); validate vendors release patches; (19) Management protocol disabling—disable IPMI, ICMP, IMPI bridges where not required; limit access to privileged users; (20) Incident response procedures—firmware compromise requires out-of-band recovery; maintain recovery media; prepare secure BIOS recovery process. The critical insight: firmware represents blind spot in modern security; isolated from OS-level monitoring; often unpatched, unupdatable, full hardware access. Remote attack vectors ubiquitous: HTTP firmware update checking over plaintext HTTP; IPMI authentication bypasses; AMT web interface vulnerabilities. Pre-OS code execution enables SMM privilege (ring -2) exploitation; compromise survives OS reinstall. Network-accessible firmware contradicts data center isolation assumptions; management network compromise enables symmetric OS compromise. Reference implementation vulnerabilities propagate widely: Tianocore DHCP buffer overflow affects multiple vendors; no vendor-specific fix needed. Vendor extensions beyond reference implementation double attack surface: HTTP boot (HP), WiFi (AMI), Bluetooth (AMI), SMTP; each custom implementation introduces unique vulnerabilities. Buffer overflow in pre-OS code enables arbitrary SMM execution: ASUS/ASROCK firmware update vulnerability demonstrates classic memory safety bugs in firmware context. Hardware debugging challenges limit firmware security research: XTP/Closed Chassis Adapter/USB3 debug required; constrains researcher community. The broader lesson: firmware security lagging OS security by decade; no standard security practices, exploit protections, or update mechanisms. Vendor fragmentation: three major firmware vendors (ASUS, ASROCK, HP) implement update checking three different ways; standardization necessary. Supply chain risk amplified: third-party component firmware often proprietary, unupdatable, unverifiable; backdoor risk. Management interface design prioritizes functionality over security: blanket remote access (KVM, power control, firmware update) enables wholesale compromise. The asymmetry: defender must patch all firmware variants; attacker needs exploit for single model. Network-accessible firmware fundamentally problematic: attack surface unavoidable; defense must focus on authentication, encryption, and signature verification. The future: firmware security requires standardized update mechanisms, exploit protections, and monitoring; currently missing across industry. Hardware debug access (physical) controls firmware security: XTP/Closed Chassis ports enable firmware modification; physical security essential. Firmware compromise persistence (SMM, BIOS survives OS wipe) demands architectural change: trusted boot, firmware attestation, secure recovery mechanisms required.

talks.title: No Royal Road … Notes on Dangerous Game
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning No Royal Road … Notes on Dangerous Game.
talks.summary:
Overview:
A cybersecurity researcher, historian, and reverse engineer associated with BlackHoodie presents a critical evaluation of nation-state threat attribution, threat hunting metaphors, and the geopolitical realities of the commercial cyber intelligence industry. Drawing on philosophical frameworks from Karl Marx's Das Kapital and Ernest Hemingway's writings on dangerous game, the speaker deconstructs the conventional 'hunter versus hunted' paradigm. The presentation examines the myth of vendor neutrality, covert state-industry information sharing, and the severe human consequences of targeted surveillance operations against activists.

Key Topics:
- Deconstructing conventional threat intelligence constructs: the limitations of the 'hunter and game' dynamic
- Challenging the neutrality of private antivirus vendors and threat intelligence firms in nation-state tracking
- Covert intelligence backchannels, withholding behavior, and coordinated disclosure with home governments
- The operational realities of targeted commercial spyware: Citizen Lab investigations and human rights targets

Technical Details:
The speaker critiques the prevailing conceptual models used in commercial threat hunting, highlighting how simplistic metaphors obscure the operational realities of nation-state conflict. Referencing Karl Marx's dictum from Das Kapital that there is 'no royal road to science,' the presentation emphasizes that rigorous cyber threat attribution requires deep contextual, historical, and geopolitical analysis rather than superficial technical indicators. Similarly, invoking Ernest Hemingway's ethical principle from Notes on Dangerous Game—that one must be prepared to shoot oneself out of the trouble one shoots into—the talk warns against over-eagerness and political naivety in public nation-state attribution campaigns.

The presentation challenges the long-standing industry assumption that commercial cybersecurity firms and antivirus vendors operate as disinterested, globally neutral arbiters. In practice, private intelligence firms maintain close, formalized relationships with intelligence agencies and law enforcement within their home jurisdictions. Citing investigative reporting by Chris Bing and public disclosures regarding Microsoft's confidential pre-notifications to the United States government, the speaker illustrates that threat intelligence dissemination is heavily shaped by domestic legal regimes and national interests. Vendors frequently exhibit 'withholding behavior,' delaying public reporting or staggering signature deployment to facilitate state operations or navigate political sensitivities, demonstrating that private firms rarely operate with true geopolitical independence.

The talk further explores how adversarial constructs collapse when tracking targeted surveillance malware against civilian targets. Examining investigations conducted by the Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto's Munk School, the speaker highlights the case of Emirati human rights activist Ahmed Mansoor. Mansoor was subjected to repeated cyber espionage campaigns employing commercial lawful interception suites developed by FinFisher, Hacking Team, and NSO Group (Pegasus). While Mansoor's cooperation with security researchers yielded landmark technical disclosures, the real-world outcome underscores the extreme asymmetry of nation-state targeting, as Mansoor was ultimately arrested and imprisoned by state authorities despite technical mitigations.

Key Takeaways:
Cybersecurity analysts and threat intelligence practitioners must incorporate geopolitical and historical context into malware attribution rather than relying strictly on technical telemetry. Security teams should recognize that commercial threat intelligence reports reflect the domestic legal obligations and national security alignments of their reporting vendors. Organizations protecting civil society and high-risk individuals must combine technical defense with operational security, recognizing that commercial spyware poses existential physical risks that software patches alone cannot neutralize.

talks.title: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the SBOM
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the SBOM.
talks.summary:
Overview: Every time you look at your inbox, there it is... SPAM! Your penis needs enlargement, a horny single girl from Russia "accidentally" emailed you, and a former Nigerian prince knows that you're just the man to safeguard his millions. But in 2007, while still a student at MIT, one particular kind caught my eye: stock spam. Those bizarre stock market "tips" that claim you should buy a particular stock because it's "about to go through the roof!!!!" Like most people, I initially thought nothing of t

Key Topics: hese ridiculous emails. That was until Kyle Vogt (now of Justin.tv) proposed the stupidest idea I had ever heard: "There has to be some way we can make money off these spammers". After trying, and failing, to prove Kyle wrong, the two of us embarked on a 4-month study into the dark depths of stock spam. In this talk, I'll explain how we went from hand-sorting tens of thousands of spam emails to developing a trading strategy able to take a piece of the spammers' profits. And how, in the process, our work produced data that disproved the results of nearly all the existing stock spam research.

talks.title: Finding Xori: Malware Analysis Triage with Automated Disassembly
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Finding Xori: Malware Analysis Triage with Automated Disassembly.
talks.summary:
## Overview

At Endgame, security teams face the challenge of triaging millions of malware samples with very few reverse engineers. To solve this, researchers Amanda Rousseau ("malware unicorn") and Rich Seymour developed **Xori** (referred to phonetically as "Zori" in the talk), an automated disassembly and triage framework designed for bulk processing. Started approximately six months prior to the presentation and comprising roughly 36,000 lines of code, the project is open-sourced under the AGPLv3 license. 

The project originated from evaluating existing disassemblers (including Capstone, Radare2, IDA Pro, Hopper, and Binary Ninja) against requirements for stability, cross-platform support (macOS, Windows, Linux), readable output, and automation capability. While Radare2 suffered frequent segfaults and other tools varied in price or automation readiness, Capstone provided high performance and LLVM/GDB header roots. Taking the best attributes from existing tooling and light emulation in QEMU, the team chose to implement Xori entirely in **Rust** for its memory safety, compiler-enforced correctness, and execution speed.

---

## Core Features and Architecture

Xori currently supports x86 (32-bit) and 64-bit architectures, targeting both Portable Executable (PE) files and x86 shellcode. Its architecture includes several dedicated components:

* **Custom PE Parser and Loader:** The team rolled their own parser to extract standard loading metadata as well as obscure artifacts (such as DOS stubs) across PE32 and PE32+ formats. The loader reconstructs the image into memory with configurable base addresses for the stack, DLLs, and system structures.
* **Memory Management:** Xori segregates memory ranges (image, stack, and dynamically added regions) to prevent out-of-bounds reads and safely handle invalid address references.
* **Dual Emulation Modes:**
  * *Light Emulation:* Default, performant mode that handles stack argument tracking during function calls and dynamically unpacks inline stack strings (similar to FLARE library behaviors).
  * *Full Emulation:* Slower mode intended for unpacking or specialized PE loading routines.
* **Dynamic Environment Simulation (TEB/PEB):** Thread Environment Blocks (TEB) and Process Environment Blocks (PEB) are serialized directly into bytes using Rust structs. This allows Xori to emulate dynamic Windows API resolution (e.g., shellcode traversing `FS:[0x30]`) and resolve calls like `LoadLibraryA` even when absent from static import tables.
* **Configurable Symbols and JSON Output:** Windows DLL export offsets can be supplied via large JSON files to map specific OS environments (Windows XP, 7, 10). Output is serialized into machine-readable JSON for integration into pipelines.

---

## Analysis Techniques and Disassembly Logic

Accurately mapping control flow and distinguishing code from data relies on several core heuristics:

* **Code vs. Data Separation:** The engine detects padding following non-returning calls (e.g., runtime initialization routines like VB5 main structures) and recognizes standard compiler padding patterns (e.g., `0xCC` int3 padding from Visual Studio). Non-returning blocks are treated as data rather than disassembled code.
* **Queue-Based Branch Traversal:** To evaluate branches, Xori prioritizes execution flow using a work queue. Jump branches are pushed to the top of the queue for immediate analysis, while non-jump (fall-through) branches are placed at the back. Currently, this path enumeration runs specifically over the `.text` section.
* **Loop Short-Circuiting:** To prevent infinite analysis loops during light emulation, Xori tracks loop iterations and terminates execution after reaching a configurable threshold (e.g., 4,000 loops).
* **Pattern Matching:** Function headers and signatures are evaluated using Rust's `regex::bytes` (byte regex), enabling IDA-style FLIRT/FLARE pattern matching across raw binary sequences.

talks.title: Great Algorithms Do Not Always Make Great Products
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Great Algorithms Do Not Always Make Great Products.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Jonathan Rivers, Chief Technology Officer at 3Pillar Global, delivers an executive-level analysis on the product engineering and commercial realities of cybersecurity software development. Drawing historical parallels to William Gibson's Neuromancer and examining a crowded market of over 2,000 security vendors, Rivers addresses the fundamental disconnect between cutting-edge algorithms and commercially viable products. The presentation outlines the strategic pitfalls that transform promising cybersecurity startups into stagnant 'zombie companies' and presents a three-pillar framework for achieving sustainable product-market fit.

Key Topics:
- Market dynamics in enterprise cybersecurity: overcoming crowded ecosystems and lengthy procurement cycles
- The 'AI algorithm trap': why superior machine learning models fail to translate into successful commercial products
- The phenomenon of 'zombie companies' and vulnerability to incumbent platform feature commoditization
- Three core pillars for software product success: data-driven decision making, customer centricity, and minimizing time to value

Technical Details:
Rivers analyzes the structural friction between technical cybersecurity innovation and commercial enterprise procurement. With more than 2,000 active security vendors and hundreds of new startups launching annually, the market is characterized by severe fragmentation where no single vendor or technological concept dominates the entire defense spectrum. Startups frequently develop innovative machine learning models or proprietary algorithms to analyze security log streams, operating under the assumption that novel intellectual property guarantees commercial success. However, enterprise cybersecurity buyers—specifically CISOs, CIOs, and corporate procurement offices—operate via slow, deliberate Request for Proposal (RFP) processes and risk-averse purchasing committees that prioritize integration, governance, and usability over theoretical algorithmic superiority.

Startups that over-index on algorithm design while neglecting end-to-end product architecture frequently stall, becoming what Rivers terms 'zombie companies.' These organizations retain a modest initial customer base but experience stagnant revenue growth, failing to secure follow-on venture funding or achieve an acquisition. Because their technology remains an unintegrated point solution rather than a holistic product, large enterprise platform bundlers inevitably replicate their core algorithmic functionality into broader product suites, commoditizing the standalone technology. Rivers highlights that the primary failure point occurs in the transition from data ingestion and machine learning processing to actionable, operational workflows that deliver concrete security outcomes.

To circumvent this lifecycle stagnation, Rivers outlines a three-step engineering framework. First, teams must implement data-driven decision-making by embedding comprehensive product analytics into application architectures. Rather than relying on executive intuition or subjective hunches, software leaders must track granular feature usage, identifying whether customer engagement is concentrated in a tiny fraction of features (such as 75% of users utilizing only one capability) and pruning neglected code. Second, engineering teams must maintain relentless customer centricity, designing interfaces around operational pain points rather than technical complexity. Third, startups must aggressively minimize time to value (TTV), deploying lightweight, usable increments that rapidly demonstrate measurable security enhancements and generate recurring enterprise revenue.

Key Takeaways:
Cybersecurity startups and product teams must avoid over-investing in raw algorithmic complexity at the expense of user experience and workflow integration. Product roadmaps must be governed by embedded product analytics and measurable customer usage data rather than subjective developer opinions or market hype. Engineering organizations must prioritize minimizing time to value, delivering fast, operational capabilities that solve immediate operational challenges before platform incumbents commoditize their features.

talks.title: Holding on for Tonight: Addiction in InfoSec
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Holding on for Tonight: Addiction in InfoSec.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Jamie, an information security and compliance professional with 17 years of experience in trust and safety and six years of sobriety, delivers a candid presentation at Black Hat USA on addiction and Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) in the infosec community. Highlighting the pervasive drinking culture at cybersecurity conferences and corporate events, the speaker deconstructs common misconceptions surrounding substance abuse. She offers practical strategies for organizations, event organizers, and colleagues to foster inclusive, psychologically safe environments that support individuals in recovery.

Key Topics:
- Epidemiological data on Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) and neurobiological disease mechanisms
- Industry-specific stressors contributing to substance abuse: on-call rotations, incident response, and cognitive burnout
- Dispelling addiction myths: lack of willpower versus complex biological, environmental, and neurological factors
- Concrete workplace and conference adaptations: "Friends of Bill W." spaces, equal-tier mocktails, and supportive management

Technical Details:
Citing data from the 2016 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, Jamie points out that 14.6 million American adults (5.9% of the population, or approximately 1 in 17 individuals) suffer from Alcohol Use Disorder. The speaker debunks the harmful myth that addiction stems merely from a lack of self-control or moral failure. Drawing from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), she explains that AUD and substance use disorders are chronic, relapsing brain diseases that physically alter neural structure and cognitive function, behaving biologically like diabetes or cardiovascular disease. While genetic predispositions and biological factors establish vulnerability, high-stress occupational environments serve as potent external catalysts.

Within the cybersecurity sector, occupational conditions exacerbate addiction risks: high-stakes on-call rotations, unrelenting incident response pressure, chronic context switching, and extended analytical troubleshooting create prolonged mental fatigue. Compounding these demands is an industry culture where alcohol is heavily integrated into professional networking, conference social events, and vendor happy hours. Jamie outlines how this creates significant barriers for professionals in recovery, who often fear career repercussions if they disclose their sobriety. To dismantle these barriers, she recommends actionable organizational measures: ensuring employee assistance programs provide functional mental wellness resources; organizing dedicated, sign-posted "Friends of Bill W." (Alcoholics Anonymous) recovery meetings in quiet rooms during conferences like Black Hat and DEF CON; and designing event menus with creative, equal-tier non-alcoholic signature drinks (such as smoothies or craft mocktails) served without stigmatizing garnishes or secondary-citizen glassware.

Key Takeaways:
Enterprise leadership and conference organizers must actively decouple professional networking and celebrations from mandatory alcohol consumption. Event planners should establish safe spaces for recovery meetings and provide quality non-alcoholic beverage options that normalize sober participation. Managers and peers should practice empathetic listening without probing personal medical disclosures, recognizing that sustainable incident response operations require proactive mental wellness support rather than reliance on unhealthy coping mechanisms.

talks.summary: Edge Side Includes (ESI) Injection: Exploiting Caching Servers for Session Hijacking and SSRF **Overview** Security researcher Louis Jamison (GoSecure, Montreal) presents Edge Side Includes (ESI) injection attacks targeting ESI-enabled caching servers, demonstrating session hijacking via HTTP-only cookie theft, arbitrary cache rewriting, and server-side request forgery (SSRF). Research originally discovered during security audit of large Montreal ISP's caching infrastructure. ESI is 17-year-old standard (2001 specification) enabling fine-grained cache invalidation at sub-page level; allows application servers to mark webpage fragments for independent caching logic (weather forecast updates hourly; labels cache permanently). Problem: ESI markup evaluated by caching server without input validation; vulnerable to injection attacks analogous to XSS. Attack vectors: (1) ESI variable injection leaking HTTP-only cookies (Apache Traffic Server, Oracle Web Cache); (2) ESI include overwriting cached files (Oracle Web Cache online tag); (3) SSRF via ESI includes to internal services. Core vulnerability: no distinction between legitimate ESI tags (from application server) and injected malicious tags (from attacker payload). Defense bypass: Apache Traffic Server cookie whitelisting circumventable via HTTP header variable. Demonstrated exploits: (1) Traffic Server: injected ESI comment referencing HTTP cookies; victim browser requests attacker server with session ID as filename; (2) Oracle Web Cache: ESI online tag overwrites jQuery cached file; injected AJAX payload sends victims' cookies to attacker. HTTP-only cookie bypass: traditional session theft requires JavaScript; ESI injection works without JavaScript. Detection: ESI comment-based detection (ESI tags consumed, non-ESI tags returned); manual testing or scanner support (Burp Suite, Acunetix, Akamai). Mitigation: OWASP CRS HTML entity encoding, proactive escaping of user input, CloudFlare Workers as safer alternative (JavaScript-based fragment assembly instead of server-side markup). Affected implementations: Apache Traffic Server, Oracle Web Cache, Squid, Varnish, Fastly, Akamai, IBM Commerce Server, and others. Research scope: six ESI implementations analyzed; null pointer dereferences, header injection bypasses, filter evasion discovered. **Technical Details** Edge Side Includes Architecture, Injection Mechanisms, and Cache Manipulation: 1. **ESI Purpose and Cache Fragmentation**: - Problem solved: monolithic webpage caching; changing one element invalidates entire page - Solution: fragment markers; mark independent cache regions; individually invalidate fragments - Example: weather website with static labels and dynamic forecast; forecast cached hourly, labels cached indefinitely - Performance benefit: reduced full-page invalidations; better cache hit ratio - Implementation: XML-like tags (esi:include, esi:vars) in HTTP response; parsed by caching server 2. **ESI Fragment Markers and Syntax**: - Format: XML-prefixed tags (esi:include, esi:inline, esi:choose, esi:vars, esi:comment) - Parsing requirement: HTTP Surrogate declares ESI support; application server must mark response with ESI-enabled header - Typical deployment: enabled by default; any response containing esi: tags processed - Injection ease: no input validation distinguishing legitimate from injected tags - Bypass: some implementations check for Surrogate-Control header; often not enforced 3. **ESI Includes (esi:include Tag)**: - Functionality: replace tag with content from specified URL; URL resolved by caching server - Cache behavior: if included resource cached, use cache entry; otherwise fetch from origin - Request flow: client requests page1 → cache miss → origin responds with esi:include tag → cache fetches page2 → concatenates response → returns to client - Scope: includes can reference any whitelisted server (or any server if whitelist not enforced) - Security: enables SSRF if attacker can control include URL 4. **ESI Variables (esi:vars Tag)**: - Functionality: attribute-less tags expanding HTTP transaction metadata - Available variables: HTTP user agent, query string, cookies, HTTP headers, custom variables - Use case: conditional caching based on client properties (language cookie → fetch French vs. English content) - Syntax: $(HTTP_HEADER{Cookie}) expands to cookie value - Vulnerability: leaks sensitive HTTP headers; HTTP-only cookies exposed 5. **Apache Traffic Server ESI Implementation**: - Deployment: used by major ISPs (Comcast confirmed, others likely) - Specification compliance: implements full ESI specification plus extensions - Cookie whitelisting: feature to restrict cookie access (cookie-named whitelist); bypass via HTTP header variable $(HTTP_HEADER{Cookie}) - Vuln erability: header variable not restricted; whitelist easily bypassed - Exploit: ESI injection → inject esi:var referencing HTTP_HEADER{Cookie} → expanded to cookie value → leaks HTTP-only cookie 6. **Oracle Web Cache ESI Implementation**: - Extensions: beyond-spec features including esi:inline, esi:online tags - esi:inline danger: arbitrary cache entry overwrite; powerful manipulation capability - Syntax: content overwrites cache entry "filename" - No whitelisting: any file name writable; application assets (jQuery, JS libraries) targetable - Consequence: injected payload in cache entry; served to all users requesting that file 7. **Session Hijacking via ESI Cookie Leakage**: - Attack scenario: vulnerable website with user input reflected in HTTP response - Injection: attacker crafts esi:var payload referencing HTTP cookies - Victim trigger: victim visits attacker's payload (forum post, comment); cache processes ESI tag - Cookie expansion: esi:var expanded to session cookie value; injected into image src attribute - Browser request: victim's browser requests image from attacker server; sends session cookie as URL parameter - No JavaScript required: browser makes request automatically (unlike XSS); HTTP-only cookie leaked 8. **Apache Traffic Server Cookie Hijacking Proof-of-Concept**: - Payload: - Injection vector: user input reflected in HTML (message board example) - Attacker self-test: attacker injects own payload; browser makes request with own session ID - Victim execution: victim views message containing payload; browser requests attacker server with victim's session ID - Attacker access: replacement of own cookie with victim's cookie; session takeover 9. **Oracle Web Cache File Overwriting via esi:online**: - Vulnerability: esi:online tag overwrites arbitrary cache entries - Target: jQuery.js or other JavaScript library cached globally - Payload: malicious_code - Scope: every user requesting jQuery.js receives malicious version - Injection vector: user input without HTML encoding; ESI parsing happens despite encoding 10. **HTML Encoding Bypass for ESI Injection**: - Mitigation attempt: HTML entity encoding (< becomes <, > becomes >) - ESI circumvention: flexible parser syntax; quotes optional; unquoted attribute values parsed - Bypass example: - Lesson: HTML entity encoding insufficient; ESI engines parse before HTML decoding - Proper mitigation: filter ESI tags before encoding; content-type aware filtering 11. **Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via ESI Includes**: - Mechanism: esi:include with URL controlled by attacker - Scope restriction: most ESI implementations whitelist allowed hosts; some allow any host - Squid, Node-ESI allow unrestricted includes; bypass whitelist via crafted URLs - Internal network access: cache server requests internal-only URLs; proxy through cache - Data exfiltration: sensitive responses from internal services returned to attacker via cache entry 12. **JSON Response Injection for SSRF**: - Attack: inject esi:include tag into JSON response (unsanitized API endpoint) - Content-type: JSON has no reason for HTML encoding; browsers ignore it - ESI parsing: caching server evaluates esi:include regardless of content-type - Proof: fetch internal API (e.g., /api/admin/status) via injected include; response concatenated into JSON - Example: {"data": ""} 13. **Manual ESI Detection Techniques**: - ESI comment test: send test; if removed, indicates ESI parsing - Payload echo-back: send test; if echoed, not ESI; if removed, likely ESI - Positive confirmation: combine with variable expansion; - Response comparison: baseline response vs. payload response; compare for sign of parsing 14. **Automated ESI Detection in Security Scanners**: - Burp Suite Active Scanner Plus: implements ESI heuristics; comment-based detection - Acunetix: similar detection mechanisms; ESI comment removal detection - Scanner limitations: may not detect all variants; false negatives possible - Burp Collaborator: out-of-band detection; hit Collaborator server via ESI include 15. **CloudFlare Workers as Modern ESI Alternative**: - Safer model: JavaScript execution in edge workers; fragment assembly programmatic - Fragment delivery: fragments sent via HTTP headers; not in response body - HTTP Response Injection: nearly impossible (headers unsigned, but harder than body injection) - Security improvement: fragments not in response; no injection attack surface - Deployment: requires CloudFlare; not universally available; trade-off for security 16. **ESI Whitelist Bypasses**: - Apache Traffic Server: cookie whitelist bypassable via HTTP_HEADER variable - Cookie naming: variable names explicitly whitelisted; HTTP_HEADER{Cookie} treats Cookie as generic header name - Lesson: whitelisting complex; specific restrictions (e.g., "allow only HTTP_HEADER{X-Custom}") required - Alternate names: some implementations allow alternative header names (HTTP_COOKIE vs. Cookie) 17. **Caching Server Implementations and Vulnerability Patterns**: - Apache Traffic Server: widely deployed; multiple vulnerability patterns - Oracle Web Cache: powerful extension (esi:online) increases exploitation impact - Squid: flexible ESI; allows unrestricted includes; SSRF vulnerability - Varnish: ESI support via modules; variable handling - Fastly: CDN-level ESI; potentially affecting high-traffic sites - Akamai: major CDN; ESI implementation details less public - IBM Commerce Server: used by e-commerce platforms; likely ESI vulnerable 18. **Real-World ESI Deployment Findings**: - Newspaper organizations: early web-enabled sites (pre-2010) retain ESI; large attack surface - Legacy systems: ESI persists despite modern alternatives (CloudFlare, etc.) - Bug bounty programs: ESI injection reports received by major vendors; exploits confirmed - Hidden usage: ESI not advertised; organizations unaware of deployment - Obscurity risk: lack of documentation and visibility; unmaintained by teams 19. **Defense: OWASP CRS (ModSecurity Core Rule Set)**: - Approach: HTML entity encoding of user input via WAF - Mechanism: esi: prefixed tags encoded; < becomes <; parser cannot interpret - Prerequisite: same character set (UTF-8, ASCII); encoding must be compatible - Scope limitation: only protects if HTML encoding applied; JSON responses not covered 20. **Proactive Escaping Strategy**: - Philosophy: filter ESI tags based on content-type awareness - JSON responses: no need for HTML encoding; block esi: tags directly - HTML responses: encode (or deny) ESI tags; validate against ESI grammar - Input validation: whitelist acceptable characters; reject control characters - Output encoding: context-aware; different for HTML, JSON, XML - Testing: fuzzing with ESI payloads; detection + prevention validation **Defense & Takeaways** Defending against ESI injection attacks in caching infrastructure: (1) Disable ESI if unused—if ESI functionality not required, disable in cache configuration; removes attack vector entirely; (2) Input validation—filter user-controlled input; reject esi: prefixed content; whitelist acceptable characters; (3) Output encoding—HTML entity encode user input if reflected; context-aware encoding for JSON/XML; (4) ModSecurity CRS—deploy OWASP Core Rule Set; encode HTML entities; validate HTTP headers; (5) WAF filtering—block esi: tag patterns at WAF level; prevent injection before cache server; (6) Content-type awareness—treat JSON differently from HTML; apply appropriate filters per content-type; (7) Cookie protection—use Secure flag on cookies; enable HttpOnly; restrict cookie scope to origin; (8) HTTPOnly enforcement—ensure session cookies marked HTTPOnly; prevents JavaScript-based exfiltration (though ESI bypasses this); (9) Cache invalidation—implement proper cache keys; prevent collision of user inputs with cache entries; (10) Header whitelisting—if using ESI variables, explicitly whitelist allowed headers; reject HTTP_HEADER access by default; (11) Variable restrictions—restrict esi:vars access; prevent expansion of sensitive variables (cookies, auth headers); (12) Include whitelist—enforce strict whitelist of allowed include URLs; reject dynamic URL generation; (13) Regular expressions—use regex to detect esi: patterns; block at earliest stage; (14) Logging and alerting—log ESI injection attempts; alert on detected patterns; correlate with cache misses; (15) Scanning tests—regularly test for ESI injection vulnerability; include in security testing protocols; (16) Vendor updates—apply security patches from cache vendors; monitor advisory databases; (17) Disable extensions—disable vendor-specific ESI extensions if not used (oracle:inline); reduce attack surface; (18) Separate development—isolate cache configuration from application code; prevent accidental ESI exposure; (19) Documentation review—audit all caching deployments; document ESI usage; identify unnecessary implementations; (20) Incident response—if ESI injection detected, revoke affected cookies; rotate session tokens; audit cache entries for malicious modifications. The critical insight: ESI injection parallels XSS but operates at cache layer, not browser layer; attacks invisible to traditional web application firewalls. Caching servers treat ESI tags as metadata, not content; no input validation distinguishing injected from legitimate tags. HTTP-only cookie bypass fundamental: browser automatically sends cookies in requests; ESI variable expansion exfiltrates cookies without JavaScript. File overwriting via esi:online demonstrates privilege escalation: arbitrary cache entry modification affects all users requesting modified resource. Whitelist bypasses common: cookie whitelisting in Apache Traffic Server bypassed via HTTP_HEADER variable; generic restriction inadequate. The broader lesson: caching infrastructure introduces new attack surface; developers often unaware of cache configuration; legacy ESI deployments persist due to organizational inertia. Seventeen-year-old specification (2001 ESI) shows vendor implementation divergence; no unified security model. Vendor extensions beyond spec (Oracle esi:online, Apache cookie whitelisting) add complexity; each extension introduces unique vulnerabilities. Input validation absent: cache servers accept ESI tags without validating source; differentiation impossible (intentional design limitation). SSRF potential: unrestricted ESI includes enable internal network access; scope restrictions often unenforced. Modern alternatives (CloudFlare Workers) demonstrate safer approach: fragment delivery via headers rather than response body; injection attack surface reduced. Obscurity provides false security: ESI ubiquitous but underdocumented; organizations unaware of deployment; no prioritized updates. The asymmetry: attacker needs single vulnerable cache configuration; defender must secure all cache implementations in infrastructure. Detection difficulty: ESI injection often invisible to application logs; cache-level processing hides attack. The risk: session hijacking without JavaScript; file overwriting affects all users; SSRF enables internal network exploration. Mitigation complexity: addressing requires understanding of cache architecture, ESI specification, and content-type semantics. The future: ESI likely to decline (CloudFlare Workers replace it); but legacy deployments persist for years; long tail of vulnerable systems.

talks.title: A Dive in to Hyper-V Architecture & Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding A Dive in to Hyper-V Architecture & Vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Joe and Nicolas Economou from the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) explore the internal architecture and guest-to-host attack surface of Microsoft Hyper-V. Motivated by Microsoft's high-tier bug bounty payouts—offering up to $250,000 for remote code execution in the hypervisor—the speakers demystify Hyper-V's partition model and isolation boundaries. The presentation details how hypercalls, virtual devices, and kernel-mode virtualization service providers interact, providing vulnerability researchers with concrete entry points for hypervisor security research.

Key Topics:
- Architectural separation between the Hyper-V standalone hypervisor and the root partition.
- Inter-partition communication mechanisms including hypercalls, traps, and GPADL.
- Categorization of guest-to-host attack surfaces: VDevs, VSPs, and Integration Components.
- Trade-offs between legacy emulated hardware and high-performance para-virtualized devices.

Technical Details:
Unlike virtualization stacks where the hypervisor operates within the host operating system's kernel, Hyper-V's hypervisor is a standalone binary executing in its own distinct physical and virtual address spaces. Guest partitions cannot access hypervisor memory directly. The hypervisor is primarily responsible for configuring Extended Page Tables (EPT/SLAT), programming virtualization hardware primitives, handling CPU intercepts, and processing hypercalls—the system call equivalent within virtualization. However, the core hypervisor binary itself exposes minimal guest-accessible attack surface, with the vast majority of actionable guest-to-host vulnerabilities residing in the root partition.

The root partition hosts the parent Windows operating system and possesses direct access to the physical memory of all child guest partitions. Because guests have zero direct access to underlying hardware, the root partition exposes services through three primary components. First, Virtual Devices (VDevs) reside in user mode within the root partition, providing either hardware emulation (such as a 25-year-old network interface operating via legacy I/O ports, motherboards, serial ports, or video cards) or para-virtualized functionality. Second, Virtualization Service Providers (VSPs) operate directly in host kernel mode to deliver high-performance para-virtualization for performance-critical subsystems, including storage, networking, video, and PCI devices. Third, Integration Components run in user mode alongside VDevs over dedicated communication channels.

To facilitate shared memory transfers without mapping arbitrary host addresses, Hyper-V relies on Guest Physical Address Descriptor Lists (GPADLs). Structurally analogous to Windows Memory Descriptor Lists (MDLs), a GPADL consists of a header followed by a list of guest physical addresses, allowing the guest to describe memory buffers for host operations. Because emulated hardware is inherently slow, attackers and researchers focus heavily on the high-performance para-virtualized VSPs and VDev channels, where complex parsing of guest physical descriptors and inter-partition ring buffers takes place.

Key Takeaways:
Hyper-V vulnerability research requires shifting focus away from the minimal core hypervisor binary toward user-mode VDevs and kernel-mode VSPs in the root partition. The para-virtualized interface—orchestrated via GPADLs and VMBus channels—represents the primary surface for guest-to-host escapes and host kernel compromise. System administrators and cloud architects must ensure hypervisor patches are rigorously deployed, while developers building virtualized drivers must validate all guest-supplied physical address descriptors against boundary violations and race conditions.
