talks.title: Chasing Foxes by the Numbers: Patterns of Life and Activity in Hacker Forums
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Chasing Foxes by the Numbers: Patterns of Life and Activity in Hacker Forums.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Christopher Ahlberg, co-founder and CEO of Recorded Future, presents a quantitative methodology for cyber threat attribution based on Pattern of Life (PoL) analysis and Activity-Based Intelligence (ABI) across dark web and underground hacker forums. Addressing scenarios where sophisticated threat actors practice rigorous operational security (OPSEC) and frequent "handle hopping" to avoid moniker-based tracking, Ahlberg demonstrates how mathematical modeling of forum metadata reveals distinct behavioral fingerprints. Analyzing a dataset of over 1.4 million forum participants across Russian, Chinese, Arabic, and Farsi communities, Ahlberg shows how temporal rhythms and event responses enable cross-persona attribution.

Key Topics:
- Limitations of moniker-based attribution and overcoming adversary "handle hopping"
- Activity-Based Intelligence (ABI) and Pattern of Life (PoL) analysis applied to forum metadata
- Temporal, cultural, and geopolitical activity signatures (diurnal curves, workweeks, religious holidays)
- Vector space mathematical clustering (42-dimensional weekly profiles) to correlate pseudonyms and actor hand-offs

Technical Details:
Ahlberg explains that traditional cyber threat intelligence attribution heavily relies on sloppy operational security, where actors reuse handles across domain registrations, social media, and technical forums (as documented in Mandiant's APT1 report tracking monikers like "UglyGorilla" and "CPYY"). However, when sophisticated adversaries practice "handle hopping"—analogous to radio frequency hopping, where actors switch monikers within and across forums—traditional string-based tracking fails. To overcome this, Recorded Future applies Pattern of Life analysis derived from counterterrorism and criminal investigative methodologies. By focusing purely on message metadata (timestamps, posting frequency, and interaction targets) across more than 100 underground forums comprising 1.4 million actors, analysts can profile adversaries without inspecting message content.

The author demonstrates that online human activity adheres to predictable diurnal and weekly rhythms. Baseline analysis reveals that forum activity mirrors standard sleep and work cycles. Across Chinese hacker forums (such as Blackhawk / Heishu), posting patterns show pronounced morning and afternoon work blocks separated by a distinct midday lunch dip. Russian criminal forums (e.g., Exploit.in) exhibit heavy night-time activity, indicating operators working after regular business hours or across multiple time zones (such as Moscow and Vladivostok). In contrast, Iranian forums (Ashiyane) reflect regional cultural work schedules, displaying peak activity on Saturdays and Sundays while dropping sharply during the Thursday afternoon and Friday weekend, with annual activity troughs occurring during the anniversary of the Islamic Revolution. Conversely, Arabic forums exhibit surges during Ramadan. Additionally, Ahlberg measures community reactions to external technical events: both Russian and Iranian exploit forums display sharp surges in vulnerability discussions on Wednesdays following Microsoft's Patch Tuesday.

To correlate separate handles belonging to the same actor, Ahlberg models an actor's temporal activity into a 42-dimensional vector (dividing each day of the week into six four-hour blocks). Applying statistical distance metrics and clustering algorithms reveals matching operational profiles across different user accounts. This mathematical modeling successfully identified pseudonym transitions: when a prominent actor ("Optimist" / "op_de_man") ceased posting, three new accounts ("peace of mind", "bank", and "happy eyes") immediately activated with statistically identical temporal profiles and topical affinities, establishing strong leads for attribution.

Key Takeaways:
Threat intelligence teams tracking disciplined threat actors must move beyond fragile moniker searches toward quantitative Pattern of Life analysis based on communication metadata. Analyzing temporal signatures, cultural workweeks, and responses to external events provides critical attribution telemetry that persists across handle changes. While adversaries can disrupt pattern analysis by introducing artificial random delays or operating in short, sporadic bursts of activity, maintaining longitudinal metadata datasets across underground forums remains an invaluable lead-generation mechanism for threat intelligence analysts and law enforcement.

talks.title: How to Fool an ADC, Part II or Hiding Destruction of Turbine with a Little Help of Signal Processing
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of How to Fool an ADC, Part II or Hiding Destruction of Turbine with a Little Help of Signal Processing.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Jose Miguel Moreno and Alexander Fornari (Harbor Lab, Madrid) presented practical attacks on analog-to-digital converters (ADCs)—critical components in industrial control systems (PLC, SCADA, ICS). Context: ADCs interface analog world (temperature, voltage, current sensors) with digital systems; compromise of ADC readings enables attacker to blind monitoring systems or inject false telemetry. Motivation: industrial systems increasingly targeted by sophisticated adversaries; safety systems rely on sensor accuracy—false readings enable attacks while fooling safety PLC (programmable logic controller). Research scope: examined 6 real devices (all using Sigma-Delta ADCs); discovered practical attack vectors: (1) amplitude attacks—injecting out-of-range voltages causing cross-channel interference, (2) frequency attacks—exploiting aliasing vulnerabilities when high-frequency signals exceed Nyquist limit. Significance: demonstrates feasibility of blind attack on safety-critical systems; attacker need not compromise PLC/network, only inject analog signals (achieved via physical proximity). Implications: ADC specifications/filtering insufficient alone; system designers must assume adversarial analog injection.

## ADC Architecture and Operational Principles

**ADC Definition and Role**: Analog-to-Digital Converter—passive electronic component translating analog world signals (voltages, currents) into digital values. Inputs: analog signals (continuously variable voltage from sensors). Outputs: discrete digital values (binary representation). Relationship: ADC bridges analog domain (physical world) and digital domain (computing systems). Example: temperature sensor outputs analog voltage proportional to temperature; ADC samples voltage, outputs digital value representing temperature.

**Key ADC Parameters**: Resolution (bit depth: 8, 12, 16-bit ADCs determine precision—12-bit = 4,096 possible values). Sampling rate (frequency at which ADC samples input signal). Reference voltage (maximum voltage range ADC can measure—e.g., 5V reference = 5V max input). Conversion type (successive-approximation, Sigma-Delta, pipeline—differ in speed/accuracy trade-offs).

**Multi-Channel ADCs**: Single IC contains multiple input channels (example: 8-channel ADC with independent voltage measurement capability per channel). Channels grouped into input-side (connected to analog signals) and output-side (serial interface to host computer). Example workflow: monitor system voltages (motor supply, heater supply, boiler control)—8 channels measure 8 independent voltages simultaneously; host computer queries ADC, receives values, makes control decisions.

**Physical Implementation**: ADC ICs in standardized packages (DIP, surface-mount). Channels exposed as accessible pins; host interfaces via serial bus (SPI, I2C) or parallel data bus. Real-world example: industrial monitoring board with 8-channel ADC, individual pins labeled for voltage inputs from different subsystems.

**Sampling Characteristics**: ADC samples input signal at regular intervals (determined by sampling frequency). Captured value held until next sample. Temporal representation: snapshots of continuously-varying analog world. Implication: sampling frequency must be sufficiently high to accurately represent signal dynamics.

## Aliasing and Nyquist Theorem

**Aliasing Definition**: Distortion artifact when signal not sampled at sufficient frequency. Result: reconstructed signal appears different from actual signal (false frequency representation). Example: visual aliasing in film (wagon wheels appearing to move backward due to frame rate misalignment with wheel rotation frequency).

**Nyquist Theorem**: Signal containing frequency components up to F_max must be sampled at minimum frequency 2*F_max (twice maximum frequency). Formula: sampling frequency ≥ 2 * maximum signal frequency. Example: 1 kHz signal requires minimum 2 kHz sampling rate. Practical: many systems sample at >2x Nyquist (safety margin for complex signals).

**Aliasing Attack Vector**: If attacker injects high-frequency signal above Nyquist limit (relative to ADC sampling rate), ADC undersamples signal, producing false low-frequency representation in output. Example: ADC sampling at 100 kHz can represent up to 50 kHz (Nyquist frequency). Attacker injects 75 kHz sine wave—ADC outputs false 25 kHz component (not present in actual signal).

**Anti-Aliasing Filters**: Analog low-pass filter placed before ADC input. Purpose: attenuate frequencies above Nyquist limit, preventing aliasing. Specification: filter cutoff frequency set to Nyquist frequency or slightly higher. Ideal filter: brick-wall response (completely blocks above cutoff, passes below). Real filters: gradual rolloff (pass band, transition band, stop band).

## Sigma-Delta ADC Architecture and Operation

**Sigma-Delta Design Concept**: Over-sampling ADC architecture. Key difference: samples signal at frequency much higher than Nyquist requirement (e.g., 20x Nyquist frequency). Purpose: achieve high accuracy with simple 1-bit quantization internally; digital filtering produces multi-bit output. Advantage: relaxed analog anti-aliasing filter requirements (wider bandwidth filter possible due to over-sampling).

**Internal Architecture Components**: (1) Modulator—continuously samples input signal at high frequency, performs 1-bit quantization (output = high/low bit stream), feeds back to input (negative feedback loop). Purpose: encode signal information in high-frequency bit stream. (2) Digital filter (low-pass)—filters over-sampled bit stream, removes high-frequency quantization noise, outputs final multi-bit digital value at lower output rate (decimation).

**Feedback Loop**: Internally-reconstructed estimate of signal fed back to modulator input; modulator compares input to estimate, outputs 1 if input > estimate, 0 if input < estimate. Feedback loop causes output to track input (delta-sigma feedback). Result: high-frequency bit stream whose density encodes signal amplitude.

**Quantization Noise Shaping**: Over-sampling + feedback loop pushes quantization noise to high frequencies (noise shaping). Digital filter attenuates high-frequency noise component. Net result: low-frequency signal accurately represented, high-frequency noise removed. Advantage: better signal-to-noise ratio than simpler ADC architectures at same resolution.

**Anti-Aliasing Filter in Sigma-Delta**: Due to over-sampling, filter requirement relaxed. Example: Sigma-Delta sampling at 200 MHz (20x nominal Nyquist for 10 MHz signal) requires filter cutoff only slightly above 10 MHz (no brick-wall requirement). Contrast: successive-approximation ADC at 20 MHz (2x Nyquist for 10 MHz signal) requires sharp filter cutoff at 10 MHz.

**Programmable Gain Amplifier (PGA)**: Optional feature in Sigma-Delta ADCs. Allows software-programmable amplification of input signal (1x, 2x, 4x gains). Purpose: acquire weak signals with better resolution (amplified signal uses more of ADC's quantization levels). Side effect: changing PGA gain shifts digital filter response (cutoff frequency changes with gain setting).

## Amplitude-Based ADC Attack

**Attack Concept**: Inject out-of-range voltage (exceeding ADC's rated input range) into one ADC channel; observe interference effects on other channels. Goal: demonstrate cross-channel crosstalk vulnerability. Attack assumption: attacker has physical access to ADC input pins or can inject via compromised sensor circuit.

**Test Setup**: Multi-channel ADC (e.g., 8-channel device) with external voltage supply connected to one channel; other channels connected to benign signal sources. Baseline: measure normal ADC output (all channels reading expected values). Attack: gradually increase injected voltage into one channel, monitor output changes on other channels.

**Attack Execution**: Connect external DC supply to ADC channel (e.g., channel 3 in examples). Supply programmable voltage (negative to positive, ramped gradually). Monitor ADC output for all channels simultaneously. Document voltage levels vs. output readings.

**Experimental Results**: Initial injection (small amplitude, e.g., 30 mV): no crosstalk observed—injected channel reads expected value, other channels unaffected. Moderate injection (100-200 mV): subtle interference appearing on neighboring channels (expected behavior from some isolation loss). High-amplitude injection (300+ mV): significant crosstalk observed—channels not directly connected to injection point show reading changes. Example: injecting negative voltage on channel 3 (out-of-range input) causes channels 1-2 to read different values than baseline.

**Cross-Channel Interference Mechanism**: ADC internal circuitry shares components (power rails, ground planes, substrate). Injection of large voltage creates electromagnetic disturbance affecting other channels. Current paths through shared substrate cause voltage drop, interfering with other channels' signal processing. Differential measurements: channel 2 baseline (2.3V) becomes 3.53V when channel 3 receives out-of-range injection—3.1V voltage shift purely from crosstalk.

**Practical Implication**: Attacker controlling one sensor (or injecting into one ADC channel) can corrupt readings from all other channels. Safety system monitoring multiple parameters (e.g., temperature, pressure, voltage) can be blinded by attacking single measurement channel. Example attack: inject excessive voltage on temperature channel; safety PLC sees corrupted temperature readings from multiple channels, potentially triggering false alarms or masking actual faults.

**Attack Feasibility**: Requires only waveform generator (affordable bench equipment or purpose-built device) and physical access to ADC inputs (via compromised sensor, exposed connector, or collocated attacker). No network access, exploitation, or PLC compromise necessary.

## Frequency-Based ADC Attack (Aliasing Exploitation)

**Attack Concept**: Exploit Sigma-Delta ADC's digital filter characteristics by injecting high-frequency signal that aliases into low-frequency output range. Goal: inject false low-frequency signal while ADC's output appears normal (frequency in accepted range).

**Digital Filter Frequency Response**: Sigma-Delta ADCs' digital filter exhibits band-pass behavior with defined cutoff frequency. At PGA gain setting G, cutoff frequency F_cutoff = F_base * G. Example: base cutoff 76 kHz, gain 1x; gain 2x → cutoff 152 kHz. Pass-band: frequencies below cutoff attenuated. Stop-band: frequencies above cutoff heavily attenuated. Transition: not brick-wall (gradual rolloff with non-ideal filter).

**Aliasing Exploitation Methodology**: (1) Identify ADC sampling frequency and digital filter cutoff. (2) Compute stop-band region (frequencies supposed to be blocked). (3) Inject signal at carefully chosen frequency in stop-band such that aliasing produces output in pass-band. (4) Attacker crafts frequency such that aliased component appears as false signal at target frequency.

**Mathematical Aliasing**: If ADC has effective sampling frequency F_s and receives input at frequency F_input > F_s/2, output contains aliased frequency: F_alias = |F_input - k*F_s| for appropriate integer k. Attacker selects F_input to produce desired F_alias.

**Experimental Attack Setup**: Equipment: function generator (creates programmable frequency signals), oscilloscope (measures signals), ADC device under test (Delta-Sigma type), data acquisition system. Signal path: function generator output → ADC input; measure both generator output (oscilloscope) and ADC output (digital readback). Sweep generator frequency across range (0 to several MHz), log ADC readings at each frequency.

**Attack Results**: Baseline (low-frequency input): ADC reads actual signal frequency accurately. Mid-range frequencies (within pass-band): ADC output follows input faithfully. Stop-band frequencies (>filter cutoff): expected behavior = ADC attenuates/blocks signal, output noise-like. Attack discovery: specific stop-band frequencies (e.g., 312.5 kHz in test example) produce unexpected clean sinusoidal output at false frequency (e.g., false 31 kHz component). Attacker-injected signal: 312.5 kHz sine wave (not present in system). ADC output: 31 kHz sine wave (false signal, appears legitimate).

**Why Aliasing Succeeds Against Sigma-Delta**: Digital filter not ideal—transition region contains partial pass-through before complete attenuation. Over-sampled bit stream from modulator contains energy at injected frequency. Digital filter partially attenuates but doesn't completely block. Aliasing mechanism: high-frequency component folds into low-frequency range via under-sampling in final decimation step. Net result: attacker's high-frequency injection appears as false low-frequency signal in output.

**PGA Gain Effect on Vulnerability**: Changing PGA gain shifts filter cutoff. Higher gain → higher cutoff frequency. Effect: stop-band region (frequencies subject to aliasing) changes. Attacker must recalculate aliasing frequencies when gain changes. Example: gain 1x (cutoff 76 kHz) vulnerable to different injection frequencies than gain 2x (cutoff 152 kHz).

## Attack Implications for Industrial Control Systems

**System Architecture Vulnerability**: Typical ICS/SCADA: physical process → sensors → ADC → PLC → decision logic → actuators. ADC blind-spot: if attacker corrupts ADC reading, PLC receives false telemetry, decisions based on false state. Safety system assuming ADC+PLC+network secure but overlooking analog attack surface.

**Attack Scenario Example**: Spinning motor monitoring system—speed sensor → ADC channel measures speed voltage. Safety PLC continuously monitors speed; if speed exceeds threshold, triggers emergency stop. Attacker injects 312.5 kHz signal into speed ADC channel → ADC outputs false 31 kHz component (not real motor speed). PLC interprets as legitimate motor running at false speed, issues wrong control commands. Actual motor may be running dangerously fast; false ADC reading masks reality. Operator monitoring sees PLC status "all green," unaware of actual hazard.

**Blind Attack Advantage**: Attacker achieves system compromise without: (1) network access, (2) PLC exploitation, (3) software modification, (4) insider knowledge of control logic. Only requirement: physical access to ADC inputs (accessible from outside secure perimeter if poorly designed). Amplifier-free attack: simple waveform generator sufficient (cost: $50-500 depending on frequency capability).

**Safety System Failure Mode**: Safety PLCs and monitoring systems designed assuming sensor data authentic. Redundancy (multiple sensors) may not help if attacker can corrupt multiple channels simultaneously (demonstrated via amplitude crosstalk). Diverse sensors (temperature, pressure) connected to same ADC → single attack compromises multiple redundant measurements.

## Defense and Mitigation Strategies

**Input Filtering Validation**: Design robust analog low-pass filters meeting Nyquist requirements. Specification: adequate attenuation in stop-band (e.g., -80dB at 2x cutoff). Practical: passive LC filters + active (op-amp) filters for adequate rolloff. Limitation: good filtering adds cost/complexity; over-designed filters may introduce latency (undesirable for real-time control).

**ADC Configuration Hardening**: (1) Disable unused channels (reduce crosstalk attack surface). (2) Use maximum practical oversampling rate (increases Nyquist frequency, reduces aliasing window). (3) Avoid programmable gain settings if fixed-gain acceptable (reduces attack surface requiring frequency recalculation). (4) Select highest-resolution ADC affordable (better signal discrimination reduces false-signal susceptibility).

**Sensor Redundancy**: Multiple independent sensors measuring same parameter; cross-check readings for consistency. Attack resistance: if attacker corrupts one ADC/sensor, redundancy detects inconsistency. Limitation: if attacker can corrupt multiple physical sensors simultaneously (e.g., collocated attack on multiple sensor inputs), redundancy bypassed.

**Rate-of-Change Monitoring**: Safety logic monitoring maximum rate of change in measurements (e.g., temperature cannot change >10°C/sec). Alasing-based false signals often exhibit unphysical frequency/rate behavior. Detection: sudden frequency jump (real analog injection at different frequency) flagged as anomaly. Limitation: sophisticated attacker can craft attack signals respecting rate limits.

**Shielding and Grounding**: Electromagnetic shielding of ADC input circuitry reduces crosstalk vulnerability. Proper grounding topology minimizes common-mode interference. Limitation: if attacker injects directly into ADC pins (not via air-coupling), shielding less effective.

**Sealed/Monitored Input Access**: Physical security: seal ADC input connectors, monitor for tampering. Limitation: requires physical inspection, doesn't prevent well-coordinated insider threat.

**System Redesign Perspective**: Consider moving signal processing analog → digital domain (digitize closer to sensor source, reducing analog attack surface). Digital signal processing offers better auditability + repeatability. Limitation: increases complexity, power consumption.

## Broader Security Implications

**Analog Attack Surface Overlooked**: Cybersecurity focus historically on network/software domains. Physical/analog domain less attention despite criticality in ICS. ADC attack represents physical-layer vulnerability—different threat model from software exploits.

**Insider Threat Risk**: Attack feasibility low-cost equipment + physical access → insider threat attractive. Disgruntled employee with maintenance access could inject ADC attacks, causing incidents while appearing external. Detection difficulty: external attack attribution requires specialized equipment (frequency analysis); may appear as sensor malfunction.

**Supply Chain Risk**: ADC vulnerability could be intentionally designed (malicious hardware implant) during manufacturing. Example: ADC firmware configured with vulnerable filter settings, exfiltrated during production. Difficult to detect during integration testing (vulnerability might activate only under specific attack conditions).

**Regulatory Compliance**: Safety-critical systems (nuclear, aviation, oil-gas) should validate ADC security. Standards (IEC 61508, etc.) may not address analog-injection attacks. Compliance gap: physical-layer attacks potentially outside traditional security audit scope.

**Evolution of Attack Sophistication**: As network-layer defenses improve, attackers adapt toward physical layer. ADC attack represents emerging threat category—low-profile, difficult to detect, high impact.

## Future Attack Research

**Hardware-Specific Vulnerabilities**: Different ADC families (manufactures, architectures) likely exhibit unique aliasing/crosstalk characteristics. Systematic survey (characterize dozens of ADC models) could map vulnerability landscape.

**Combination Attacks**: Amplitude + frequency attacks combined; amplitude injection masks frequency-attack detection systems (disruption via crosstalk hides aliasing exploit).

**Real-Time Exploitation**: Live attack against functioning industrial system (requires careful lab replication of real PLC environment) to demonstrate end-to-end attack success (ADC compromise → PLC decision → actuator malfunction).

Temporal representation: snapshots of continuously-varying analog world. Implication: sampling frequency must be sufficiently high to accurately represent signal dynamics.

## Aliasing and Nyquist Theorem

**Aliasing Definition**: Distortion artifact when signal not sampled at sufficient frequency. Result: reconstructed signal appears different from actual signal (false frequency representation). Example: visual aliasing in film (wagon wheels appearing to move backward due to frame rate misalignment with wheel rotation frequency).

**Nyquist Theorem**: Signal containing frequency components up to F_max must be sampled at minimum frequency 2*F_max (twice maximum frequency). Formula: sampling frequency ≥ 2 * maximum signal frequency. Example: 1 kHz signal requires minimum 2 kHz sampling rate. Practical: many systems sample at >2x Nyquist (safety margin for complex signals).

**Aliasing Attack Vector**: If attacker injects high-frequency signal above Nyquist limit (relative to ADC sampling rate), ADC undersamples signal, producing false low-frequency representation in output. Example: ADC sampling at 100 kHz can represent up to 50 kHz (Nyquist frequency). Attacker injects 75 kHz sine wave—ADC outputs false 25 kHz component (not present in actual signal).

**Anti-Aliasing Filters**: Analog low-pass filter placed before ADC input. Purpose: attenuate frequencies above Nyquist limit, preventing aliasing. Specification: filter cutoff frequency set to Nyquist frequency or slightly higher. Ideal filter: brick-wall response (completely blocks above cutoff, passes below). Real filters: gradual rolloff (pass band, transition band, stop band).

## Sigma-Delta ADC Architecture and Operation

**Sigma-Delta Design Concept**: Over-sampling ADC architecture. Key difference: samples signal at frequency much higher than Nyquist requirement (e.g., 20x Nyquist frequency). Purpose: achieve high accuracy with simple 1-bit quantization internally; digital filtering produces multi-bit output. Advantage: relaxed analog anti-aliasing filter requirements (wider bandwidth filter possible due to over-sampling).

**Internal Architecture Components**: (1) Modulator—continuously samples input signal at high frequency, performs 1-bit quantization (output = high/low bit stream), feeds back to input (negative feedback loop). Purpose: encode signal information in high-frequency bit stream. (2) Digital filter (low-pass)—filters over-sampled bit stream, removes high-frequency quantization noise, outputs final multi-bit digital value at lower output rate (decimation).

**Feedback Loop**: Internally-reconstructed estimate of signal fed back to modulator input; modulator compares input to estimate, outputs 1 if input > estimate, 0 if input < estimate. Feedback loop causes output to track input (delta-sigma feedback). Result: high-frequency bit stream whose density encodes signal amplitude.

**Quantization Noise Shaping**: Over-sampling + feedback loop pushes quantization noise to high frequencies (noise shaping). Digital filter attenuates high-frequency noise component. Net result: low-frequency signal accurately represented, high-frequency noise removed. Advantage: better signal-to-noise ratio than simpler ADC architectures at same resolution.

**Anti-Aliasing Filter in Sigma-Delta**: Due to over-sampling, filter requirement relaxed. Example: Sigma-Delta sampling at 200 MHz (20x nominal Nyquist for 10 MHz signal) requires filter cutoff only slightly above 10 MHz (no brick-wall requirement). Contrast: successive-approximation ADC at 20 MHz (2x Nyquist for 10 MHz signal) requires sharp filter cutoff at 10 MHz.

**Programmable Gain Amplifier (PGA)**: Optional feature in Sigma-Delta ADCs. Allows software-programmable amplification of input signal (1x, 2x, 4x gains). Purpose: acquire weak signals with better resolution (amplified signal uses more of ADC's quantization levels). Side effect: changing PGA gain shifts digital filter response (cutoff frequency changes with gain setting).

## Amplitude-Based ADC Attack

**Attack Concept**: Inject out-of-range voltage (exceeding ADC's rated input range) into one ADC channel; observe interference effects on other channels. Goal: demonstrate cross-channel crosstalk vulnerability. Attack assumption: attacker has physical access to ADC input pins or can inject via compromised sensor circuit.

**Test Setup**: Multi-channel ADC (e.g., 8-channel device) with external voltage supply connected to one channel; other channels connected to benign signal sources. Baseline: measure normal ADC output (all channels reading expected values). Attack: gradually increase injected voltage into one channel, monitor output changes on other channels.

**Attack Execution**: Connect external DC supply to ADC channel (e.g., channel 3 in examples). Supply programmable voltage (negative to positive, ramped gradually). Monitor ADC output for all channels simultaneously. Document voltage levels vs. output readings.

**Experimental Results**: Initial injection (small amplitude, e.g., 30 mV): no crosstalk observed—injected channel reads expected value, other channels unaffected. Moderate injection (100-200 mV): subtle interference appearing on neighboring channels (expected behavior from some isolation loss). High-amplitude injection (300+ mV): significant crosstalk observed—channels not directly connected to injection point show reading changes. Example: injecting negative voltage on channel 3 (out-of-range input) causes channels 1-2 to read different values than baseline.

**Cross-Channel Interference Mechanism**: ADC internal circuitry shares components (power rails, ground planes, substrate). Injection of large voltage creates electromagnetic disturbance affecting other channels. Current paths through shared substrate cause voltage drop, interfering with other channels' signal processing. Differential measurements: channel 2 baseline (2.3V) becomes 3.53V when channel 3 receives out-of-range injection—3.1V voltage shift purely from crosstalk.

**Practical Implication**: Attacker controlling one sensor (or injecting into one ADC channel) can corrupt readings from all other channels. Safety system monitoring multiple parameters (e.g., temperature, pressure, voltage) can be blinded by attacking single measurement channel. Example attack: inject excessive voltage on temperature channel; safety PLC sees corrupted temperature readings from multiple channels, potentially triggering false alarms or masking actual faults.

**Attack Feasibility**: Requires only waveform generator (affordable bench equipment or purpose-built device) and physical access to ADC inputs (via compromised sensor, exposed connector, or collocated attacker). No network access, exploitation, or PLC compromise necessary.

## Frequency-Based ADC Attack (Aliasing Exploitation)

**Attack Concept**: Exploit Sigma-Delta ADC's digital filter characteristics by injecting high-frequency signal that aliases into low-frequency output range. Goal: inject false low-frequency signal while ADC's output appears normal (frequency in accepted range).

**Digital Filter Frequency Response**: Sigma-Delta ADCs' digital filter exhibits band-pass behavior with defined cutoff frequency. At PGA gain setting G, cutoff frequency F_cutoff = F_base * G. Example: base cutoff 76 kHz, gain 1x; gain 2x → cutoff 152 kHz. Pass-band: frequencies below cutoff attenuated. Stop-band: frequencies above cutoff heavily attenuated. Transition: not brick-wall (gradual rolloff with non-ideal filter).

**Aliasing Exploitation Methodology**: (1) Identify ADC sampling frequency and digital filter cutoff. (2) Compute stop-band region (frequencies supposed to be blocked). (3) Inject signal at carefully chosen frequency in stop-band such that aliasing produces output in pass-band. (4) Attacker crafts frequency such that aliased component appears as false signal at target frequency.

**Mathematical Aliasing**: If ADC has effective sampling frequency F_s and receives input at frequency F_input > F_s/2, output contains aliased frequency: F_alias = |F_input - k*F_s| for appropriate integer k. Attacker selects F_input to produce desired F_alias.

**Experimental Attack Setup**: Equipment: function generator (creates programmable frequency signals), oscilloscope (measures signals), ADC device under test (Delta-Sigma type), data acquisition system. Signal path: function generator output → ADC input; measure both generator output (oscilloscope) and ADC output (digital readback). Sweep generator frequency across range (0 to several MHz), log ADC readings at each frequency.

**Attack Results**: Baseline (low-frequency input): ADC reads actual signal frequency accurately. Mid-range frequencies (within pass-band): ADC output follows input faithfully. Stop-band frequencies (>filter cutoff): expected behavior = ADC attenuates/blocks signal, output noise-like. Attack discovery: specific stop-band frequencies (e.g., 312.5 kHz in test example) produce unexpected clean sinusoidal output at false frequency (e.g., false 31 kHz component). Attacker-injected signal: 312.5 kHz sine wave (not present in system). ADC output: 31 kHz sine wave (false signal, appears legitimate).

**Why Aliasing Succeeds Against Sigma-Delta**: Digital filter not ideal—transition region contains partial pass-through before complete attenuation. Over-sampled bit stream from modulator contains energy at injected frequency. Digital filter partially attenuates but doesn't completely block. Aliasing mechanism: high-frequency component folds into low-frequency range via under-sampling in final decimation step. Net result: attacker's high-frequency injection appears as false low-frequency signal in output.

**PGA Gain Effect on Vulnerability**: Changing PGA gain shifts filter cutoff. Higher gain → higher cutoff frequency. Effect: stop-band region (frequencies subject to aliasing) changes. Attacker must recalculate aliasing frequencies when gain changes. Example: gain 1x (cutoff 76 kHz) vulnerable to different injection frequencies than gain 2x (cutoff 152 kHz).

## Attack Implications for Industrial Control Systems

**System Architecture Vulnerability**: Typical ICS/SCADA: physical process → sensors → ADC → PLC → decision logic → actuators. ADC blind-spot: if attacker corrupts ADC reading, PLC receives false telemetry, decisions based on false state. Safety system assuming ADC+PLC+network secure but overlooking analog attack surface.

**Attack Scenario Example**: Spinning motor monitoring system—speed sensor → ADC channel measures speed voltage. Safety PLC continuously monitors speed; if speed exceeds threshold, triggers emergency stop. Attacker injects 312.5 kHz signal into speed ADC channel → ADC outputs false 31 kHz component (not real motor speed). PLC interprets as legitimate motor running at false speed, issues wrong control commands. Actual motor may be running dangerously fast; false ADC reading masks reality. Operator monitoring sees PLC status "all green," unaware of actual hazard.

**Blind Attack Advantage**: Attacker achieves system compromise without: (1) network access, (2) PLC exploitation, (3) software modification, (4) insider knowledge of control logic. Only requirement: physical access to ADC inputs (accessible from outside secure perimeter if poorly designed). Amplifier-free attack: simple waveform generator sufficient (cost: $50-500 depending on frequency capability).

**Safety System Failure Mode**: Safety PLCs and monitoring systems designed assuming sensor data authentic. Redundancy (multiple sensors) may not help if attacker can corrupt multiple channels simultaneously (demonstrated via amplitude crosstalk). Diverse sensors (temperature, pressure) connected to same ADC → single attack compromises multiple redundant measurements.

## Defense and Mitigation Strategies

**Input Filtering Validation**: Design robust analog low-pass filters meeting Nyquist requirements. Specification: adequate attenuation in stop-band (e.g., -80dB at 2x cutoff). Practical: passive LC filters + active (op-amp) filters for adequate rolloff. Limitation: good filtering adds cost/complexity; over-designed filters may introduce latency (undesirable for real-time control).

**ADC Configuration Hardening**: (1) Disable unused channels (reduce crosstalk attack surface). (2) Use maximum practical oversampling rate (increases Nyquist frequency, reduces aliasing window). (3) Avoid programmable gain settings if fixed-gain acceptable (reduces attack surface requiring frequency recalculation). (4) Select highest-resolution ADC affordable (better signal discrimination reduces false-signal susceptibility).

**Sensor Redundancy**: Multiple independent sensors measuring same parameter; cross-check readings for consistency. Attack resistance: if attacker corrupts one ADC/sensor, redundancy detects inconsistency. Limitation: if attacker can corrupt multiple physical sensors simultaneously (e.g., collocated attack on multiple sensor inputs), redundancy bypassed.

**Rate-of-Change Monitoring**: Safety logic monitoring maximum rate of change in measurements (e.g., temperature cannot change >10°C/sec). Alasing-based false signals often exhibit unphysical frequency/rate behavior. Detection: sudden frequency jump (real analog injection at different frequency) flagged as anomaly. Limitation: sophisticated attacker can craft attack signals respecting rate limits.

**Shielding and Grounding**: Electromagnetic shielding of ADC input circuitry reduces crosstalk vulnerability. Proper grounding topology minimizes common-mode interference. Limitation: if attacker injects directly into ADC pins (not via air-coupling), shielding less effective.

**Sealed/Monitored Input Access**: Physical security: seal ADC input connectors, monitor for tampering. Limitation: requires physical inspection, doesn't prevent well-coordinated insider threat.

**System Redesign Perspective**: Consider moving signal processing analog → digital domain (digitize closer to sensor source, reducing analog attack surface). Digital signal processing offers better auditability + repeatability. Limitation: increases complexity, power consumption.

## Broader Security Implications

**Analog Attack Surface Overlooked**: Cybersecurity focus historically on network/software domains. Physical/analog domain less attention despite criticality in ICS. ADC attack represents physical-layer vulnerability—different threat model from software exploits.

**Insider Threat Risk**: Attack feasibility low-cost equipment + physical access → insider threat attractive. Disgruntled employee with maintenance access could inject ADC attacks, causing incidents while appearing external. Detection difficulty: external attack attribution requires specialized equipment (frequency analysis); may appear as sensor malfunction.

**Supply Chain Risk**: ADC vulnerability could be intentionally designed (malicious hardware implant) during manufacturing. Example: ADC firmware configured with vulnerable filter settings, exfiltrated during production. Difficult to detect during integration testing (vulnerability might activate only under specific attack conditions).

**Regulatory Compliance**: Safety-critical systems (nuclear, aviation, oil-gas) should validate ADC security. Standards (IEC 61508, etc.) may not address analog-injection attacks. Compliance gap: physical-layer attacks potentially outside traditional security audit scope.

**Evolution of Attack Sophistication**: As network-layer defenses improve, attackers adapt toward physical layer. ADC attack represents emerging threat category—low-profile, difficult to detect, high impact.

## Future Attack Research

**Hardware-Specific Vulnerabilities**: Different ADC families (manufactures, architectures) likely exhibit unique aliasing/crosstalk characteristics. Systematic survey (characterize dozens of ADC models) could map vulnerability landscape.

**Combination Attacks**: Amplitude + frequency attacks combined; amplitude injection masks frequency-attack detection systems (disruption via crosstalk hides aliasing exploit).

**Real-Time Exploitation**: Live attack against functioning industrial system (requires careful lab replication of real PLC environment) to demonstrate end-to-end attack success (ADC compromise → PLC decision → actuator malfunction).

talks.title: WiFi-Based IMSI Catcher
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for WiFi-Based IMSI Catcher.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Piers O'Hanlon and Ravishankar Borgaonkar demonstrate how mobile subscriber identities can be captured over unlicensed Wi-Fi frequencies without using traditional cellular interception hardware. While conventional IMSI catchers (such as StingRays) operate on licensed cellular bands and require specialized radio equipment, the authors reveal that smartphones inadvertently expose their International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) during automated Wi-Fi authentication. The talk details exploitation vectors across carrier Wi-Fi offloading and Wi-Fi Calling protocols, illustrating how this technique circumvents modern operating system MAC address randomization.

Key Topics:
- International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) functions and cellular tracking risks.
- Comparative analysis between cellular IMSI catchers (StingRays) and Wi-Fi-based approaches.
- Cleartext IMSI leakage in EAP-SIM, EAP-AKA, and VoWiFi (Wi-Fi Calling) protocols.
- Circumvention of mobile OS Wi-Fi MAC address randomization across iOS and Android.

Technical Details:
The International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) is a globally unique 15-digit number stored in the Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) card that serves as the primary subscriber identifier for cellular network authentication and billing. Conventional cellular IMSI catchers (such as StingRay devices or rogue femtocells) broadcast cellular beacons across licensed GSM, 3G, or 4G bands, often deploying radio frequency jamming to force mobile devices into downgrading to 2G GSM protocols where mutual authentication is absent. Once attached, these devices harvest subscriber IMSIs and IMEIs or intercept voice and data communications, but require expensive software-defined radios and regulatory spectrum licenses.

The authors introduced a low-cost alternative that captures IMSIs over unlicensed Wi-Fi spectrum using standard off-the-shelf Wi-Fi hardware. The attack exploits two distinct carrier-integrated features: automatic carrier Wi-Fi offloading and Wi-Fi Calling (Voice over Wi-Fi / VoWiFi). Under carrier offloading specifications, mobile devices automatically connect to public carrier Wi-Fi hotspots using Extensible Authentication Protocol methods backed by the SIM card (EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA). In standard implementations, when the rogue Wi-Fi access point challenges the mobile device with an EAP-Request/Identity frame, the smartphone responds with an EAP-Response/Identity frame containing its permanent cleartext IMSI prior to establishing an encrypted tunnel or receiving an encrypted pseudonym.

A similar exposure occurs during Wi-Fi Calling initialization, where IPsec IKEv2 exchanges over untrusted Wi-Fi connections expose subscriber identity tokens. Crucially, this Wi-Fi IMSI catching technique completely defeats modern operating system privacy enhancements. While iOS (since iOS 8), Android, and Windows Mobile deploy Wi-Fi MAC address randomization to prevent physical tracking across Wi-Fi probe requests, the underlying subscriber IMSI remains constant. Because the IMSI is tied permanently to the SIM card hardware, harvesting the IMSI allows an attacker to continuously track a target's physical movements and link ephemeral MAC addresses back to a persistent real-world identity.

Key Takeaways:
Automatic network attachment protocols must not transmit persistent hardware identifiers in cleartext before establishing authenticated, encrypted sessions. Mobile network operators and standards bodies must mandate the universal use of encrypted identities or temporary pseudonyms (such as IMSI encryption in 5G or protected EAP-AKA') during Wi-Fi offloading and VoWiFi negotiations. Operating system vendors and users should restrict automatic Wi-Fi connection behaviors and disable unencrypted carrier offloading profiles to protect subscriber privacy in public spaces.

Overview: MacOS has a strong reputation for security and comes with many restrictions such as the usage of an App Store to prevent malicious code being installed. However, we have found that since MacOS is the minority platform for many software packages and security platforms, it rarely gets the same attention from security vendors as Windows. This workshop will teach you to exploit that lack of attention from software like Microsoft Office and security platforms like a leading EDR solution to break in a

We will walk you through how to use open source tools, both unmodified and customized, can be used to take advantage of the difference in capability, e.g., script detection, between Windows and non-Windows platforms. We will show you how to map out an environment, how to gain code execution in multiple ways, grab credentials, find files, collect screenshots and webcam shots and exfiltrate the loot while remaining undetected. The key takeaway is that despite the myriad of operating system security features present in MacOS and Linux, and the addition of

Takeaways: ll be compromised by a diligent attacker using open source tooling. This workshop will show you how! [Unfortunately we cannot provide an EDR system for you to play with, so please bring your own or practice the techniques without that particular opponent.]

talks.title: Pocket-Sized Badness: Why Ransomware Comes as a Plot Twist in the Cat-Mouse Game
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Pocket-Sized Badness: Why Ransomware Comes as a Plot Twist in the Cat-Mouse Game.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Stefano Zanero (Politecnico di Milano, Trend Micro SDR research) presented comprehensive analysis of mobile ransomware evolution on Android, focusing on detection methodologies and real-world case studies. Context: ransomware transformed from theoretical crypto-virology concept (20 years prior) to billion-dollar criminal enterprise post-Cryptolocker (2012-2013). Motivation: mobile ransomware largely under-researched compared to desktop variants; Trend Micro SDR investigated Android malware and discovered >1 order-of-magnitude increase in samples (2015-2016). Research includes: retrospective analysis of ransomware evolution, case studies of representative mobile families (Locker, Color, SD Fang, LockDroid), static-analysis-based detection of characteristic ransomware features, tool release implementing detectors. Key findings: mobile ransomware uses diverse techniques (soft-button-hijacking for screen locking, device-administration API abuse, encryption, threatening text in 60+ languages), detection feasible via combination of NLP (natural-language processing) + static dataflow analysis without requiring dynamic execution. Significance: demonstrates ransomware detection scalable to large malware repositories; enables rapid identification of emerging ransomware variants; reveals defensive strategies against prevalent mobile threat.

## Ransomware Evolution and Cryptovirology Foundation

**Crypto-Virology Origin (20 Years Prior)**: Academic term coined at Oakland Security/Privacy Symposium describing malicious use of cryptography for extortion-based attacks. Prescient element: paper's authors explicitly predicted role of electronic currency in ransomware ecosystem. Quote: "specialized crypto virus could search for e-money nodes and encrypt them, effectively kidnapping digital money." Reality: while not literally encrypted electronic currency, ransomware uses cryptocurrency (Bitcoin) as payment medium, exactly as predicted.

**Pre-Cryptolocker Era (2000-2011)**: Isolated ransomware cases (few families, minimal outbreak impact). Severity: limited because payment collection infeasible (no anonymous payment channels).

**Cryptolocker Watershed (2012-2013)**: Game-changing malware family combining RSA encryption with Bitcoin ransom. Impact: transformed ransomware from curiosity to mature criminal business model—millions in extortion revenue. Ecosystem consequence: exponential growth in ransomware families post-Cryptolocker as cybercriminals replicated proven model.

**Desktop Ransomware Dominance (2012-2014)**: Extensive academic/commercial focus on desktop/server ransomware; mobile ransomware largely ignored despite early 2014-2015 Android variants. Research gap: mobile platform presents different threat model, techniques, and defenses compared to desktop.

**Mobile Ransomware Emergence (2014-2016)**: Specialized Android ransomware families began appearing; growth trajectory steep. Data: Trend Micro SDR analysis of internal data (2015-2016) shows >10x increase in submitted ransomware samples. Geographic variation: certain regions (Australia, Singapore) experience higher ransomware prevalence depending on criminal group targeting/client base.

**Market Diversification**: Ransomware taxonomy: (1) traditional encryption-based (steals data, demands payment), (2) screen-locking variants (simpler—no encryption, just UI hijacking), (3) hybrid (combination techniques). Market pressure: competition drives feature enhancement (better encryption, multilingual threatening text, obfuscation).

## Mobile Ransomware Families and Exploitation Techniques

**Locker Family (Simple Locker)**: One of first Android screen-locking ransomware. Predominant technique: soft-button-event hijacking (prevents home/back button functionality). Encryption rare (only ~50 samples of thousands analyzed). Variant: recent evolution uses encryption with third-party device key (external key server), SMS for C&C communication. Significance: demonstrates screen-locking variant economic viability (victim cannot navigate OS, forced to interact with ransom UI).

**Color Family**: Renowned for sophisticated threatening text (main attack vector = psychological pressure). Localization effort: threatening text translated to 60+ languages; law-enforcement references customized per country (unique police logos/terminology for each jurisdiction). Implication: suggests professional-level malware development (significant translator/linguist involvement), indicates market targeting diverse geographic victims. Text structure: accusation-based (victim violated law/accessed prohibited content), authority-impersonation (police/regulatory threats). Analysis: sophisticated localization implies economic viability—criminals investing resources in user experience, suggesting profitability.

**SD Fang Family**: Started as banking trojan (1M USD fraud), operator switched to ransomware business model. Significance: demonstrates criminal-career progression (banking -> ransomware—higher ROI, lower technical complexity). Capability: real encryption (actual symmetric/asymmetric cryptography, not fake screen lock). Technique: device-administration API abuse (newer method than soft-button hijacking). Victim base: evolved from banking targets to general population (broader attack surface).

**LockDroid Family**: Recent variant (September 2016) using device-administration API in novel way. Attack: reset-password API (part of device-admin framework) called with random password, password sent to C&C, then device locked. Consequence: legitimate device owner locked out (password changed without consent). Mitigation: Google patched Android N—reset-password API restricted to single-call maximum (prevents repeated calls). Side effect: breaks legitimate remote-device-administration use case but effectively prevents LockDroid variant.

## Screen Locking Techniques and Detection

**Soft-Button-Event Hijacking Method**: Android programming: activities override onKeyDown/onKeyUp methods to handle button presses. Standard flow: button press → OS generates key event → dispatches to focused activity → activity's onKeyDown method called → activity returns true/false. Return value significance: true = event consumed (stop propagation); false = event propagates to next handler. Exploitation: malware overrides onKeyDown, checks if pressed button matches target (home, back), if matched returns true (blocking event). Consequence: normal button functionality blocked—user cannot navigate OS or exit malware UI.

**Implementation Details**: Malware extends Activity class, overrides onKeyDown/onKeyUp, adds conditional logic checking for key codes (KeyEvent.KEYCODE_HOME, etc.), conditionally returns true. Detection: reverse engineer APK, identify Activity subclasses overriding key-handling methods, analyze method body for conditional statements returning true on specific key codes.

**Dialog-Based Locking (Rare)**: Create non-cancellable dialog (setOnCancelListener(null)), fullscreen dialog occludes normal OS UI. Less common than button hijacking; equally effective but requires more code.

**Device-Administration API Abuse (Modern Technique)**: Declared in AndroidManifest.xml: receiver element requesting BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN permission. Receiver references separate XML resource file (device-admin-policy.xml) specifying capabilities. Capabilities available: password policies, reset password, lock device, wipe device, force lock after timeout. Legitimate use: enterprise device management (mobile device management solutions), remote lock/wipe for lost devices. Malicious use: lock device with random password (LockDroid), encrypt storage (Simplocker variant), remote wipe sensitive data. Detection: identify AndroidManifest.xml receiver with BIND_DEVICE_ADMIN, parse policy XML, search bytecode for calls to dangerous APIs (lockNow(), resetPassword(), wipeData()).

## Threatening Text Detection via NLP and Machine Learning

**Text Extraction Strategies**: Primary source—plain-text strings in APK (decompile, extract ASCII strings from classes.dex/resources). Secondary source—runtime text extraction via sandbox execution (capture strings from logcat, network traffic decoding, API monitoring). Fallback—optical character recognition (OCR) on screenshots during execution (text visible in UI but not easily statically extractable).

**Language Preprocessing Pipeline**: Language detection (identify French/English/etc.) → segmentation (split text into sentences/phrases) → stop-word removal (filter non-semantic words like "the," "a") → stemming (reduce words to root form: "locked"→"lock," "safety"→"safe"). Output: vector of semantic word features.

**Machine Learning Classification**: Custom lightweight classifier using weighted word-category scoring. Training: curate representative ransomware/non-ransomware text samples, manually categorize into threat categories (money-related, law-related, accusation-related, other). Scoring function: for each sentence, calculate similarity to each category (presence of category-indicative words weighted). Decision: threshold-based classification—if score exceeds threshold for money category, classify sentence as money-related threat.

**Threshold Calibration**: Set thresholds using separate corpus of known ransomware vs. legitimate text (books, websites, etc.). Objective: maximize true-positive rate (ransomware text correctly identified) while minimizing false positives (legitimate text misclassified as threatening).

**Threatening Text Characteristics**: Clear, convincing language (victims not expected to be experts—text must be understandable). Coercion techniques: legal/authority references, accusation framing (violation of specific laws), payment instructions (enable victim compliance). Avoidance of detection: no excessive grammar errors, consistent fonts, proper spelling (unlike spam emails). Expectation: legitimate-looking threat message, not obviously malicious.

**Category-Specific Analysis**: Money-related phrases ("pay fine," "bitcoin payment," "fund transfer"). Law-related phrases (citations of legal codes, references to specific crimes). Accusation-based (victim framing—inappropriate content access, legal violations). Combination detection: if sentence scored high for multiple categories, likely ransomware (legitimate text rarely combines accusations + payment demands).

## Device-Administration API Abuse Detection

**Manifest Extraction**: Parse AndroidManifest.xml, search for receiver element with intent-filter matching device-admin intent actions. If found, identify associated device-admin policy XML file (usually res/xml/device-admin-policy.xml). Extract policy directives (capabilities requested by malware).

**Policy Analysis**: Dangerous policies include: resetPassword (changed device password), forceLock (device locked immediately), wipeData (factory reset), disableCamera (disable camera). Detection: if policy XML specifies dangerous capabilities, flag as potential abuse.

**Bytecode Dataflow Analysis**: Traditional static analysis: search CFG (control-flow graph) for calls to dangerous methods (lockNow(), resetPassword(), wipeData()). Entry point: receiver's onReceive method (dispatches device-admin commands). Trace dataflow from command dispatch to dangerous API calls. If path found, API abuse confirmed.

**Reflection Resolution**: Malware may obfuscate method calls via Java reflection (not direct method invocation, but dynamic dispatch via reflection API). talks.title: Ghost in the PLC: Designing an Undetectable Programmable Logic Controller Rootkit
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Ghost in the PLC: Designing an Undetectable Programmable Logic Controller Rootkit.
talks.summary:
Overview:
This presentation introduces an undetectable rootkit architecture targeting the pin control subsystem of Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) in industrial critical infrastructure. The researchers evaluate the efficacy of current PLC attack vectors and defensive mechanisms, focusing on low-overhead host-based protections. The talk demonstrates how manipulating physical I/O pin multiplexing at the hardware level bypasses conventional memory attestation and control-flow integrity defenses without altering operating system binaries or ladder logic.

Key Topics:
- Critical infrastructure threat landscape and PLC operational mechanics (RTOS, logic execution, I/O processing)
- Taxonomy of PLC attacks: Firmware modification, logic alteration, control flow hijacking, and ICS malware (Stuxnet)
- Evaluation of host-based PLC defenses: Memory attestation (Doppelgänger) and control-flow tracking (Autoscopy Jr.)
- Pin control rootkit design: Hardware pin multiplexing manipulation and zero-overhead evasion

Technical Details:
Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) form the foundational automation layer for critical infrastructure, including nuclear power plants, water treatment facilities, power grids, gas distribution, and transportation. These embedded systems run real-time operating systems (RTOS) that execute industrial control logic in cyclical loops: reading physical sensor inputs (such as temperature gauges), processing control routines, and writing outputs to actuators and alarms. Historical state-sponsored campaigns, such as Operation Olympic Games (Stuxnet) and research on the "Damn Vulnerable Chemical Process," demonstrate that adversaries compromise these devices to manipulate physical industrial processes while masking anomalies from human operators.

Existing PLC attacks generally fall into distinct categories: firmware modification (flashing backdoored firmware), logic tampering (altering ladder logic code), control-flow attacks (memory corruption and buffer overflows), credential bypasses (hardcoded default credentials), and SCADA-level malware. To counter these threats without requiring hardware modifications or virtualization (which most commercial PLCs lack), researchers have developed lightweight host-based defenses. The speakers categorize these into trivial solutions (static firmware and logic checksumming) and non-trivial host intrusion detection systems. They specifically analyze Doppelgänger—which enforces memory attestation by scanning executable memory and placing dynamic hardware watchpoints to verify memory checksums—and Autoscopy Jr., which profiles execution paths (function pointers, return addresses, and parameters) into a "trusted location list" (TLL) to detect control-flow anomalies.

The authors propose a novel rootkit paradigm that operates beneath these software-centric defenses by targeting "pin control." Microcontrollers within PLCs use hardware pin control and multiplexing registers to dynamically assign physical processor pins to internal peripherals, GPIOs, or communication buses. By directly manipulating these hardware pin configuration registers, the rootkit alters the physical voltage, sensor inputs, and actuator outputs directly at the silicon interface. Because this manipulation requires no modification of executable memory regions, application logic, or CPU control flow, it completely evades memory attestation tools like Doppelgänger and control-flow monitors like Autoscopy Jr., creating a stealthy, cross-platform persistence mechanism.

Key Takeaways:
Software-based host intrusion detection and memory attestation are fundamentally insufficient to protect PLCs if microarchitectural pin multiplexing registers remain accessible to attackers. Embedded hardware vendors must incorporate hardware-enforced write locks and physical isolation for pin configuration and peripheral multiplexing registers once the RTOS completes initialization. Industrial defense strategies should integrate out-of-band physical process monitoring and electrical signal validation to detect actuator discrepancies independent of controller software telemetry.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

## Overview

Quentin Meffre (independent security researcher, top contributor to Pwn2Own) presented sophisticated exploitation techniques for use-after-free (UAF) vulnerabilities in Adobe Flash Player. Context: for 3+ years, classical Flash exploits relied on vector-length corruption (vector object contains length field; overflow corrupts length; inflated length enables arbitrary memory access). Adobe mitigations (2015): isolated heap (separate memory partition for Flash objects vs. system allocations), length field relocation (moved to metadata section separate from vector buffer), verification fields (XOR-based integrity checks). **Flash v22 Memory Protector Mitigation**: Adds guards against arbitrary executable-bit setting (addresses wrapper-function ROP chain exploitation). Mitigation: intercepts VirtualProtect calls from exploit-controlled code paths, rejects PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE on untrusted memory regions. Workaround: (1) find alternative gadget chains not blocked by memory protector, (2) exploit vulnerability pre-v22 deployment (transitional period), (3) combine multiple vulnerabilities (use UAF for read, exploit different bug for executable-bit setting).

## Strategic Exploitation Implications

**Mitigation-Adaptation Cycle**: Mitigations deployed (isolated heap, verification fields, ASLR), attackers adapt (UAF-based approach). Cycle continues: new mitigations (memory protector), new adaptations (alternative gadgets). Arms race inherent in vulnerability-exploitation landscape.

**Sophistication Asymmetry**: Vulnerability developers (Adobe) must secure *all* code paths; attackers need only find *one* viable path. Attacker advantage: time-unlimited exploitation research post-vulnerability discovery; vulnerability developers facing time-constrained patch deployment (balance security vs. user friction).

**Heap Spray Limitations and Evolution**: Heap spray—effective for predictable memory layout—becomes unreliable as heap randomization improves. Exploit code requires adaptive strategies (object spraying, flag-searching, multiple occupation cycles). Modern exploits more complex than classical ones; implies higher skill barrier but still within reach of motivated adversaries.

**Undocumented/Legacy Code Risk**: P SDK vulnerability discovered in undocumented, legacy code path. Adobe initially removed package (v20), reintroduced after 6 months (v21) without comprehensive security review. Risk: legacy features carry historical security debt; reintroduction without re-auditing propagates vulnerability.

**Tool Development and Democratization**: Exploitation techniques once limited to elite researchers (Hacking Team exploit code revealed) now teachable via academic presentation. Open-source exploitation frameworks (Metasploit, etc.) incorporate techniques, enabling less-skilled attackers. Effect: vulnerability exploitation window widens post-disclosure.

## Windows Version Specific Considerations

**Windows 7 Exploitation (Favorable Conditions)**: Predictable heap allocation (sequential allocation from free list). Single occupation sufficient for UAF-based exploitation. Minimal randomization in heap base addresses. Exploitation timeline: seconds (quick memory reuse, straightforward type confusion). Platform end-of-support (Jan 2020) limits relevance but illustrates exploitation principles.

**Windows 10 Exploitation (Adversarial Conditions)**: Randomized free-list selection, multiple free-list cycles required. Increased code randomization, metadata object spraying necessary. Exploitation timeline: slower due to multiple allocation cycles. However: exploitation still feasible (confirmed via research experimentation). Implications: modern exploit complexity, but not complexity that defeats determined attacker.

**Variant Strategies by Windows Version**: Exploit code requires version detection (via WMI query, version API calls) to adapt strategy at runtime. Different code paths for Windows 7/10 handle heap allocation variance. Unified exploitation framework supporting multiple Windows versions adds significant complexity but ensures broad applicability.

talks.title: Stumping the Mobile Chipset
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Stumping the Mobile Chipset.
talks.summary:
Overview:
A security researcher from Intel presents an in-depth vulnerability analysis of Qualcomm chipset drivers and kernel modifications within the Android operating system. The presentation outlines the Android supply chain, demonstrating how closed-source chipset components introduce system-wide privilege escalation vulnerabilities across multiple device manufacturers. The author details two major vulnerabilities: an input verification bypass in Qualcomm's Ashmem driver extension and security exposures in the AF_MSM_IPC kernel router.

Key Topics:
- Android hardware and software supply chain dynamics: Linux kernel, AOSP, OEMs, and chipset vendors
- Systemic risk of Qualcomm chipset modifications across heterogeneous Android devices
- Ashmem architecture, file-descriptor verification flaws, and OBB filesystem exploitation
- Qualcomm IPC Router (AF_MSM_IPC) architecture, socket types, and unprivileged access vectors

Technical Details:
The Android ecosystem relies on a multi-tiered supply chain comprising the upstream Linux kernel, Google's Android Open Source Project (AOSP), device OEMs (such as Samsung, LG, and HTC), and chipset manufacturers like Qualcomm. Because Qualcomm dominates the mobile ARM market, custom driver code developed by the chipset vendor executes at the lowest, most privileged levels of the Android kernel across hundreds of device models. Consequently, vulnerabilities within Qualcomm's proprietary modifications bypass OEM-specific security boundaries, posing systemic privilege escalation risks.

The speaker first analyzes a vulnerability in Qualcomm's extension of Android Shared Memory (Ashmem), termed "Ashmem Devil." Ashmem provides inter-process shared memory using file-descriptor-based APIs (/dev/ashmem). Qualcomm added a kernel helper function designed to extract internal shared memory structures directly from a user-supplied file descriptor (int fd). The function converts the file descriptor into a kernel struct file *, attempts to verify that the target is a genuine Ashmem object, and casts file->private_data to access private fields. Rather than adhering to standard Linux kernel conventions—which verify file types by comparing file operations (f_op) function pointers—Qualcomm's code merely verified whether the file's path string ended with /ashmem from its mount root.

Exploiting this path validation flaw from an unprivileged context posed a challenge, as / resides on a read-only RAM disk and unprivileged apps cannot create system mount points. The researcher bypassed this restriction using Android's Opaque Binary Blob (OBB) feature, a legacy mechanism used by large applications (like games exceeding 100MB) to mount external filesystem containers. The author created a custom OBB image containing an arbitrary file named ashmem at its root directory, mounted it via standard Android APIs without special privileges, and passed its file descriptor into Qualcomm's API. The driver misinterpreted the arbitrary file's private_data pointer as an Ashmem allocation, enabling controlled kernel memory corruption. The talk also details Qualcomm's IPC Router subsystem (AF_MSM_IPC, socket family 27), revealing that unprivileged applications could open client and control ports via ioctl to monitor system endpoints and manipulate inter-processor communications before Google restricted socket access via SELinux.

Key Takeaways:
Kernel drivers must validate internal object types by verifying function pointers in kernel operation tables (f_op) rather than relying on untrusted, user-manipulable file path strings. Platform maintainers should audit third-party chipset vendor code with the same scrutiny applied to core kernel components, ensuring proprietary extensions adhere to Linux kernel security best practices. Coordinated disclosure timelines must synchronize vendor patch releases with public advisories to prevent window-of-exposure vulnerabilities prior to carrier and OEM patch deployment.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: The Path Less Traveled: Abusing Kubernetes Defaults
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding The Path Less Traveled: Abusing Kubernetes Defaults.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In the Black Hat presentation *"The Path Less Traveled: Abusing Kubernetes Defaults,"* speakers Ian Coldwater (Lead Platform Security Engineer at Heroku) and Duffy Cooley (Staff Cloud Native Architect at VMware) examine the security posture of out-of-the-box Kubernetes installations. The speakers emphasize that assuming Kubernetes or applications deployed on it are secure by default is a mistake. 

While there is no single universal set of defaults—configurations vary across distributions and cloud providers—the demonstration environment relies on `kind` (Kubernetes in Docker) using `kubeadm`. `kubeadm` rationalizes and provides a relatively secure baseline compared to many out-of-the-box setups; however, inherent architectural mechanisms and default behaviors still present a substantial attack surface.

## Kubernetes Architecture and Attack Surface

Kubernetes operates as both an application with configurable binaries and an API-driven platform defined via YAML. Understanding its loosely coupled distributed architecture is essential for identifying exploit opportunities across its core components:

* **etcd:** The key-value store holding all cluster state, including configuration files and ConfigMaps. Because etcd is writable and represents the cluster’s ultimate source of truth, an attacker targeting it can exfiltrate sensitive data (such as cloud metadata and credentials) or write directly to it to manipulate cluster state.
* **API Server:** The central communication hub. All internal services, worker nodes, and external clients route requests through the API server, which performs authentication, authorization, and manifest validation. As the only component communicating directly with etcd, compromising the API server provides near-total administrative control over the cluster.
* **Kubelet:** The node agent responsible for running workloads by interfacing with the container runtime (e.g., Docker or containerd). It maintains its own API to interact with the API server. Gaining access to the kubelet allows attackers to modify authorization settings, create users or service account roles, and execute commands—vector patterns seen in historical attacks such as the Tesla incident.
* **Controller Manager & Scheduler:** The scheduler assigns pods to nodes, while the controller manager runs control loops that break down high-level abstractions (like Deployments) into pods. From an attacker's perspective, these components are frequently bypassed.

## Attack Vectors and Exploitation Techniques

The speakers outline specific methodologies and historical vulnerabilities that target these architectural interactions:

* **Social Engineering via Manifests:** Because Kubernetes configuration is managed declaratively via tools like `kubectl` (`kubeclt apply`), convincing an administrator or developer to apply an unvetted YAML file gives an attacker immediate execution within the cluster.
* **Bypassing the API Server (CVE-2018-1002105):** The speakers highlight this critical vulnerability—a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw involving `Connection: Upgrade` requests. Because the API server failed to properly validate error codes, an attacker could establish a direct WebSocket tunnel to the backend kubelet, bypassing API server authentication and authorization entirely.
* **Direct Node Scheduling & etcd Compromise:** Rather than waiting for the scheduler to place a workload, an attacker can specify a `nodeName` directly in a pod specification, effectively bypassing the scheduler and controller manager. In environments bootstrapped with `kubeadm`, control plane nodes also run a kubelet alongside etcd. The speakers demonstrate using this direct scheduling technique to place a pre-configured `etcdctl` client pod directly onto the control plane node, allowing them to access etcd directly, dump cluster secrets, and extract sensitive data.

talks.title: Command Injection in F5 iRules
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Command Injection in F5 iRules.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Christoffer Jerkeby, a security consultant at F-Secure Sweden, presents research on command injection vulnerabilities within F5 BIG-IP application delivery controllers caused by insecure iRules scripts. The talk explains the role of BIG-IP appliances in high-traffic enterprise architectures, managing session load balancing, TLS termination, and traffic manipulation. The author analyzes how user-authored iRules scripts, built upon F5's simplified Tool Command Language (Tcl) runtime, inadvertently introduce critical command injection flaws due to improper syntax evaluation.

Key Topics:
- F5 BIG-IP architecture: Load balancing, session management, TLS termination, and internet exposure
- Architectural purpose and syntax of iRules event-driven scripts (when HTTP_REQUEST)
- Evolution of iRules from Tcl 8.4 and security trade-offs of command filtering
- Tcl command injection mechanisms, double evaluation risks, and global attack surface mapping

Technical Details:
F5 BIG-IP devices serve as foundational infrastructure in modern networks, operating as application delivery controllers, traffic gateways, session state managers, and load balancers. They handle heavy enterprise traffic loads, terminate TLS connections, manage session cookies, and route HTTP/HTTPS requests to backend server pools. A global scan conducted by the researcher revealed thousands of internet-exposed BIG-IP appliances identifiable by default response headers (such as Server: BigIP or BigIP strings served during HTTP redirects and /favicon.ico requests).

To provide fine-grained control over network traffic, F5 incorporates iRules, an event-driven scripting engine. Administrators use iRules to enforce custom traffic routing, sanitize headers, perform localized language redirection, cache static resources directly on the controller, and filter denial-of-service traffic. The iRules execution engine was originally forked from Tcl (Tool Command Language) version 8.4 in 2001. F5 modified the Tcl dialect, intentionally stripping low-level file system manipulation and OS-level execution commands to simplify the scripting environment and prevent scripts from destabilizing the underlying appliance.

Despite these restrictions, vulnerabilities arise from Tcl's fundamental parsing model, specifically command and variable substitution ("double evaluation"). In Tcl, commands and expressions enclosed in brackets ([...]) or quotes are evaluated dynamically by the interpreter. If an iRule script incorporates unvalidated user input (such as HTTP query parameters, URI paths, or request headers) into an unquoted or improperly braced command—such as dynamic redirection handlers, logging statements, or conditional blocks—Tcl treats embedded brackets within the input as nested sub-commands. Attackers can inject arbitrary Tcl syntax, bypassing intended control flow and executing unauthorized logic inside the BIG-IP execution environment. While iRules supports Tcl exception handling via catch statements, unhandled injections disrupt load balancer operations or compromise internal session contexts.

Key Takeaways:
Administrators writing F5 iRules must strictly adhere to secure Tcl coding practices, specifically enclosing all script arguments, expressions, and variable evaluations in curly braces to prevent double evaluation. Enterprise security teams should audit custom and third-party iRules configurations for unsafe command substitutions where untrusted HTTP headers or URI strings are directly interpolated. Organizations should suppress disclosure headers (such as Server: BigIP) to limit reconnaissance by external adversaries scanning for vulnerable load balancers.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)
